cards.context:
An accepting branch serves as a certificate that a string belongs to a nondeterministically accepted language. Complement closure asks whether negative answers always admit certificates within some exponential-time bound as well; the exponent may change.

The polynomial-time analogue is TCS-0002, NP versus coNP: \(\mathrm{NP}\) uses polynomial rather than exponential time, and \(\mathrm{coNP}\) consists of its complement languages. The known implication \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\Rightarrow\mathrm{NEXP}=\mathrm{coNEXP}\) makes a separation here a stronger conclusion than separating NP from coNP.

TCS-7232, Asser’s problem, concerns \(\mathsf{NE}=\mathsf{coNE}\). Here \(\mathsf{NE}\) permits nondeterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\), and \(\mathsf{coNE}\) consists of its complement languages. The present card instead permits \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), so it records the requested NEXP formulation separately.

Thapen’s 2025 paper studies consistency of the conjectured separation with specified formal arithmetic theories: whether those theories can prove the opposing inclusion. Its Theorem 2 uses the paper’s parameter-free formalization of \(\mathrm{coNEXP}\), a qualification discussed in Section 3. This result concerns what those theories can prove and does not establish an unconditional separation of the ordinary machine classes.

With polynomial-length advice, the corresponding classes are equal: \(\mathrm{NEXP/poly}=\mathrm{coNEXP/poly}\). For a language \(L\in\mathrm{NEXP/poly}\), supplement its length-\(n\) advice with the \(n+1\)-bit integer \(|L\cap\{0,1\}^n|\). A nondeterministic exponential-time machine can guess that many distinct length-\(n\) members, together with accepting computations under the original advice, and check that its input is absent from the list. Distinctness can be enforced by guessing the members in lexicographic order. The exact count forces the list to contain all members. This decides the complement with polynomial advice and exponential time; it does not remove the advice or settle the uniform question.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.

cards.title: Containment of PPAD in PLS
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PPAD}\subseteq\mathrm{PLS}\) under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions? Here PPAD represents directed endpoint search and PLS represents potential-based local search, with precise definitions below. Equivalently, do there exist uniform deterministic polynomial-time computable maps \(F,G\) that transform every End-of-Line input \(I\) into a Localopt instance \(F(I)\), and transform every accepted Localopt answer \(w\) for that instance into an accepted End-of-Line answer \(G(I,w)\)? This asks only the displayed direction of containment.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is given by an explicit topologically ordered list of gates over fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, and constants 0 and 1, with listed input nodes and ordered output nodes. Counts, gate types, wire indices and delimiters use an unambiguous binary encoding. All lists are part of the input, rather than a program generating them; the numbers of input and output bits therefore contribute to the encoding length. The notation \(\{0,1\}^n\) denotes length-\(n\) bit strings, and \(0^n\) is the all-zero string.

Polynomial time means one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a bound \(a(N+1)^d\), for fixed integers \(a,d\ge1\), on inputs of complete bit length \(N\). All bit operations and output bits count. Machines receive and may inspect full circuit gate lists; they have no advice, oracle or randomness unless randomness is explicitly allowed below. A malformed circuit encoding is efficiently recognizable. For a search task with such an input, INVALID is its only accepted answer, and INVALID is forbidden on valid inputs. Tags and bit strings in all answers have a fixed unambiguous binary encoding.

A total NP search problem is a relation \(R(x,y)\) on bit strings with a valid answer on every input \(x\), a fixed polynomial bound on the length of every accepted answer \(y\), and a deterministic polynomial-time test of \(R(x,y)\). TFNP denotes the class of these relations. A deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of maps \(F,G\) such that, for every \(x\) and every valid \(Q\)-answer \(z\) on \(F(x)\), the output \(G(x,z)\) is a valid \(R\)-answer on \(x\). Both maps are uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms, with time measured in their full input bit lengths. Here FP means total search relations admitting a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that selects a valid answer, without requiring a unique answer.

An End-of-Line input consists of circuits \(S,P:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), for \(n\ge1\). The input is valid when \(P(0^n)=0^n\) and \(S(0^n)\ne0^n\), conditions checked by circuit evaluation. An answer is any \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[P(S(v))\ne v\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(v\ne0^n\ \text{and}\ S(P(v))\ne v\bigr).\]
Thus zero is accepted only for the first condition, not merely for being the designated start. Failed input conditions, like malformed encodings, have only the answer INVALID. No global inverse promise is imposed. The graph intuition uses an edge \(u\to v\) when \(u\ne v\), \(S(u)=v\) and \(P(v)=u\); the displayed answer relation is authoritative. Answers need not lie in the component of zero. The directed endpoint principle guarantees an answer. PPAD, short for Polynomial Parity Argument, Directed, is the subclass of TFNP reducible to this End-of-Line task by the many-one search reductions just defined.

A Localopt input consists of circuits \(T:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}^m\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}^r\), where \(m,r\ge1\). Read the output of \(V\) as an unsigned binary integer with the first output bit most significant. A valid answer is any \(w\in\{0,1\}^m\) satisfying
\[V(T(w))\ge V(w).\]
The circuit \(T\) proposes a next state and \(V\) assigns its cost; a solution is a state where that proposal does not improve the cost. A global minimum of \(V\) is always an accepted answer. There is no specified starting state or reachability restriction. Malformed encodings have only INVALID as an answer. Allowing distinct state and cost widths is polynomially equivalent by padding to the equal-width formulation in the cited source. PLS, short for Polynomial Local Search, is the subclass of TFNP reducible to Localopt by the specified many-one search reductions.

The required maps \(F,G\) are fixed for all circuit sizes. The output of \(F\) must be a well-formed Localopt instance even on a malformed End-of-Line encoding; such inputs can be sent to a fixed trivial instance, and \(G\) must then return INVALID. For every other input, correctness must hold for every accepted Localopt witness, not only for one chosen minimum or one reachable state. The time and output length of \(F\) are polynomial in \(|I|\); the time and output length of \(G\) are polynomial in \(|I|+|w|\). Consequently all output circuit sizes and the parameters \(m,r\) are polynomially bounded by \(|I|\). Neither map uses an oracle for solving either search task. This is one many-one reduction, not an adaptive sequence of calls. Since End-of-Line and Localopt are the defining complete tasks, existence of these maps is equivalent to the stated class containment.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the specified maps F and G exist, including their polynomial bounds and correctness for every target answer, or prove that no such pair exists in the ordinary uniform model. A single hard-looking example, an oracle separation, a query lower bound or a conditional cryptographic claim is insufficient. A positive proof need not provide an efficient algorithm for solving Localopt. Establishing only the reverse containment does not answer this card.
cards.why: Determine whether every directed parity search problem can be expressed as potential-based local search through an ordinary polynomial-time reduction. This resolves a central relationship between two major total-search classes, and would identify PPAD with their known intersection CLS if affirmative.

cards.context:
Directed endpoint search guarantees another endpoint from a known start. Local search instead guarantees a state where a proposed move does not decrease an integer cost. PPAD and PLS collect the total search relations reducible to these two mechanisms; Definitions specifies the exact tasks and reduction.

Papadimitriou explicitly asks whether PPAD is contained in PLS. This is not the reverse containment and is not a demand for a polynomial-time algorithm that solves Localopt. A positive answer would show that local search can represent every directed parity task with a correct translation of every solution.

CLS denotes Continuous Local Search, a class built around continuous potential-based search. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani prove that CLS is exactly the intersection of PPAD and PLS. Their theorem makes this card equivalent to CLS = PPAD. CLS versus FP, where FP means efficient solution algorithms, remains a different question.

The literature discusses PPAD and PLS as conjecturally incomparable and gives oracle evidence. An oracle separation restricts access to a hidden function and does not by itself rule out a reduction that inspects explicit circuits. The target allows such circuit inspection and requires an ordinary-model conclusion.

A polynomial-time solver for End-of-Line would imply the requested containment by letting the output translator solve the original input directly. Thus a negative answer here would also separate PPAD from FP. It would not, by itself, settle the reverse containment of PLS in PPAD.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm{P}\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

cards.context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.

cards.context:
If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

source_formulation.text: This retains the existing arbitrary-real-weight randomized APSP question and its comparison-addition model with ordinary logarithmic-size word operations. It makes uniformity, primitive operations, the graph promise and joint output guarantee explicit. The cited equivalence literature also states integer-weight theorems with a logarithmic dependence on the weight range; its strongly polynomial reduction is identified separately rather than silently equating all weight and machine conventions.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

cards.context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+N)^c.\]
Here \(N\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
cards.definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(N\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,N\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+N\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(N\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
cards.why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

cards.context:
In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
cards.definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

cards.context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.

cards.title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(N\) is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(N\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(N+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,N\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.
cards.why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.

cards.context:
Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. cards.title: Additive-one approximation for bin packing
cards.formal:
Is there a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for one-dimensional offline bin packing that uses at most one more bin than optimum? Explicitly allowing randomization, the target is one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every finite input list \(I=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n})\) of rational sizes \(0<s_{i}\le1\), \(A\) runs within \(p(N)\) steps for every coin sequence, always outputs a feasible packing, and satisfies
\[
\Pr\bigl[B(A(I))\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+1\bigr]\ge\tfrac23.
\]
Here \(N\) is the total binary input length, \(B\) is the number of bins used, and probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits for each fixed input. A deterministic algorithm with the same bound on every input also qualifies.
cards.definitions:
All items and their sizes are given before computation starts. Each item is listed separately, including repetitions. Write \(s_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i},b_{i}\) are positive binary integers and \(a_{i}\le b_{i}\). Input length includes the item list, numerators, denominators and separators; arithmetic precision is not free.

A packing partitions the item indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty bins \(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q}\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in B_{j}}s_{i}\le1\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Items are indivisible and must each appear in exactly one bin. The output explicitly assigns every item to a bin. The integer \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum feasible number \(q\); the empty input has optimum zero and can be packed in zero bins. Zero-size items, if allowed by an alternative convention, can be handled separately without changing the existence question.

Running time is worst-case bit complexity on a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine. There is no input advice, supplied optimal packing or promise on the size distribution, number of distinct sizes or optimum. The input is an explicit list, not binary multiplicities representing exponentially many separate output items.

The additive allowance is exactly one bin with capacity exactly 1. It does not grow with the instance, and it is not a multiplicative factor \(1+\varepsilon\). Neither larger bin capacities nor discarding an item is permitted. The target concerns the integer optimum of the packing problem, not the optimum of a fractional relaxation.

The probability convention makes explicit an algorithmic interpretation that includes randomized approximation algorithms, as in the later logarithmic-additive result. Its theorem gives expected polynomial runtime with its quality guarantee; that is a separately reported form of the known result. For the target here, the output must always be feasible and only the one-extra-bin guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give one algorithm and a proof of all stated time, feasibility and probability guarantees, or refute the existence of such an algorithm. A negative answer must exclude the allowed randomized algorithms. If the exclusion uses an additional complexity hypothesis, that hypothesis must also be proved. An \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) bound with unspecified constant \(C>1\), an asymptotic approximation scheme, or a nonconstructive fractional-integrality-gap bound alone does not meet the target.
cards.why: A one-extra-bin algorithm would show that a strongly NP-hard packing problem can nevertheless be solved to a uniformly tiny additive error. The question tests a much sharper notion of approximation than a ratio tending to one and is a long-standing benchmark for understanding the structure of feasible packings.

cards.context:
Problem 3 asks whether bin packing can join problems that admit polynomial-time solutions within one unit of their integer optimum. The book separately highlights a constant number of extra bins as significant progress. This card keeps the one-bin endpoint as its main target.

The book recalls the Karmarkar–Karp additive \(O((\log n)^{2})\) guarantee. Hoberg and Rothvoss later give a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial runtime and at most \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+2))\) bins, where \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is the fractional packing optimum. In particular this gives \(\operatorname{OPT}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}+2))\) bins, without establishing a constant additive bound.

The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Its objective is the total fractional number of bins. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

Bounds of the form \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_{\varepsilon}\) can approach multiplicative ratio 1 while retaining an unbounded or larger additive loss. They therefore do not imply the requested one-extra-bin guarantee on every instance.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.
cards.why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.

cards.context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.
