cards.title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.
cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(q=|\Sigma|\ge2\) and identify \(\Sigma\) with \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), represented by fixed-length binary symbols. For each height \(N\), an encoder defines maps \(C_N:\{0,1\}^{\le N}	o\Sigma^{\le N}\) with \(|C_N(x)|=|x|\), \(C_N(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\), and prefix consistency: if \(u\) is a prefix of \(x\), then \(C_N(u)\) is the prefix of \(C_N(x)\) of length \(|u|\). Thus an output symbol cannot depend on future input bits. For every \(N\ge1\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and distinct \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\), let \(j\) be the first input position where \(x_j
e y_j\). The tree-distance requirement is \[ igl|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:C_N(x)_t
e C_N(y)_t\} igr|\ \ge\ \delta(\ell-j+1).\] Divergence is defined using the input histories, even if some output labels coincide. For equal-length \(u,v\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(\ell\ge1\), define suffix distance \[d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(u,v)=\max_{1\le j\le\ell} rac{|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:u_t
e v_t\}|}{\ell-j+1}.\] A decoder receives \(1^N\) and any \(w\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and returns a binary string of length \(\ell\), or a failure symbol. For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\ell\), if \(d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(w,C_N(x))\le\alpha\), the output must be exactly \(x\). No correctness requirement is imposed outside this promise, but the decoder must still halt within its time bound. The promise bounds errors in every suffix of the received prefix. It is not a bound on total Hamming error alone, which would not separate paths that diverge close to their end. The encoder and decoder are two fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine programs, with constants \(K,k\), each using at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit steps per invocation on valid inputs. Encoding receives \(1^N\) and the currently available input prefix \(x\), and outputs \(C_N(x)\). The known horizon \(N\) is allowed; the code families for distinct horizons need not agree. All preprocessing, symbol calculations and output writes count toward the time bound, and there is no separately supplied table, advice, random seed, oracle or graph of the exponentially large tree. Constants and programs are independent of \(N\), \(\ell\), \(x\) and \(w\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the fixed alphabet, positive constants, uniform encoder and decoder, and proofs of prefix consistency, the distance inequality, the promised decoding guarantee and polynomial bit complexity; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such collection exists. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.
cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.

The 2018 interactive-coding paper defines efficient tree-code decoding through suffix distance: a received prefix is decoded when every suffix has sufficiently few errors. This supplies a concrete promise for the otherwise unspecified decoding clause in the source question.

The checked May 2026 version of Cohen, Schulman and Srivastava records that constant-rate positive-distance tree codes exist nonconstructively, while the explicit constructions discussed there achieve rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) at constant distance. That rate tends to zero as the horizon grows.

Their rate–immediacy theorem rules out constant rate for codes satisfying an additional immediacy property under the theorem’s hypotheses. General tree codes need not satisfy that property, so the result does not prove impossibility of the encoder and decoder requested here.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.

cards.context:
The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.

cards.title: Černý conjecture
cards.formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with \(n\ge1\) states have a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? The statement quantifies over all finite nonempty alphabets. A reset word sends every possible initial state to the same state, under the transition model below.
cards.definitions: An automaton is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)\), where \(|Q|=n\ge1\), \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet and \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) is total. Extend it to words by \(\delta(q,\epsilon)=q\) and \(\delta(q,wa)=\delta(\delta(q,w),a)\). A word \(w\) is a reset word if \(|\{\delta(q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\); its length is its number of letters. Synchronizing means that at least one reset word exists. Its final state is not prescribed. Initial and accepting states play no role, and the empty word handles \(n=1\). There is no strong-connectivity, fixed-alphabet or other structural promise. Partial or nondeterministic automata, and synchronization of only a prescribed subset of states, are different models. No time bound for constructing the word is imposed. In the context, \(T(n)\) denotes the maximum shortest-reset-word length over all such synchronizing automata with \(n\) states; duplicate letter transformations can be removed, so this maximum exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every synchronizing \(n\)-state automaton has a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\), or exhibit a synchronizing automaton and prove that every word up to that length fails to reset it.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

cards.context:
The selected binary question is the Černý conjecture. Its \((n-1)^2\) upper bound would match the classical worst-case family. A counterexample to the universal bound also answers this card; it need not determine the entire extremal function.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(L(D)=L(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma^{*}\), and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

cards.context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(L=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(L=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(L\subseteq \Sigma^{*}\) such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in L(E)\) and \(v\in L(F), \Sigma^{*}\setminus L(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(L(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(L)=\min \{h(E):L(E)=L\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(L)>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

cards.context:
Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma^{*}ab\Sigma^{*})^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma^{*}\) by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.

cards.title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
cards.definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.
cards.why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.

cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

cards.context:
This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

An equality has a finite certificate: a sequence of contextual applications of the defining relation connecting the two words. Inequality has no analogous certificate supplied by the presentation itself. A long search with no successful derivation does not decide whether one exists, since intermediate words can have unbounded length.

Length-preserving relations, where \(|u|=|v|\), form a decidable special case. The general problem allows length-changing replacements. Termination of an oriented shortening rule is not sufficient by itself: different irreducible words may still represent the same element. The requested algorithm has no efficiency requirement, so a large computable time bound would still be a positive answer.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.

Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(L_{0}a_{1}L_{1}\cdots a_{r} L_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(L_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(L_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(L(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(L(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.

cards.context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

cards.title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
cards.definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(P_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.

cards.context:
An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence \(\forall x\,\bigl(P_a(x)\Rightarrow\exists y\,(\operatorname{Desc}(x,y)\land P_b(y))\bigr)\). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

Bojańczyk and Segoufin decide definability in \(\Delta _{2}\), the languages having both an existential-then-universal and a universal-then-existential definition. They do not decide arbitrary first-order definability. Blumensath’s 2024 finite-tree work supplies decidable necessary and sufficient conditions separately, but no one condition that is both. A necessary condition can fail to reject every nondefinable language, while a sufficient condition can fail to accept every definable language. The remaining gap is a complete test.

The 2025 automata characterization studies first-order logic over unordered infinite trees. The August 2026 result decides a common fragment of particular branching-time and linear-time temporal logics. Their domains or logical restrictions differ from the full finite ordered-tree question. They do not supply the all-input terminating test requested here. A solution would turn an expressiveness boundary into a mechanically checkable property of finite-state tree specifications.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
A ranked alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminal symbols with ranks \(r(a)\in\mathbb N\). Simple types are finite expressions generated by a base type \(o\) and the arrow constructor \(\tau\to\sigma\), associating to the right. A terminal of rank \(r\) has the type with \(r\) arguments of type \(o\) and result \(o\); rank zero means type \(o\). A scheme has a finite set of typed nonterminals, one distinguished start nonterminal \(S:o\), and exactly one rule \[F x_1\cdots x_k\longrightarrow t\] for each nonterminal \(F:\tau_1\to\cdots\to\tau_k\to o\). Here the distinct variables \(x_i:\tau_i\) are the only variables allowed in \(t\), and \(t:o\) is a finite well-typed applicative term over terminals, nonterminals and these variables. Terms are symbols or applications \(uv\), with \(u:\alpha\to\beta\) and \(v:\alpha\) giving \(uv:\beta\); application associates to the left. Rules may be mutually recursive and may duplicate or discard parameters. There are no data tests, constructor equations, pattern matching or nondeterministic alternatives. No syntactic restriction called safety is required.

Starting at the closed ground term \(S\), expose the head constructor by repeatedly replacing a fully applied head nonterminal \(F u_1\cdots u_k\) by \(t[u_1/x_1,\ldots,u_k/x_k]\). When a terminal head \(a u_1\cdots u_{r(a)}\) is exposed, output a node labeled \(a\) with the ordered child trees obtained in the same way from the ground terms \(u_i\). If the head unfolding never exposes a terminal, output a single \(\bot\) node with no children. In particular, unfolding does not require finishing a constructor's arguments before exposing that constructor. This defines \(\operatorname{Tree}(G)\) over \(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). A node address is a finite sequence of positive integers specifying successive child positions, starting with the empty address at the root. A terminal of rank \(r\) has precisely children numbered \(1,\ldots,r\), and \(\bot\) has none. Equality means the same set of addresses and the same label at every address. The number of unfolding steps and the names of internal nonterminals are not observable.

Type order is defined by \(\operatorname{ord}(o)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(\tau\to\sigma)=\max\{\operatorname{ord}(\tau)+1,\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\}\). A scheme's order is the maximum order of its nonterminals; the two input orders need not agree. An input explicitly lists the finite alphabet and ranks, type syntax trees, nonterminal symbols, start symbols and rule syntax trees, with binary indices and delimiters. Well-typedness and the syntactic conditions are effectively checked; invalid descriptions are rejected. The sought machine must work uniformly over all valid encodings, alphabets, finite orders and rule sizes. It returns an exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error, an oracle, or any additional time or space requirement beyond termination.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability of the input language defined above. A positive answer must supply one effective algorithm and prove its termination and correctness on every valid pair, including equal infinite trees and divergent schemes, uniformly in the finite input orders. A negative answer must prove that no total computable decider exists; undecidability for one fixed order already suffices for this unrestricted problem. A positive algorithm only for a restricted order or safety class, model checking of one tree, or a theorem conditional on another unresolved decision problem is not a full positive answer. No finite-depth approximation to tree equality is accepted.
cards.why: This is a central comparison problem for finite programs with higher-order recursion. Their complete output can be an infinite tree, and strong logical properties of each individual tree are already decidable. Deciding equality would establish an effective method for identifying identical observable recursive behavior across different finite descriptions; undecidability would locate a fundamental boundary beyond single-program verification.

cards.context:
A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, generated trees have finite-state descriptions and equality is decidable. At order one, equivalence is interreducible with deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. The higher-order setting permits functions as parameters of recursive definitions. Jochems’s §5 explicitly distinguishes this unresolved general problem from the established order-one result.

Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre prove that recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata describe the same classes of trees, with effective translations at each order. A collapsible pushdown automaton has a nested stack structure with links allowing restoration of earlier stack contents. The paper transfers value-tree equality to language equivalence for deterministic machines of this kind, but its final discussion explicitly leaves that comparison problem open. Equivalence of two representation models does not itself decide equality of two represented objects.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems’s 2021 result is a conditional decidability theorem: a specified semidecidability property of coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses would imply decidability of scheme equivalence. These clauses describe relations using higher-order logical rules with a greatest-model interpretation. The required semidecidability remains an assumption in Theorem 4.1, so the paper does not provide a completed equality algorithm.

The same paper proves that allowing explicit divergence leaves does not change the decidability question: its transformation to divergence-free trees preserves and reflects equality. The present formulation retains divergence because it is part of the semantics of an arbitrary input scheme, with no productivity promise. A productive infinite tree and a computation that never exposes a constructor remain distinct outputs.

The April 2026 polyregular result proves undecidability for equality of functions at higher-order types in a calculus with list operations and extensional semantics over function arguments. The paper’s language has no recursion and its programs terminate. Its comparison problem is different from equality of closed, possibly infinite constructor trees generated by the recursion rules in this card; no reduction between the two problems is assumed.

The July 2026 probabilistic-verification result decides almost-sure termination for a type-restricted class of probabilistic recursion schemes. That is a question about a termination probability in a restricted model. It does not settle equality of deterministic value trees at arbitrary finite orders.

cards.title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
cards.formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an input DFA is \(A=([n],[a],\delta,s,F)\), where \(\delta:[n]\times[a]\to[n]\) is total, \(s\in[n]\), and \(F\subseteq[n]\). Its explicit input consists of \(n\), \(s\), the \(an\) transition targets, and \(n\) accepting-state bits, one target or bit per input word. Extend \(\delta\) to finite words by \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ub)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),b)\). The recognized language is \(\{u:\delta^*(s,u)\in F\}\). The output is an explicit complete DFA \(B=([k],[a],\delta',s',F')\), \(1\le k\le n\), recognizing exactly that language, with \(k\) minimal among all complete DFAs over the same alphabet. Unreachable input states may be discarded; no equivalence partition for them is required. Both input and output transitions are explicitly represented.

Use one sequential deterministic word-RAM with word length \(w=\lceil2\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), addressed word memory and finitely many registers. Reading or writing one addressed word, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by an amount less than \(w\), comparisons and conditional branches each cost one step. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle instruction or externally supplied lookup table is available. The finite program may depend on the fixed alphabet size but not on the input size. All algorithmic preprocessing, auxiliary-table construction, initialization and output writing are charged to the running time; memory beyond the input has a fixed blank initial value. The asymptotic target is considered for \(n\ge n_a\ge a\), so the explicit \(an\)-word transition table fits the chosen word address space. Finitely many smaller sizes for each fixed alphabet are finite exceptions to the asymptotic claim. This spells out the input-addressing convention without changing the saved logarithmic word formula. The cost is in word operations, not bit operations: the input uses \(\Theta(n)\) words for fixed \(a\). There is no randomization, expected-time qualification, distribution on inputs, language approximation or promise on the transition graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation, including correctness, minimality, explicit output and the stated RAM cost. A positive proof must cover every fixed \(a\ge2\) by a uniform-in-\(n\) finite program and fixed constants. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(a\ge2\), every correct program in this full RAM model fails an \(O(n)\) worst-case bound: no constants \(C,n_0\) work for all sufficiently large inputs. A lower bound restricted to partition refinement, a comparison model or one particular minimization algorithm does not prove this negation. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional version.
cards.why: DFA minimization is a basic preprocessing step for recognizers, regular-language operations and finite-state verification. Its classical algorithm is almost linear, and the logarithmic factor has resisted removal for general transition graphs. Resolving the target would distinguish an inherent cost of the problem from the cost of the partition-refinement paradigm.

cards.context:
Two reachable states are equivalent exactly when every continuation word is either accepted from both or rejected from both. A smallest recognizer retains one representative of each such behavior. The task asks for the resulting explicit automaton, not merely a test of whether the input is already minimal.

Hopcroft’s algorithm minimizes a complete DFA in \(O(an\log n)\) time. For a fixed alphabet this is \(O(n\log n)\), while the input and a largest possible minimal output each occupy only linearly many words. The target is therefore removal of one logarithmic factor in worst-case sequential time.

Partition refinement begins with blocks distinguished by acceptance and repeatedly separates states whose transitions lead to different blocks. The 2023 lower-bound paper formalizes costs of such refinements and proves a logarithmic-factor obstruction even on deterministic systems with two actions. Its theorem quantifies over that method class, not over all multiplication-capable word-RAM programs.

Unary automata have a functional-graph structure that admits linear-time methods outside ordinary partition refinement. The saved target deliberately starts at alphabet size two, where two successor functions can interact. The successful unary case cannot be substituted for the multi-letter statement.

There are also linear-time results for special transition graphs, such as those whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles. These are meaningful positive cases but do not impose the arbitrary transition-graph guarantee requested here.

The source concerns symbolic automata, where transitions can carry predicates describing large or infinite alphabets. This card uses only its ordinary finite-alphabet minimization baseline. The precise word operations, input layout and uniformity convention are editorial choices already present in the saved target; they are not attributed as a conjecture made verbatim by the source authors.

cards.title: Separating words problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that any two distinct binary words of length \(n\ge1\) can be distinguished by a deterministic finite automaton with at most \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states? Distinguishing means accepting exactly one of the two words, with unrestricted behavior on all other words. The automaton may depend on the pair, and its complete one-pass transition model is defined below.
cards.definitions:
The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton.

Precisely, write
\[
s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}
\min\bigl\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\bigr\}.
\]
The maximum and minimum use the model above. A complete DFA recognizing one fixed length-\(n\) word has at most \(n+2\) states, so \(1\le s(n)\le n+2\).

The assertion \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) is expressed for all positive lengths using \(\log_2(n+1)\). One universal constant must cover every length and every pair of distinct words; no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing the separating automaton.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) works for every pair of distinct equal-length binary words. To refute the bound, show that for every \(C>0\) some pair requires more than \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states.
cards.why: Determining the polynomial exponent would quantify the worst-case finite-state memory needed to distinguish two long binary words, while separating polynomial growth from finer logarithmic factors.

cards.title: A logic capturing polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.
cards.why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.
