cards.context:
A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.
cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.

references.title: A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences
references.authors: Piotr Bacik; Toghrul Karimov; Florian Luca; Joris Nieuwveld; Joël Ouaknine; David Purser; James Worrell
references.locator: Author PDF dated 26 July 2026, 59 pp., linked from Ouaknine’s publication page as submitted. Full §1 pp. 1–4, Problem 2, Theorem 5, rational-to-integer scaling, simple/non-degenerate conventions; §9.1 p. 48 other domains. Inspected 14 September; no newer date is inferred from the access date.

cards.context:
Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.status_note: The unrestricted integer Skolem problem is explicitly open in the corrected 17 July 2026 low-order paper, the 16 July general conditional paper and the joint survey dated 26 July 2026. Revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no unconditional resolution. The new general decidability argument is conditional on its stronger good-prime gap conjecture; density-one index coverage does not cover every possible zero. Source statements and their scopes were checked, not all cited proofs independently verified.

progress.text: The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem describes zero sets as finitely many arithmetic progressions plus a finite set; the inspected primary papers explain why this is not an effective solution of the decision problem.
The MFCS paper gives a procedure for simple recurrences with unconditional correctness certificates upon termination, but termination on every input depends on two number-theoretic conjectures.

The SODA low-order result places order at most four in coRP; the inspected third arXiv version of 17 July corrects Lemma 3.2. Its bounded-index result for each fixed order retains the index bound as input.
The general conditional decidability paper uses a strengthened Cramér–Granville hypothesis and separately gives an unconditional Universal Skolem Set of density one.
The new joint survey explicitly retains the unrestricted integer Skolem problem as open and separates Positivity, Bi-Skolem and other settings.

sentences: The Skolem problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide if any given integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term.
The input lists its order, coefficients and initial values in binary, with no restriction on order or repeated characteristic roots and no upper bound on the index.
Every single term can be computed, but a decision procedure must also finish when the infinite sequence has no zero.
The question is a basic exact reachability problem in linear dynamics with connections to program verification and automata.
A complete Lean proof must establish decidability or undecidability for all inputs; conditional termination, low-order algorithms and density-one index sets do not settle that target.

problem_origin.note: Historical origin in Skolem’s 1930s work on zeros of recurrences. The modern uniform decision problem is its algorithmic form, not a verbatim 1934 formulation.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(N+1)^c\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(N\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.
cards.why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).

cards.context:
The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(N+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.

cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
cards.definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the card’s encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.
cards.why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.

cards.context:
Tarski’s decision theorem covers polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals with arbitrary first-order quantifiers. Adding the single function \(\exp\) asks whether that global decidability survives beyond polynomial arithmetic. The input remains a finite symbolic formula: a quantified real is part of the semantics, not a real number that must somehow be supplied as an infinite input string.

The target includes exact equalities and unrestricted quantifier alternation. For example, \(\forall x\,(x>0\Rightarrow\exists y\,\exp(y)=x)\) expresses surjectivity onto the positive reals; the implication here is an abbreviation for a disjunction in the specified syntax. Individual familiar identities are decidable, but they do not supply a machine for every sentence. Approximating an exponential value is also a different task: arbitrarily accurate approximations need not by themselves decide whether a given expression is exactly zero.

Wilkie proved model completeness of the real exponential theory in 1996: every formula is equivalent, in that theory, to an existential formula. The structure is also o-minimal, meaning that every definable subset of the real line is a finite union of points and intervals. These are strong finiteness properties, but neither statement alone certifies an algorithm for exact truth. The June 2026 paper recalls both results and distinguishes model completeness from completeness and effective axiomatization.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability assuming the real form of Schanuel’s conjecture. That hypothesis says that whenever \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the field \(\mathbb Q(a_1,\ldots,a_n,\exp(a_1),\ldots,\exp(a_n))\) has transcendence degree at least \(n\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Linear independence means that a rational linear combination is zero only when every coefficient is zero; transcendence degree is the maximum number of elements algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\), meaning that no nonzero rational polynomial in those elements vanishes. Wilkie’s 1997 exposition explicitly describes the decidability result as conditional. The stronger conjecture about complex tuples is not required for this real-theory implication.

The algorithmic survey distinguishes Schanuel’s transcendence conjecture from a weaker effective separation statement equivalent to decidability. For integer polynomials \(p,q_1,\ldots,q_n\) in \(2n\) variables, set \(F_p(x)=p(x_1,\ldots,x_n,\exp(x_1),\ldots,\exp(x_n))\), and define \(F_{q_i}\) similarly. The weak statement asks for a computable positive integer \(\eta\) such that every common zero \(\gamma\) of the \(F_{q_i}\) with invertible derivative matrix \((\partial F_{q_i}/\partial x_j)(\gamma)\) satisfies \(|F_p(\gamma)|\leq1/\eta\Rightarrow F_p(\gamma)=0\). The source explains that some such separation value exists; the unresolved requirement is its uniform computability. Consequently, failure of the stronger Schanuel conjecture would not by itself establish undecidability.

Berarducci and Gallinaro’s revision of 23 June 2026 gives a new axiomatization of the full real exponential theory under the real Schanuel hypothesis. Its unconditional theorem concerns model completeness for axioms of a restricted exponential function: this function equals \(\exp(x)\) on \((-1,1)\) and zero outside that interval. Completeness for their axiom systems, including the unrestricted exponential system, still uses the conjecture. Thus the unconditional theorem is not an unconditional decision procedure for the full language on this card.

One application comes from weighted automata assigning nonnegative rational values to finite words. The CONCUR 2020 source asks whether two initial states define functions \(f,g\) with \(f(w)\leq Cg(w)\) for every word \(w\) and some constant \(C>0\). The general problem is undecidable, but when both positive-weight languages are bounded—each contained in a product \(w_1^*\cdots w_k^*\) of repetitions of finitely many fixed words—the source reduces the comparison to real-exponential arithmetic and obtains conditional decidability. Decidability of the present card would make that application unconditional; the unrelated undecidability result for arbitrary automata does not refute this theory’s decidability.

progress.text: Tarski’s published decision theorem for polynomial real arithmetic establishes the starting point; the exponential extension is the further question described in the checked later primary literature.

Wilkie proves model completeness, and Macintyre–Wilkie prove decidability subject to the real Schanuel conjecture. The conditional result is described directly in Wilkie’s 1997 exposition and reviewed with exact hypothesis distinctions in the later sources.
The CONCUR weighted-automata paper invokes decidability of real-exponential arithmetic to obtain its bounded-language comparison result conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture.

The publisher releases the algorithmic-applications survey online, in a volume carrying a 2026 citation year. Section 3.1 distinguishes the stronger transcendence assumption from the weaker effective separation property equivalent to decidability.

Berarducci–Gallinaro v2 retains the real Schanuel assumption in Theorems 14.2 and 14.4; Theorem 12.4 is an unconditional model-completeness theorem for restricted-exponential axioms. This is the latest listed arXiv version as checked on 14 September 2026.

The input is finite symbolic syntax with no arbitrary real constants or real-number oracle, and quantifiers range over all reals.
Acceptance requires a complete Lean-checked proof of total correct decidability or a proof of undecidability, with no time bound and no unresolved extra hypothesis.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
cards.definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

cards.context:
The two ingredients are separately decidable: plain word equations by Makanin’s theorem and integer linear arithmetic by Presburger’s theorem. Their combination constrains both letter alignment and numerical size, and neither theorem alone settles their interaction.

Length identities can omit crucial content. For distinct letters \(a,b\), the word equation \(Xa=bX\) has no finite-word solution, although its induced length equality \(|X|+1=1+|X|\) is always satisfied. This illustrates why the target concerns a common word substitution, not merely a consistent length vector.

Restrictions on counts of individual letters, full Parikh vectors or additional quantifier alternation can yield different decidability results. Those predicates do not occur in the present input language. The distinction is explicit in Ciobanu’s survey.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on their solution lengths. Quadratic means each unknown appears at most twice across the equation. Their RP 2025 paper appeared online in November 2025; its proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. This restricted theorem does not cover an arbitrary system with unrestricted variable occurrences.

The IJCAR 2026 paper gives a sufficient termination condition and a partial converse for extended Nielsen transformations. The theorem concerns a specific procedure and a graph condition on an extended equation; it does not establish that every input of the unrestricted satisfiability problem is decidable. Its full preprint explicitly retains the general open question.

The checked July 2026 preprint states NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints over two letters. Its NEXP-completeness theorem concerns existential arithmetic with divisibility. These are distinct claims, and neither is a decision procedure or an undecidability proof for the current card.

The saved target is a conjunction, while that lower-bound corollary permits disjunctions. Finite expansion relates their decidability questions, but need not preserve polynomial input size; the corollary is therefore not presented here as a checked NEXP lower bound for the exact conjunction encoding. Allowing empty substitutions is likewise kept distinct from the preprint’s nonerasing convention.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time decider that, given a finite simple stochastic game \(G\), start vertex \(s\) and binary rational \(r\in[0,1]\), accepts exactly when \(v_G(s)>r\)? Here \(v_G(s)=\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\Pr_s^{\sigma,\tau}[\text{eventually reach sink }1]\). Time is measured in the total encoded bit length of the game, start vertex and threshold.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

cards.context:
This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

The exact branch formerly indexed as TCS-2427 asks for a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm returning optimal positional strategies for a finite, explicitly given, two-player zero-sum turn-based game. Each state is owned by one player; every available action has a rational reward to Max and a rational probability distribution over successor states. Min receives the opposite reward. A common rational discount multiplier \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is part of the binary input, and Max's objective is \(\mathbb E[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_t]\). Multiplication by \(1-\gamma\) leaves optimal strategies unchanged. The factor is constant during a play but may approach one across inputs. Time must be polynomial in the complete encoding length, including \(\gamma\); polynomial dependence on \(1/(1-\gamma)\) alone is insufficient. Exact solving of this class and simple stochastic games are polynomial-time equivalent. The source's additional approximation branch has no precision selected here.

The 2023 source explicitly separates the known constant-discount algorithms from the input-dependent discount question. The checked 2024 paper invokes the reduction of discounted game values and optimal policies to SSGs. These connections motivate consolidating the exact branch into the present threshold problem; they do not establish that its polynomial-time target is solved.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
cards.definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.
cards.why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.

cards.context:
Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.

context_blocks.text: Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.

cards.title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite propositional MELL sequent \(\Gamma\) in the calculus below, halts and answers yes exactly when \(\vdash \Gamma\) has a finite derivation? There is no promised bound on formula size or exponential nesting and no requested time bound beyond termination on every input.
cards.definitions: Use atoms \(p_{i}\) and their distinct dual literals \(p_{i}^{\perp}\) for integers \(i\ge 0\). Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by \(A ::= p_{i} | p_{i}^{\perp} | 1 | \perp  | (A\otimes A) |\) (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent \(\Gamma\) is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes \(\vdash p_{i},p_{i}^{\perp}\). The unit rule has no premises and concludes \(\vdash 1\). Tensor takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) and \(\vdash \Delta ,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\Delta ,A\otimes B\). Par takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\)⅋B. The other unit rule takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\perp\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Weakening takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Contraction takes \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A,?A to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Promotion takes \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,!A\), where every formula in ?\(\Gamma\) has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.
cards.why: MELL combines resource-sensitive composition with controlled reuse. Its decision problem connects automated proof search to branching counter systems and tests a fundamental boundary of algorithmic reasoning about resources.

cards.context:
Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.
cards.why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.

cards.context:
Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

cards.title: Decidability of branching-VASS reachability
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm deciding reachability in branching vector addition systems with states when the dimension is part of the input? Given a finite system \(B\) as defined below and a target configuration \(q(x)\), decide whether \(q(x)\) is the root of a finite valid derivation tree of \(B\).
cards.definitions: The input dimension is an integer \(d\geq1\). A \(d\)-dimensional branching vector addition system with states (\(d\)-BVASS) has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\) and finite rules \((S,a,q)\), where \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) consists of a state \(q\) and vector \(x\in\mathbb N^d\). A rule with \(S=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\) combines one configuration \(q_i(x_i)\) for each input state into \(q(a+x_1+\cdots+x_k)\), provided all coordinates of this output are nonnegative. All child configurations must themselves have nonnegative coordinates. Input states in one rule are distinct, following the source’s set convention. When \(S\) is empty, the rule supplies the initial configuration \(q(a)\) if \(a\geq0\) coordinatewise. A derivation is a finite rooted tree: each node uses one rule, has exactly its rule’s specified children, and its label is obtained by the preceding sum. Leaves therefore use empty-input rules. A target is reachable if some such tree has that target as root. Derivations may use the same rule any finite number of times; there is no global stock of initial tokens shared between different branches. The number of children and the dimension are unbounded input parameters. States, rules, child-state sets and target are listed explicitly, with signed binary integers for displacement coordinates and binary nonnegative target coordinates. There are no equality or zero tests, resets, counter multiplication, probability or additional acceptance conditions. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine that halts and answers correctly on every valid finite encoding, with no running-time bound requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm for the stated arbitrary-dimensional finite-tree reachability problem, or prove in Lean that it is undecidable. A dimension-dependent result covering only some fixed dimensions, a coverability algorithm, or a procedure that terminates only on reachable targets does not decide this problem. Finite derivation trees must satisfy every branch and every exact target coordinate.
cards.why: Branching VASS extend the Petri-net style of counter computation to recursive combinations of resources. Settling exact reachability in arbitrary dimension would identify a central decidability boundary between path computations and branching derivations in infinite-state verification.

references.title: Bridging the Gap Between Plain VASS and Branching VASS
references.authors: Clotilde Bizière; Jérôme Leroux; Grégoire Sutre
references.locator: Version 1, 14 September 2026; extended FOSSACS 2026 paper. §1 introduction, §2.3 model, §5 Theorem 5.2/Proposition 5.3/Remark 5.4, §6 discussion preceding Proposition 6.4, §7 Theorem 7.3 and §8 conclusion.

cards.context:
A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

The extended FOSSACS 2026 paper proves that every BVASS reachability set is a section of a VASS reachability set: one intersects with specified semilinear constraints and projects selected counters. The theorem is a structural existence statement. The paper does not obtain a general effective construction that would turn it into a reachability decider, and Remark 5.4 explicitly explains this distinction.

Its low-dimensional result gives effectively semilinear reachability sets for two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional BVAS. A BVAS here is the single-control-state version, so the five-dimensional theorem must not be attributed to arbitrary-state BVASS. The conclusion again identifies arbitrary-dimensional exact reachability as open. The retained 2025 rule conventions and decision target are unchanged.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated logspace-uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth search circuits on all simple undirected graphs, or prove that no such family exists. A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
