references.title: Maximum Matching and Related Problems in Catalytic Logspace
references.authors: Srijan Chakraborty; Samir Datta; Aryan Kusre; Partha Mukhopadhyay; Amit Sinhababu
references.locator: Revision 1, 1 June 2026; abstract and Theorem 1.1: construction in polynomial-time catalytic logspace, with no claimed general NC algorithm

cards.context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

cards.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. Use [synchronous LOCAL rounds](definitions.html#distributed-rounds) with unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.
cards.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.

references.title: Triangle-Free Coloring in LOCAL via Resilient Lovász Local Lemma
references.locator: Posted 13 August; manuscript 14 August 2026; §§1.3, 2.2 and 6.1 distinguish bounded degree, resilient applications and general LLL

cards.context:
The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

progress.text: Brandt and coauthors prove \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) lower bounds for sinkless orientation and distributed LLL under the stated criterion hypotheses.
Fischer–Ghaffari obtain \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  \log  n})}\) rounds at low dependency degree under polynomial slack and explicitly record the Chang–Pettie \(O(\log  \log  n)\) conjecture.
Davies gives \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) rounds under polynomially strengthened criteria, with a broader probability-versus-degree tradeoff.

Davies-Peck and Zhang extend efficient resilient-LLL applications to triangle-free coloring. Their general-degree discussion does not resolve the fixed-degree linear-log-log target.

Processors know local portions of this dependency structure and communicate in synchronous LOCAL rounds.
The question asks for \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds with high probability when the dependency degree is constant and the probability criterion has sufficiently strong constant polynomial slack.
The guarantee must bound the worst finishing time over all nodes.
An algorithm that achieves only a small average finishing time would leave the central coordination issue unresolved for the last remaining bad events.

cards.title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following conjecture true? For every fixed sublinear local-memory exponent \(0<\delta<1\), every uniform randomized MPC algorithm \(A\) that distinguishes a single cycle of length \(n\) from two disjoint cycles of length \(n/2\), with high probability and linear total memory as specified below, requires \(\Omega(\log n)\) worst-case synchronous rounds. More precisely, for every fixed positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), there must be constants \(c_{A,h}>0\) and \(n_{A,h}\) such that
\[T_A(n,h)\ge c_{A,h}\log_2 n\]
for every even \(n\ge n_{A,h}\). Correctness has probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\) on each promised graph and every admissible initial placement of its edge list.
cards.definitions:
The input is an edge list of a simple undirected graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for even \(n\ge6\). It is promised to consist either of one cycle through all \(n\) vertices or of exactly two disjoint cycles, each through \(n/2\) vertices. Every edge appears once as its pair of endpoints; the orientation of that pair and list order are arbitrary. Both cases have exactly \(n\) edges and degree two at every vertex. The vertex names carry no order around a cycle. Inputs outside the promise impose no correctness requirement.

Here is a fixed finite-word version of linear-total-space MPC. For a fixed \(\delta\), use \(p(n)=\lceil n^{1-\delta}\rceil\) machines, indexed from one to \(p(n)\). For each fixed \(h\), the algorithm may choose constants \(K_h\ge4\) and an integer \(B_h\ge2\), independent of \(n\). A word has \(B_h\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Each machine can store at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words, including its input, work state and communication buffers. Thus the sum of memory capacities is \(O(n)\) words for fixed \(h,\delta\). Initially each edge record is placed on one machine, and every placement fitting these local capacities is allowed. Other mutable memory is initially blank. Each machine knows \(n,p(n),h\) and its own index; fixed model parameters are part of the program.

Each synchronous round allows arbitrary finite local computation within that memory and communication with arbitrary other machines. Each machine sends at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words in total and receives at most that many; words may encode arbitrary information rather than whole graph records. Recipient addresses count as part of the communicated data. The algorithm must respect both send and receive bounds on every promised input and every random tape. Messages arrive before the next round. Local computation must terminate but has no time bound. Machines have private independent fair random bits and may additionally use a common read-only fair random tape; random bits retained for later use occupy memory. There is no further advice or oracle.

All machines execute one finite program with their indices as input. The program is uniform over \(n,h\); it can depend on the fixed exponent. It suffices to quantify over rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\), so all machine counts and capacity bounds are effectively specified: any fixed smaller real exponent is dominated by a rational exponent below one, and a lower bound for every rational exponent covers it. Constants in the resource bounds may depend on the program and fixed confidence parameter, but not on the input or placement.

Machine one must eventually output ONE or TWO. On every promised input and placement, the output must be correct with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), jointly over all random bits. No machine may exceed the resource bounds even on a tape leading to an incorrect answer. Let \(T_A(n,h)\) be the supremum of the number of synchronous rounds until this output, over all promised inputs with exactly \(n\) vertices, all initial placements and all random tapes. Eligible algorithms have finite \(T_A(n,h)\) for each \(n,h\). The target is a worst-case round bound, not expected time.

High probability means that every fixed positive integer \(h\) can be requested as an input parameter; integer parameters also imply every fixed real failure exponent. The lower-bound constants may depend on \(h,\delta,A\). No component-stability, comparison-only or indivisible-record restriction is imposed. In particular, graph distance does not bound the distance a message can travel between machines.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal logarithmic lower bound or of its full negation. A uniform \(o(\log n)\)-round algorithm for one fixed \(\delta<1\), with the stated correctness and space bounds for every fixed confidence parameter, suffices to refute it. The literal negation can also be witnessed by failure of the eventual lower bound along an unbounded subsequence; a refutation need not be little-o at every size. A bound only for restricted encodings, component-stable algorithms, geometric embeddings or larger total memory does not prove the stated conjecture.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.

cards.title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate \(P\) of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing \(P\) has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
cards.definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(P(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.
cards.why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.

references.title: What Can We Compute in a Single Round of the Congested Clique?
references.locator: PODC 2023; revision 4, 31 January 2024 abstract. One-round MST algorithms require Ω(log³ n) link bandwidth, hence at least two rounds with O(log n) messages; a constant lower bound and a multi-edge output task.

cards.context:
Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.

cards.title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A\), taking a positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), such that for every fixed \(h\ge1\), on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with \(n\ge2\), its vertex outputs form a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), and its worst-case elapsed round count \(T_A(n,h)\) satisfies
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T_A(n,h)}{\log_2 n}=0?
\]
The guarantee ranges over all degrees, all valid distinct identifier assignments and all port numberings. Local computation, storage and message lengths are unrestricted; vertices have private random bits and may know \(n\) and the maximum degree.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\); disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are included. Vertex \(v\) eventually outputs a bit \(b_v\). Set \(I=\{v:b_v=1\}\). Independence requires that no edge have both endpoints in \(I\), and maximality requires that every vertex outside \(I\) have a neighbor in \(I\). Maximal does not mean maximum cardinality. For the one-vertex graph the algorithm must output its vertex, without an asymptotic restriction beyond finite time.

Vertices have pairwise distinct identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). Each vertex initially knows its own identifier, its degree, the identifiers of its neighbors, the exact \(n\), the exact maximum degree \(\Delta\), and \(h\). An arbitrary port numbering bijectively labels each vertex's incident edges by the integers from one to its degree. The two endpoints need not give an edge the same port number. Knowing neighbors initially instead of after an identifier-exchange round changes the count by at most one round and does not change the little-o target.

The LOCAL model runs in synchronous rounds. Each vertex can send a different finite binary message of arbitrary length along each incident edge, with messages delivered before the next round. There are no other channels, graph preprocessing, advice strings or shared random tape. Each vertex runs the same finite program with its own sequence of independent fair random bits. Local storage and intermediate computation are unbounded but must be finite and terminate on every random tape between rounds. The program is uniform over \(n,\Delta,h\) and vertex identifiers. After a vertex emits its output it may send fixed dummy messages until all vertices have finished.

For fixed \(n,h\), \(T_A(n,h)\) is the supremum of the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, over every graph with exactly \(n\) vertices, identifiers, ports and random tapes. This supremum must be finite. The displayed success probability concerns the entire output labeling simultaneously on each particular input, not each vertex separately. The time guarantee holds even on tapes on which the output is wrong.

The limit means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every fixed integer \(h\ge1\), some \(n_0\) has \(T_A(n,h)\le\varepsilon\log_2n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on \(h,\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, degrees or identifiers. Positive integer confidence parameters suffice for every requested real constant failure exponent. No common bound uniform in unbounded \(h\) is required. This explicit confidence-input convention realizes the saved high-probability requirement.

A bound on awake rounds, expected rounds, node-average rounds, or graphs avoiding short cycles is not the all-input worst-case elapsed-round bound in the question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of such a uniform algorithm, including maximality, joint success probability and the little-o limit for every fixed confidence parameter; or prove the negation of this existential statement in the specified model. A lower bound for a restricted algorithmic technique, a sublogarithmic bound only for some graph classes, or a merely expected-time bound does not settle the target.
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.

cards.title: Depth-first search in NC
cards.formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.
cards.why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.

references.title: Nearly Work-Efficient Parallel DFS in Undirected Graphs
references.authors: Mohsen Ghaffari; Christoph Grunau; Jiahao Qu
references.locator: Abstract states depth Õ(√n) and work Õ(m+n); the 2025 paper explicitly identifies this algorithm as randomized. Abstract and later paper’s statement checked, not the proof.

cards.context:
Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. context_blocks.text: Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.
The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth.
Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target.
A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

cards.title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized priority-CRCW PRAM algorithm \(A_a\), constants \(C_a\ge1\) and \(B_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge a+3}\), and a function \(h_a:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to[1,\infty)\) with
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h_a(N)}{\log N}=0,
\]
such that the following holds? On every explicitly given directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le n^a\), the algorithm outputs an exact integral maximum flow with probability at least \(2/3\), and every execution satisfies
\[
 W\le C_a(m+n)h_a(m+n),\qquad
 D\le C_a h_a(m+n).
\]
Here \(W\) is total work and \(D\) is parallel depth in the word model below. In asymptotic notation the requested simultaneous bounds are \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Input memory contains \(n,m,s,t\) and an explicit ordered array of arcs \(E\), each with its two endpoint labels and integer capacity. There are no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. The range is \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\), and isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and zero capacities are permitted. No planarity, acyclicity, density or expansion promise is assumed. The fixed integer \(a\) specifies the admitted capacity regime and may be built into the program.

A feasible output is an integer \(f_e\) for every original arc, in input order, such that \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) and
\[
 \sum_{(v,z)\in E}f_{(v,z)}=
 \sum_{(z,v)\in E}f_{(z,v)}
 \quad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}).
\]
Its value is outgoing flow minus incoming flow at \(s\). It must maximize that value over all feasible flows. Integral capacities admit an integral maximum flow. Any maximizing flow is acceptable, but the entire arc vector must be output explicitly. A maximum-flow value, a cut or an implicit flow alone is not the required output. If no positive flow is possible, the exact optimum is zero.

The computational model is a synchronous parallel random-access machine with shared memory and priority concurrent reads and writes (priority CRCW PRAM). Simultaneous reads of one cell are allowed. If multiple processors try to write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes at most one word-RAM instruction per round, using its own local registers and the shared memory. Processor identifiers and memory addresses are word values. Processors follow one finite program with their identifiers available; there is no input-length advice or precomputed table. Processor activation and all program-controlled initialization count as work; a hidden computation cannot be assigned to an uncharged processor. Initially only the explicit input and fixed machine constants are present, and unused memory and registers are zero.

Words have length
\[
 w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Each processor may generate a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one instruction; all such random words are mutually independent. Operations on longer integers are implemented by multiple charged instructions. There are no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic operations or real-number oracles. The chosen \(B_a\) must accommodate every processor identifier and address used by the algorithm.

Work \(W\) is the sum of all executed processor instructions, including activation, input access, preprocessing, random generation and output writes. Depth \(D\) is the number of synchronous rounds until the complete output is available. Both resource bounds must hold on every execution, including executions returning an incorrect answer. Correctness means that the whole vector is feasible and exactly optimal, with probability at least \(2/3\) over the machine's coins for each fixed input. The success probability is not averaged over graphs, and resources are not merely bounded in expectation. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case.

The program, word constant, multiplicative constant and overhead function may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its input ordering or its capacities. One algorithm for the fixed \(a\) must achieve the asymptotic bounds over all sizes. In particular, for every \(\delta>0\), its work is eventually at most \((m+n)^{1+\delta}\) and its depth at most \((m+n)^\delta\), after increasing a size threshold depending only on \(a,\delta\). Allowing a different algorithm for each \(\delta\) would be a different claim. The overhead function is an analytic bound, not advice supplied to the machine.

Subpolynomial depth is the requested target; polylogarithmic depth would suffice but is not required. The same computation must have almost-linear total work. An algorithm with small depth and polynomially more work, or with almost-linear work and a fixed positive power of \(n\) in its depth, does not meet the simultaneous endpoint. Using \(m+n\) accounts explicitly for the vertex set even when the graph contains few arcs.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation.

A positive answer must cover every fixed capacity exponent \(a\), with a uniform algorithm for that exponent, the simultaneous worst-case work and depth bounds, and the per-input probability of an exact explicit integral maximum flow. A result with stronger bounds also qualifies if it supplies this full output and model guarantee.

A negative answer must prove that for at least one fixed \(a\) no admissible algorithm and constants satisfy the target. A conditional obstruction, a lower bound for one algorithmic framework, or a difficulty confined to a more demanding capacity model does not establish the unconditional negation. An approximation algorithm, a restricted graph-family result, or a reduction to another task alone is insufficient unless the remaining task is also solved with the required resources.
cards.why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.

cards.context:
Sequential almost-linear-time algorithms do not guarantee few dependent computation stages. This question asks whether exact directed flow can retain almost-linear total work while reducing those stages to subpolynomial depth.

The DAG-projection result gives efficient parallel reductions between exact directed flow and suitable approximation tasks on directed acyclic graphs. A reduction transfers a future algorithm; it does not itself supply the missing endpoint.

The August 2026 revision of the dense-instance result gives \(\widetilde O(m+n^{3/2})\) work and \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) depth. Its work is near-linear on sufficiently dense inputs, but its depth is still polynomial in graph size.

The separate strongly polynomial parallel result supports arbitrary real capacities with \(\widetilde O(mn)\) work and \(\widetilde O(m)\) depth. Neither bound supplies the almost-linear-work and subpolynomial-depth combination asked for here.

Approximate flow in undirected graphs is a different regime in the source’s classification. Exactness, direction and the simultaneous resource limits are essential parts of this card.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

references.authors: Amir Azarmehr; Soheil Behnezhad; Lily Chung; Alma Ghafari; Jane Lange; Ronitt Rubinfeld

cards.context:
Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

cards.title: Fault-adaptive Byzantine agreement at optimal resilience
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic synchronous protocol and an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(t\ge0\), with \(n=2t+1\) named processes and trusted ideal signature setup as defined below, the protocol solves binary strong Byzantine agreement against every adaptive adversary corrupting at most \(t\) processes, and every execution with \(f\le t\) actual corruptions has total communication at most
\[
C\,n(f+1)
\]
words sent by processes while they follow the protocol? The protocol receives \(n,t\), identities and the setup, but not the eventual value of \(f\). The bound includes communication after a process decides. No bound on the number of rounds is imposed beyond eventual decision by every never-corrupted process.
cards.definitions:
Processes have distinct identities \(1,\ldots,n\), know the membership and threshold \(t\), and each starts with one input bit. Every pair has a reliable authenticated channel. Time is divided into synchronous rounds known to all processes. A message sent by a noncorrupted process to another noncorrupted process is delivered by the end of that round. A send to each of several recipients is charged separately; there is no free broadcast primitive.

An adversary may choose which processes to corrupt as the execution develops, after observing communication, with at most \(t\) distinct processes ever corrupted. Corruption is permanent and reveals the process’s state and signing capability. Corrupted processes may send inconsistent messages, omit messages, or stop. They cannot impersonate an uncorrupted sender or create signatures forbidden by the ideal signing interface. Honest messages already sent retain the stated reliable-delivery guarantee. Let \(f\) be the total number of distinct processes corrupted during the execution. Correct processes for agreement, termination and validity are those never corrupted.

Each correct process must eventually decide one bit, once and irrevocably. Agreement requires that all such decisions are equal. Strong unanimity requires that, if every correct process’s original input is the same bit \(b\), their decision is \(b\), regardless of the inputs and messages of corrupted processes. With mixed correct inputs, either bit is permitted.

The trusted setup occurs before the measured execution and supplies public verification information and private signing capabilities. Ordinary signatures are publicly verifiable and can be produced only by the named signer; once produced, they may be copied and forwarded. For any publicly specified threshold \(q\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), an ideal threshold-signature instance permits each process to create a share on a specified message. Shares from at least \(q\) distinct processes on that same message can be combined locally into one constant-size publicly verifiable certificate. A certificate can be created only from the required distinct shares, or copied if already available. Corrupted signers can provide their own shares on arbitrary messages. This idealization rules out forgery exactly; it does not assert unconditional security of a physical cryptographic implementation. Setup and local signature operations incur no communication charge beyond transmitting their inputs or outputs.

A word carries a constant number of input bits, ordinary signatures, signature shares or threshold certificates, together with \(O(\log(n+2))\) ordinary control bits. These constants are fixed independently of \(n,t,f\). An arbitrary list of signers, values or certificates is charged for all its contents; compression into one threshold certificate is allowed only through the stated interface. Every nonempty message costs at least one word. Local computation is unrestricted. A protocol is uniform if a single finite algorithm specifies each process’s behavior from its identity, input, parameters, setup and local history. It uses no random choices outside the ideal setup.

The communication measure counts every word sent while a process is uncorrupted, including words sent by a process that is later corrupted, and all permitted protocol traffic after decisions. Arbitrary traffic sent after corruption is excluded. The bound holds in every allowed execution, not merely in expectation or in the worst case \(f=t\). The case \(t=0,n=1\) is included.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive benchmark answer requires a complete Lean-checked protocol, correctness proof and uniform \(C n(f+1)\) word bound in the specified ideal model. A negative answer would require a Lean-checked impossibility proof for this quantified assertion. The target is binary existence with an asymptotic resource guarantee, so no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance applies. Published mathematics now gives the positive answer; this archived record does not claim that the protocol has already been formalized in Lean.
cards.why: Worst-case quadratic communication can obscure much cheaper runs with few failures. This question asks for such savings all the way to the honest-majority resilience threshold, while preserving agreement and validity against adversarial behavior.

cards.context:
Strong unanimity requires a common input of all correct processes to be preserved even when faulty processes submit conflicting values. This is stronger than requiring unanimity only when there are no faults. The source uses binary values and the optimal honest-majority threshold.

The word measure matters because a threshold certificate can encode many endorsements in constant space. A lower bound on the number of individual signatures does not automatically become the same lower bound on transmitted words. The trusted setup and certificate interface are part of the model.

The 2022 source achieves \(O(n(f+1))\) words for Byzantine broadcast and a weaker agreement variant. For binary strong agreement it gives \(O(n)\) words when \(f=0\), with a quadratic fallback in other cases, and leaves full adaptivity open.

The 2023 STRONG result attains adaptive word complexity with \(n=(2+\Omega(1))t+1\). That fixed resilience gap prevents it alone from settling the exact \(n=2t+1\) question.

The 2024 DARE work reaches the honest-majority threshold for general strong multi-valued agreement with adaptive word complexity. Its general strong-validity implementation uses multiverse threshold signatures; the later binary theorem provides a direct match to the standard threshold-signature interface.

Published PODC 2026 Theorem 3.1 gives the requested deterministic synchronous binary protocol with \(O(n(f+1))\) words and also \(O(f+1)\) decision rounds. The result applies at \(n=2t+1\), includes fault-free runs, and counts bounded protocol traffic after decisions. The separate large-system bounds involving dispersers are not needed for this resolution.

cards.title: One-pass approximation scheme for random-order streaming matching
cards.formal:
Is there one uniform randomized streaming algorithm, an integer \(c\ge0\) and a total computable function \(g:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N_{>0}\) with the following guarantee? For every \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), the algorithm takes \(\varepsilon\) as input and reads the edges once in uniformly random order. On every run it uses at most \(g(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) working bits and returns a matching \(M\) of \(G\). Over the edge order and the algorithm’s coins,
\[\Pr\bigl[|M|\ge(1-\varepsilon)\nu(G)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
cards.definitions:
G is any fixed simple undirected graph on a known labelled vertex set [n]. Its m distinct edges arrive once each in a uniformly random permutation, independently of the algorithm’s coins. The adversary may choose G but not condition the stream order on those coins. The algorithm receives \(n\) in binary and the numerator and positive denominator of the reduced fraction \(\varepsilon\) on separate read-only binary inputs. It reads edges sequentially without rewinding, and outputs an actual edge set M after the final edge. A matching has no two edges sharing a vertex; \(\nu(G)\) is the largest matching cardinality.

Space includes stored edge endpoints, counters, retained random bits, and the final output buffer. The output must be a valid matching on every run; the approximation may fail with probability at most 1/3, over both permutation and internal randomness. All copies of the read-only parameters retained in working memory count toward the space bound. The program, the space coefficient function \(g\) and the logarithmic exponent \(c\) are fixed before the accuracy and graph are chosen. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is demanded, and no processing-time target beyond termination is imposed. Thus the question is about space at each fixed positive accuracy, not an exact matching algorithm obtained by setting \(\varepsilon\) to 1/n at uniform near-linear cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof with one algorithm, one exponent \(c\) and one computable bound \(g\) satisfying the displayed guarantees on the entire domain, or prove the negation of that statement. A lower bound using a sequence \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon(n)\) must rule out the permitted dependence on \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\).
cards.why: The target asks how much random order can improve a severe streaming-memory constraint.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
cards.why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

cards.context:
Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision directly claims a strongly polynomial algorithm for general LP; Lemma 7.1 asserts a linear bound on its iteration count. A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation. This review has not certified the proof or located independent primary validation in bounded searches.

Truffet’s current August 2026 revision also states a general strongly polynomial solution in Theorem 2.1. Its opening revision note acknowledges a logical error in earlier versions and asserts a correction; the current theorem remains a claim requiring verification. This review read that note, the theorem and the stated complexity conclusion, without certifying their proof or the full bit-complexity requirements. These unresolved claims are why the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
cards.definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.
cards.why: Komlós asks whether controlling the Euclidean size of each vector is enough to balance all coordinates by signs with a dimension-independent error. This is a central link between vector geometry and simultaneous rounding of linear constraints. It would imply the Beck–Fiala bound for sparse set systems and strengthen discrepancy-based guarantees in optimization.

cards.context:
Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.

sentences: Komlós asks whether every collection of real vectors of Euclidean norm at most one can be assigned signs so that every coordinate of their sum is bounded by one universal constant.
The dimensions and entries are arbitrary, and the same complete choice of signs must control all coordinates simultaneously.
The positive answer requires some finite constant, without determining the best one or giving an efficient algorithm.
Such a theorem would imply the Beck–Fiala discrepancy bound and strengthen rounding and optimization guarantees.

A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or unbounded discrepancy; the 10 September 2026 preprint claims the full positive bound, but this review has not independently verified its proof.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.
cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.
