cards.context:
Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.

source_formulation.text: This is the retained editorial near-input-size variant of the general sparse-system complexity question. Polynomial conditioning, logarithmic input coefficient lengths, inverse-polynomial residual accuracy, an explicit rational output and the word-RAM cost convention make the broad direction precise. Peng–Vempala and Nie supply the general finite-precision context; the Simons workshop report asks narrower benchmark and numerical-analysis questions. The proposition is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report, and does not ask the already resolved question of beating matrix multiplication.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The retained proposition is an explicitly editorial near-linear target, not a named conjecture or the already resolved faster-than-matrix-multiplication question. Inspected primary results improve general polynomial bounds or handle structured families; the August 2026 report retains narrower scalable-solver and finite-precision questions. Bounded later-work searches found no matching universal solver or unconditional impossibility proof. This status assessment does not independently certify the cited proofs.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng establish nearly linear expected-time solvers for symmetric diagonally dominant systems, with an energy-norm guarantee and a finite-precision analysis; the expanded solver paper appears in 2014.

Peng and Vempala give a general finite-precision sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication in suitable sparsity regimes; preprint v2 is dated 7 January 2021 and the conference version is SODA 2021.
Nie improves the matrix anti-concentration result and the associated sparse-system running time; the current preprint is v2 from 2 December 2021 and the conference version is STOC 2022.
The ICALP paper establishes sparse-linear-equation completeness for Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes.
The Peng–Vempala work appears in JACM; this publication does not replace the near-linear target by the already achieved matrix-multiplication improvement.
Version 3 of the Simons workshop report records status through 20 August and retains broader scalable-solver and finite-precision questions.

sentences: A sparse linear system explicitly stores only the nonzero matrix entries and its right-hand side.
The question asks whether every nonsingular rational system with polynomial conditioning can be approximately solved in nearly linear time in the number of nonzeros.
Coefficient lengths and residual accuracy are bounded on a logarithmic scale, and the output must list every rational coordinate.
The fixed word-RAM model charges preprocessing, precision, randomness and output, with a worst-case time bound and success probability at least two thirds.
Known structured solvers and general improvements over matrix multiplication motivate the target but do not provide its universal near-linear guarantee.

problem_origin.note: Nearly linear solving of general sparse systems was a natural frontier by the early nearly-linear Laplacian breakthroughs. The unrestricted problem has older numerical-linear-algebra roots.

cards.title: Crouzeix’s sharp numerical-range inequality
cards.formal: Does the inequality \[\|p(A)\|_2\le 2\max_{z\in W(A)}|p(z)|\] hold for every integer \(n\ge1\), every complex matrix \(A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) and every scalar polynomial \(p\in\mathbb C[z]\)?
cards.definitions:
The numerical range is \(W(A)=\{x^*Ax:x\in\mathbb C^n,\ \|x\|_2=1\}\), where \(x^*\) denotes conjugate transpose. The vector norm is Euclidean, and the induced matrix norm is \(\|B\|_2=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Bx\|_2\). For \(p(z)=\sum_{j=0}^m c_jz^j\), set \(p(A)=\sum_{j=0}^m c_jA^j\) with \(A^0=I\). Compactness of \(W(A)\) ensures that the scalar maximum exists.

The constant 2 must work for every dimension, scalar polynomial and matrix, including nonnormal and nondiagonalizable matrices. The inequality is an assertion about complex matrices, with no input-encoding convention. Allowing a matrix of polynomials \([p_{ij}]\) of arbitrary block size yields the stronger complete conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: A Lean proof of the universal scalar-polynomial inequality establishes the affirmative answer recorded below. Its sharpness follows by taking \(p(z)=z\) and the \(2\times2\) matrix with a single nonzero entry \(J_{12}=1\). Then \(\|J\|_2=1\) and \(\max_{z\in W(J)}|z|=1/2\).
cards.why: A sharp dimension-independent bridge from scalar approximation on the numerical range to norms of functions of nonnormal matrices; retained as a recently resolved foundational problem.

benchmark_eligibility.reason: The July 2026 scalar Crouzeix claim predates the independent August proof. Retain existing expert-assessment and pending-peer-review caveats.

references.authors: Per Åhag; Rafał Czyż; Jani Virtanen
references.locator: Posted 27 August, revised 9 September 2026; complete conjecture for matrices of order at most three and related stronger scalar COR results

cards.context:
This saved open problem has been resolved in the scalar form stated here, according to two 2026 proof manuscripts and an explicit expert assessment. Jin’s first preprint was posted on July 27, and Lorist–Schwenninger’s independent proof on August 4. In an August 15 report, Townsend and Greenbaum state that they and Crouzeix checked Jin’s argument thoroughly and believe it correct. The catalogue therefore marks this entry resolved while recording that formal journal review was still pending in the inspected repository.

The underlying issue is the behavior of functions of a nonnormal matrix. For a normal matrix, a unitary diagonalization reduces the norm of p(A) to the largest |p(λ)| over eigenvalues λ. For a nonnormal matrix, eigenvalues alone can miss substantial amplification. The nilpotent matrix J in the answer criterion has only the eigenvalue zero, yet J itself has norm one. Taking p(z)=z shows why a bound based only on scalar values at the spectrum cannot work universally.

The numerical range incorporates all quadratic forms x*Ax on unit vectors, rather than only eigenvectors. For the same J, x*Jx=conjugate(x₁)x₂. Its maximum modulus is 1/2, attained when the two coordinates have equal modulus. Thus replacing the spectrum by the numerical range gives meaningful information, but still requires the factor two. This small example establishes sharpness independently of the general proof.

A numerical-range estimate transfers scalar approximation to matrix approximation. For example, if two scalar polynomials p and q differ by at most ε throughout W(A), the theorem gives ‖p(A)−q(A)‖₂≤2ε. That is useful when a matrix polynomial is applied to a vector: the same bound controls the resulting vector error relative to its norm. The role in matrix functions and polynomial or rational Krylov methods is discussed in the expert report.

The dimension-independent nature of the constant was already a major achievement before sharpness was settled. Crouzeix obtained the bound 11.08 in 2007, and Crouzeix–Palencia reduced it to 1+√2 in 2017. The inherited Ransford–Schwenninger paper clarifies the latter proof using the numerical-range functional calculus. The remaining gap from approximately 2.414 to 2 was small numerically but resisted the existing estimates.

Jin’s proof uses a positive-real completion theorem for a matrix-valued function. In the August 7 version, the key argument is organized around an auxiliary eigenbasis and a mass parameter; the numerical-range double-layer construction has mass two. The manuscript then uses approximation by matrices with simple spectrum and suitable convex outer domains to obtain the general statement. The theorem itself is stated for every finite complex matrix and scalar polynomial, exactly matching this card.

Lorist and Schwenninger use an operator-theoretic perturbation lemma. In their notation, T has a contraction dilation with error terms E_n=2V*Q^{*n}V−T^{*n}. Uniform boundedness of these errors and their commutation with T force ‖T‖≤2. Their proof exploits all powers n through a telescoping estimate, rather than only the first power. Applying this to T=f(A) and the double-layer representation proves the scalar spectral-set bound.

The two arguments are valuable for more than lowering a constant: they identify additional structure in the earlier functional-calculus estimates that had not been sufficient when used one power at a time. The Lorist–Schwenninger manuscript explicitly acknowledges Jin’s independent proof, and its August 17 revision adds exposition and remarks rather than a restriction to a special matrix class. The exact scalar theorem and main lemma were inspected for this catalogue; no local Lean verification was performed.

The complete version remains a separate question because it asks for a bound after replacing scalar polynomial values by matrices of polynomial values, uniformly in that additional matrix size. A proof for each scalar p does not automatically supply this stronger simultaneous norm estimate. Åhag, Czyż and Virtanen’s September 9, 2026 revision proves the complete conjecture for matrices A of order at most three and develops related square-function estimates. That result must not be presented as the all-dimensional complete theorem.

The original question is retained because it records a fundamental sharp relation between a scalar geometric set and nonnormal matrix computation, together with a very recent change in mathematical status. It also provides a useful test of catalogue freshness: an entry based only on the 2018 or 2024 references would incorrectly describe the scalar conjecture as still open. New work on complete bounds or related spectral sets should receive its own precise statement.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm{P}\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
cards.definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm{P}\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.
cards.why: Semidefinite constraints underlie many successful optimization relaxations, yet their unrestricted exact decision complexity is still unsettled. This problem isolates whether finite rational input admits a polynomial-time decision even when numerical separation and small explicit witnesses are unavailable.

cards.context:
A semidefinite constraint requires a quadratic form to be nonnegative in every direction. Diagonal matrix inequalities include ordinary linear inequalities. Exact decision asks whether the feasible region is empty, which is different from obtaining a useful approximate optimizer on well-conditioned instances.

De Klerk–Vallentin’s inspected approximation theorem is supplied with a rational feasible center and quantitative inner and outer radius information. Its runtime also depends on requested accuracy. This is a polynomial bit-complexity result under explicit geometric assumptions, not an unrestricted exact emptiness test.

Approximate feasibility need not imply exact feasibility. For example,
\[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\]
has determinant \(-1\), so it is never positive semidefinite. Nevertheless its negative eigenvalue \((t-\sqrt{t^2+4})/2\) tends to zero as \(t\) tends to positive infinity. This infeasible affine family has distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone in the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries.

A rational input can also have only irrational feasible parameters. The rational affine block-diagonal matrix
\[\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\2&2x\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}2&x\\x&1\end{pmatrix}\right)\]
is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x=\sqrt2\). Replacing the real domain by rational substitutions would change the answer to this instance.

Even when rational feasible points exist, all of them can require exponentially many bits relative to the number of variables. Pataki–Touzov study the structural occurrence of such examples and questions about compact representations. This explains an obstacle to algorithms that must explicitly output a point; it does not itself lower-bound the complexity of the decision bit requested here.

General exact decision is possible through real-algebraic methods. Henrion–Naldi–Safey El Din develop symbolic algorithms accommodating degenerate feasible sets. Their optimization analysis retains generic auxiliary choices and objectives, and its displayed bounds count arithmetic operations. Bounds polynomial when one dimension is fixed do not establish one polynomial bit bound when both dimensions and coefficient lengths vary.

Ramana’s exact alternative replaces infeasibility by feasibility of another semidefinite system of polynomial description size. In the Turing model it implies that the problem lies in NP if and only if it lies in coNP; neither membership is thereby established on its own. The separate NP-intersect-coNP result over exact real-number machines uses a different model of computation.

Pataki’s October 2025 treatment retains this complexity distinction and gives a fuller description of the exact dual’s feasible set. A polynomial-size dual system is not automatically a polynomial-size binary certificate: its real variables still have to satisfy semidefinite constraints.

Slot–Steurer–Wiedmer obtain effective solution bounds and polynomial-time approximate minimization of convex polynomials over polyhedra. The constraints in that result are linear, and the authors explicitly contrast their result with general semidefinite programming. It does not make arbitrary linear matrix inequalities decidable in polynomial bit time.

The September 2026 higher-order Newton paper of ter Voert–de Klerk explicitly retains the unknown exact SDP complexity. Its iteration analysis uses a derivative oracle and real-number computation, and fixed-accuracy SDP subproblems require stated regularity. A reduction of an iteration to an SDP is therefore not a solution of this unrestricted Turing-model decision question.

cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(N\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(N\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.
cards.why: Simplex is a central optimization method whose practical effectiveness has long exceeded its general worst-case guarantees. The question isolates whether exact polynomial-time linear optimization is compatible with its required improving basis exchanges, including degeneracy, and with efficiently choosing every exchange.

cards.context:
General linear programming has polynomial-time algorithms measured in the binary input size. This card imposes the additional requirement that the computation reach its answer through legal simplex pivots on the given program from the supplied basis. The August 2026 full version of the ranking-based paper still poses the unrestricted pivot-rule question as open.

A short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short improving path to an optimum. A polynomial bit-time rule would bound both the number of its basis exchanges and the work required to choose them. Its bound may depend on coefficient bit lengths; it would not by itself establish a strongly polynomial LP algorithm or a polytope diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy allows many bases to represent one point. Kukharenko and Sanità bound consecutive degenerate improving pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n-m-1\), with efficient implementation when an improving feasible direction is available. Their result controls a block of stalling at that vertex; it does not give a dimension-independent or polynomial-in-input bound on the total number of distinct vertices visited by an arbitrary simplex run.

Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a two-phase shadow-vertex simplex method. The expectation is over Gaussian perturbations around an arbitrary input, with polynomial dependence on dimensions and on \(1/\sigma\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the relative perturbation scale. This does not bound the deterministic worst-case bit time on every unperturbed rational input.

The ranking-based results restrict the information a rule may use. One theorem gives a superpolynomial iteration lower bound in \(n\) for index-ranking rules with \(o(n/\log n)\) memory states. The other gives \(\Omega(2^{\sqrt K})\) iterations for the stated memoryless class based only on rankings by index, reduced cost and objective increase, where \(K\) counts nonzero constraint-matrix entries. The definitions also require choices to respect ranking-preserving relabelings. Memory states are not bits of memory, and \(K\) is not this card's binary input length \(N\). These restricted-information theorems do not exclude algorithms with full numerical access and general polynomial-time history.

Disser and Mosis obtain an all-pivot-rules lower bound for the active-set method with higher-degree polynomial objectives on a hypercube. Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen this to convex quadratic maximization. The objective is nonlinear and the optimization direction is maximization; neither theorem is an all-rules lower bound for the linear objective required here.

Black and Steiner’s April 2026 revision proves that finding a shortest monotone pivot sequence is NP-hard, already for simple polytopes where vertices are nondegenerate. Thus a polynomial-time algorithm for always finding a shortest sequence would imply P = NP. This card asks for some polynomial-time legal run and does not require its number of pivots to be minimum, so shortest-path hardness alone does not answer it negatively.

cards.title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one uniform classical deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge0\), every explicitly given rational matrix \(Q\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) and every rational vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), the machine correctly decides whether
\[
 \exists x\in\mathbb Z^n\quad Qx\le b
\]
within at most
\[
 2^{Cn}(N+1)^c
\]
bit operations, where \(N\) is the total binary encoding length of the input? The inequalities are componentwise, and there is no boundedness or coefficient-size promise beyond the finite explicit encoding.
cards.definitions:
The dimension parameter \(n\) is the number of integer variables, and \(m\) is the number of inequalities. Both are supplied with the input. The matrix entries and right-hand-side entries are given exactly as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators, with explicit lengths or delimiters; entries need not be reduced to lowest terms. The entire matrix is listed in row-major order, followed by \(b\). The encoding length \(N\) includes all coefficients, dimensions, signs, denominators and delimiters. There is no succinct circuit or oracle representation of the inequalities.

The inequality \(Qx\le b\) means
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}x_j\le b_i
 \quad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Every coordinate of \(x\) must be an integer, with no a priori bound on its magnitude or sign. Nonnegativity restrictions are present only if encoded among the inequalities. The underlying real polyhedron may be empty, unbounded, lower dimensional, or contain lines; the matrix may be rank deficient. No bound is imposed on the number of inequalities, determinant magnitudes or width of the feasible region. There is no objective function.

For \(n=0\), \(\mathbb Z^0\) contains the single empty vector, and feasibility means \(0\le b_i\) for every row. For \(m=0\), the conjunction of inequalities is empty and the instance is feasible. These conventions also cover the completely empty system.

The output is one exact Boolean answer: YES if an integer solution exists, and NO otherwise. Producing a feasible point or a separate infeasibility certificate is not required by this decision target. A positive answer cannot be based solely on real feasibility or on satisfying relaxed or numerically perturbed inequalities.

The computation uses a fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, independent of \(m,n,N,Q,b\). Time is the number of bit-level machine steps. All reading, parsing, exact integer or rational arithmetic, storage operations and output are charged. Arithmetic on an arbitrarily large number is not one operation. Randomness, nonuniform advice, real-number primitives and uncharged optimization or separation oracles are not available.

The constants \(C\) and \(c\) are universal for that one program. In particular, the polynomial exponent on \(N\) may not depend on \(n\), and the exponential base may not grow with \(n\), coefficient magnitude or the number of rows. A polynomial factor in numerical coefficient or determinant magnitude can be exponential in its binary encoding length and therefore is not automatically permitted. Any implementation that uses such a factor must prove that its full bit cost nevertheless meets the displayed bound on every input.

The phrase single-exponential dependence on dimension refers to the factor \(2^{Cn}\). Bounds of the form \((\log(n+2))^{Dn}\) with a fixed \(D>0\) have a growing base and do not meet that dependence as stated. A family of unrelated algorithms, one for each fixed dimension, also does not suffice without one uniform machine and the required universal bounds.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated deterministic algorithm's existence or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

A positive answer must establish exact feasibility decisions and the total bit-operation bound for every encoded rational system, including unbounded and lower-dimensional cases. If the method first converts the input to another formulation, its cost, encoding growth and dependence on the number of integer variables must all be accounted for. An optimization algorithm is sufficient only if its proved guarantees include this feasibility task and the specified bound.

A negative answer must rule out every admissible uniform deterministic program and all fixed constants \(C,c\) in the statement. A lower bound conditional on ETH, \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or another unproved assumption does not establish this unconditional negation. Excluding subexponential time \(2^{o(n)}\) does not exclude the requested single-exponential bound.

A randomized algorithm, an algorithm restricted to bounded coefficients or a special block structure, an approximate integer-feasibility procedure, or a bound exponential in a different parameter does not decide the selected target without a proved extension.
cards.why: Integer feasibility is a general optimization primitive. A fixed exponential base in the number of variables would sharpen the dimension dependence of a widely used fixed-parameter algorithmic tool without restricting the coefficients or constraint structure.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.
cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

references.title: Equality of ordinary and symbolic powers and the Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture for (n−2)-uniform clutters
references.locator: Version 2, 11 November 2025; abstract states the restriction to clutters on n vertices with every edge of size n−2.

cards.context:
Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

For the member-by-element incidence matrix \(A\), whose entry \(A_{F,e}\) is one precisely when \(e\in F\), the corresponding fractional problems are \(\min\{w^{\mathsf T}z:Az\ge\mathbf1,\ z\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le w,\ y\ge0\}\). The conjectured equality concerns integer solutions, and hence is stronger than ordinary linear-programming duality. It asks for integral optima on both sides for every integer weight.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

Roy and Saha report a proof for \((n-2)\)-uniform clutters: every member has size exactly \(n-2\) when the ground set has \(n\) elements. Arbitrary clutters can have unrelated member sizes, so this subclass result leaves the stated universal implication unchanged.

cards.title: Smale’s seventh problem
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.

references.title: Characterization of Logarithmic Fekete Critical Configurations of at Most Six Points in All Dimensions
references.authors: Diego Armentano; Leandro Bentancur; Federico Carrasco; Marcelo Fiori; Matías Valdés; Mauricio Velasco
references.locator: 22 March 2026 revision, Journal of Symbolic Computation DOI 10.1016/j.jsc.2026.102570; exact small-cardinality results and restricted seven-point case

cards.context:
Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm that solves every rational P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial bit time? More precisely, are there a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded rational input
\[n\in\mathbb N_{>0},\qquad M\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad q\in\mathbb Q^n,\]
the machine halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below, and whenever \(M\) is a P-matrix it outputs \(z,w\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying
\[w=Mz+q,\qquad z_i\ge0,\quad w_i\ge0,\quad z_iw_i=0\quad(1\le i\le n)?\]
A P-matrix has strictly positive determinant for every nonempty principal submatrix. No certificate of this promise is supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize it. The constants \(B,k\) and the program are shared by all dimensions and all rational coefficients.
cards.definitions:
Matrix promise. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), the principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) consists of the rows and columns with indices in \(S\), both in increasing order. Thus the promise is
\[\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n],\ \det M[S,S]>0.\]
Here the determinant is the usual alternating sum of products, evaluated exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). Strict positivity is essential. There is no symmetry, sparsity, triangularity, positive-semidefiniteness or nondegeneracy assumption. In particular, a valid solution may have both \(z_i=w_i=0\) in some coordinate.

Equations and output. The matrix product is \((Mz)_i=\sum_{j=1}^nM_{ij}z_j\), and all inequalities use the ordinary rational order. With \(z,w\ge0\), coordinatewise complementarity is equivalent to \(z^Tw=\sum_{i=1}^n z_iw_i=0\). A solution is the complete pair of vectors, with exact rational coordinates. An interval, floating-point vector or small residual is not an exact solution under this task. The guarantee is a search guarantee: returning only a yes/no answer about existence is insufficient.

Binary encoding. To make the bit model definite, encode a nonnegative integer \(t\) by
\[u(t)=1^{b(t)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(t+1),\qquad b(t)=\lfloor\log_2(t+1)\rfloor+1,\]
where \(\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) is its binary expansion without leading zeroes, of length \(b(t)\). The initial run of ones specifies that length. A rational number is written uniquely as \(p/d\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\gcd(|p|,d)=1\), and is encoded by a sign bit, then \(u(|p|)\), then \(u(d)\). The sign bit is zero for nonnegative \(p\), including zero, and one for negative \(p\). Thus zero uses numerator zero and denominator one. The input concatenates \(u(n)\), all \(n^2\) entries of \(M\) in row-major order, and the \(n\) entries of \(q\). Every entry, including a zero entry, is explicitly present. A syntactically valid input has exactly this form and no trailing bits. Its total binary length is \(N\). The output concatenates the \(n\) rational encodings of \(z\), followed by those of \(w\), in index order; \(n\) is already known from the input. Other usual explicit binary rational encodings are polynomially equivalent to this convention.

Computation. The same finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program is used for every input. One transition costs one step. Reading input, rational arithmetic, comparisons, intermediate representations and writing the entire output are all charged. There are no oracles, real-number unit-cost operations, randomness, nonuniform advice or free preprocessing. The polynomial time bound applies to every syntactically valid rational input, including matrices that fail the P-matrix promise. On those nonpromised inputs any halting output is allowed; detecting a violated principal minor is not required. Behavior on malformed input strings is unrestricted. A polynomial bound only on promised inputs is equivalent for this existence question, since a known polynomial bound can be enforced with a clock and arbitrary output after timeout. The bound may depend polynomially on coefficient bit lengths through \(N\); this is not a demand for a strongly polynomial number of arithmetic operations independent of those lengths.

Quantifier order. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists B,k\,\forall(n,M,q)\) with the time guarantee above and correctness whenever \(\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\). Coefficient magnitudes, dimension, degeneracy and numerical conditioning may vary without restriction; they do not permit selecting a different program or polynomial for each input.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this algorithm-existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish one program, one polynomial bit-time bound and exact correctness on every promised input, including degenerate instances. Any internal approximation procedure must be proved to recover and output the exact rational solution within that bound. A negative answer must show that every uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs fails to output the required solution on some P-matrix instance. Exponential examples for one pivot rule, hardness of recognizing P-matrices, a lower bound in a restricted oracle model, or a conditional complexity-theoretic barrier alone do not prove that negation. An algorithm for a proper matrix subclass or with an uncontrolled condition-parameter factor does not establish the positive answer.
cards.why: The P-matrix promise guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side, and that solution has a short rational description. The remaining difficulty is finding it efficiently despite the coupled choices of which coordinates vanish. A polynomial algorithm would resolve a central structured search problem that sits between tractable linear optimization and more general complementarity systems.

cards.context:
Complementarity imposes a discrete choice within linear equations: each coordinate must have \(z_i=0\), or \(w_i=0\), or both. For \(M=I_n\), the solution is \(z_i=\max\{0,-q_i\}\) and \(w_i=\max\{0,q_i\}\). For a general P-matrix, the coordinates interact through \(Mz\), so this coordinate-by-coordinate formula no longer applies.

The classical P-matrix characterization states that the linear complementarity system has exactly one solution for every real right-hand side if and only if all principal minors are positive. Uniqueness concerns the vector pair, not the choice of a complementary basis; degenerate instances can have several bases representing the same solution. The existence and uniqueness theorem does not itself give the polynomial algorithm requested here.

Rational exact output does not require an exponentially long description. In a solution, let \(S=\{i:z_i>0\}\). Then \(z_{[n]\setminus S}=0\), \(w_S=0\), and \(M[S,S]z_S=-q_S\); this principal matrix is nonsingular. Clearing input denominators and applying determinant bounds shows that its rational solution and the resulting \(w\) have polynomial bit length. If \(S\) is empty, \(z=0\) and \(w=q\). The difficult part is finding a valid pattern efficiently.

P-matrix recognition is co-NP-complete, but this card supplies the property as a promise. Gordon and Shu give polynomial conversions between different certificates that a matrix violates the promise. Such certificate results do not make recognition part of this task, and recognition hardness does not prove that promised solution finding is hard.

Fearnley, Gordon, Mehta and Savani place the promised problem in a class based on finding the endpoint of a unique, implicitly represented path whose potential increases along it. Their total-search variants permit a certificate of a violated promise as an alternative output. These complexity-class containments organize the search problem but do not give polynomial-time solution finding. The present card requires a solution only on P-matrix inputs.

Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for Hessenberg P-matrices, which have zero entries beyond the first off-diagonal on one side; tridiagonal matrices are included. Their \(O(n^5)\) arithmetic-operation bound combines polynomially many basis tests with linear-system solves. Exact rational linear algebra gives polynomial bit complexity for these subclasses. The general matrix in this card has no such zero pattern.

The ICALP 2024 paper “Two Choices Are Enough” reduces generalized complementarity instances to the ordinary binary-choice problem and relates them to geometric search problems. This equivalence extends the reach of P-matrix LCP; it is not a polynomial solver for it. ETH’s 2025 activity report continues to list general polynomial-time solution finding as open.

E.-Nagy and Végh’s June 2026 revision gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input length and in the optimized handicap \(\widehat\kappa^\star(M)\), the best handicap attainable by positive diagonal row scaling. The handicap measures departure from the inequality \(x^TMx\ge0\). Their general upper bound on the unscaled handicap is exponential in input bit complexity, and the algorithmic theorem does not give a polynomial input-length bound on the optimized parameter. It therefore does not settle the all-P-matrix target.

Then \(z_{[n]\setminus S}=0\), \(w_S=0\), and \(M[S,S]z_S=-q_S\); this principal matrix is nonsingular. Clearing input denominators and applying determinant bounds shows that its rational solution and the resulting \(w\) have polynomial bit length. If \(S\) is empty, \(z=0\) and \(w=q\). The difficult part is finding a valid pattern efficiently.

P-matrix recognition is co-NP-complete, but this card supplies the property as a promise. Gordon and Shu give polynomial conversions between different certificates that a matrix violates the promise. Such certificate results do not make recognition part of this task, and recognition hardness does not prove that promised solution finding is hard.

Fearnley, Gordon, Mehta and Savani place the promised problem in a class based on finding the endpoint of a unique, implicitly represented path whose potential increases along it. Their total-search variants permit a certificate of a violated promise as an alternative output. These complexity-class containments organize the search problem but do not give polynomial-time solution finding. The present card requires a solution only on P-matrix inputs.

Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for Hessenberg P-matrices, which have zero entries beyond the first off-diagonal on one side; tridiagonal matrices are included. Their \(O(n^5)\) arithmetic-operation bound combines polynomially many basis tests with linear-system solves. Exact rational linear algebra gives polynomial bit complexity for these subclasses. The general matrix in this card has no such zero pattern.

The ICALP 2024 paper “Two Choices Are Enough” reduces generalized complementarity instances to the ordinary binary-choice problem and relates them to geometric search problems. This equivalence extends the reach of P-matrix LCP; it is not a polynomial solver for it. ETH’s 2025 activity report continues to list general polynomial-time solution finding as open.

E.-Nagy and Végh’s June 2026 revision gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input length and in the optimized handicap \(\widehat\kappa^\star(M)\), the best handicap attainable by positive diagonal row scaling. The handicap measures departure from the inequality \(x^TMx\ge0\). Their general upper bound on the unscaled handicap is exponential in input bit complexity, and the algorithmic theorem does not give a polynomial input-length bound on the optimized parameter. It therefore does not settle the all-P-matrix target.

source_formulation.text: The retained question is ordinary deterministic polynomial bit-time solution of rational LCP under the P-matrix promise. It asks neither for recognizing that promise nor for a strongly polynomial arithmetic algorithm. The literature’s unique-sink and total-search formulations supply context; they do not add an obligation to produce non-P-matrix certificates here.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
cards.why: KLS asks whether covariance normalization alone controls the relation between global variation and local change for every log-concave distribution. Its equivalent geometric expansion principle is central to concentration inequalities and the analysis of random walks used for sampling, integration and convex optimization.

cards.context:
Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
cards.definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The parameter \(N\) is the length of the supplied finite encoding. A standard indexing uses \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, with the crossing-free code handled separately. It is neither the smallest possible crossing number of the knot nor the length of a compressed program describing a larger diagram.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the algorithm’s correct answer on every valid diagram and one polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative proof must exclude every deterministic polynomial-time recognizer in this input model, rather than only a selected algorithm or simplification rule. Short certificates, polynomial-length move sequences and successful finite experiments do not by themselves prove deterministic polynomial running time. The existence statement is binary and has no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.

cards.context:
A complicated knot diagram can represent a circle that has merely been drawn in an awkward way. The task is to distinguish such projections from actual knots, using a finite description of crossings and planar incidence. No physical model of rope or numerical geometry is involved.

Both positive and negative instances have short efficiently checkable certificates. The NP theorem certifies unknottedness, and the coNP theorem certifies knottedness. These are existence statements about verifiable evidence; they do not show how to find the evidence in deterministic polynomial time.

Thus the problem belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\). Here NP consists of decision problems with polynomial-size witnesses verifiable in polynomial time, and coNP contains their complements. NP-hardness of this particular problem under polynomial-time reductions would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\); a proof that it is outside P would in particular separate P from NP.

Lackenby proves that an unknot diagram with \(n\) crossings admits a simplification using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local changes of diagrams that preserve knot type. The theorem bounds a successful sequence’s length, while an algorithm must determine appropriate moves without an uncontrolled search.

The March 2021 Oxford announcement states a recognition algorithm with running time \(n^{O(\log n)}\). The checked SoCG 2025 article still describes that result as announced. Such a quasipolynomial bound allows a growing exponent and therefore does not give the fixed exponent requested here.

cards.title: Planar k-set growth exponent
cards.formal: Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le Cn(k+1)^a\}.\] Here \(K_2(n,k)\) is the largest number of distinct \(k\)-point subsets strictly separable by a line in an \(n\)-point planar set with no three collinear points. Its full definition is below. The bound must be uniform in both integer parameters. Logarithmic factors and exact extremal counts are not requested.
cards.definitions:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]


The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points. The requested exponent is \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le C n(k+1)^a\}.\] The integer parameter domain is the same as above. The coefficient \(C\) may depend on \(a\), but not on either parameter or the point configuration. The cited upper bound ensures \(0\le x_{\mathrm{kset}}\le1/3\). The infimum need not be attained. Thus a value zero permits subpolynomial dependence on \(k\) and does not assert a linear bound \(O(n)\). This records the exponent of the dependence on subset size after factoring out the linear dependence on the number of points; it does not assert a two-sided power-law asymptotic.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{kset}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. For each feasible exponent, one coefficient \(C\) must work for every legal pair \((n,k)\). To exclude an exponent, show that every proposed \(C>0\) fails at some such pair. The infimum need not be attained. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.
