cards.context:
A linear cut realizes only a restricted collection of subsets of a point set. Fixing the subset size measures this restriction more precisely than counting all possible cuts together. The planar problem already exhibits the persistent gap in the broader higher-dimensional question.

For \(k=1\), the separable points are precisely the vertices of the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing \(P\). Their maximum number is \(n\). The unresolved part concerns how the count grows when the selected subset size grows too.

Point-line duality relates these counts to levels in arrangements of lines. A level follows the positions with a prescribed number of arrangement lines below them. Such complexity bounds occur in geometric selection and parametric optimization, where the preferred solution changes with a parameter.

Dey’s general upper bound is \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the domain of this card. Tóth’s constructions give \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets. Thus the existing upper and lower estimates do not differ by only a universal constant when \(k\) increases.

In the plane, k-sets correspond to directed \((k-1)\)-edges. For even \(n\), subsets of size \(n/2\) therefore correspond to the two orientations of undirected halving edges. Consequently \(K_2(n,n/2)\) is twice the maximum number of halving edges. The index \((n-2)/2\) counts points on one side of a halving edge, not the size of a halving subset.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves lower-order and finite-size terms while retaining the leading four-thirds upper power in the balanced case. Such lower-order changes do not themselves determine the uniform exponent selected here.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite simple graph \(H\), there exists a real constant \(C_H\ge1\) such that, for every nonempty finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with no \(H\) minor and every edge-length function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
d_{G,w}(u,v)\le
\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f(u)_j-f(v)_j|
\le C_H\,d_{G,w}(u,v)
\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V?
\]
The constant may depend only on \(H\). The dimension and map may depend on the whole weighted graph, with no bound on dimension or on the time needed to construct them.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called edges. Connected means every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, followed by removal of loops and duplicate edges, can produce a graph isomorphic to \(H\). Exclusion concerns the underlying unweighted graph.

The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. The shortest-path distance \(d_{G,w}(u,v)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(d_{G,w}(u,u)=0\). Positivity and finiteness make this a finite metric. A one-vertex graph is allowed and satisfies the target trivially.

The target space is finite-dimensional \(\ell_1^m\): the vector space \(\mathbb R^m\) with distance \(\|a-b\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\). The first inequality fixes a noncontracting normalization, and the second allows expansion by at most \(C_H\). Allowing an arbitrary common scaling factor instead gives the same distortion notion.

All edge lengths are arbitrary positive real numbers. Neither graph size nor the ratio of the largest to the smallest edge length may affect \(C_H\). There is no requirement that the graph or its lengths be efficiently encoded, since this is a mathematical existence question. All pairs must satisfy the inequalities simultaneously for the same map.

The source also allows zero edge lengths and hence zero distances between different vertices. That convention is equivalent for this conjecture: contract each component of zero-length edges, retain the shortest parallel edge when necessary, and map the original vertices through this quotient. The quotient is still a minor of the original graph. The positive-length statement above avoids treating distinct points at distance zero as a metric space.

No Euclidean target, restriction to selected terminals, average-distance guarantee, or transformation of the distances by a power is part of this statement. Here a terminal, when used in the context, simply means a selected vertex whose distances must be preserved.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain a finite constant for every fixed excluded minor, uniformly over all weighted graphs in that class and all vertex pairs. It need not determine the best constant or construct the embeddings efficiently. A negative answer must give one fixed graph \(H\) such that for every real \(C\ge1\), some finite connected positively weighted \(H\)-minor-free graph admits no map into any finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) space satisfying both inequalities with factor \(C\). Failure at one fixed distortion value is insufficient if a larger uniform value remains possible. This binary existence claim has no additive numerical tolerance.

cards.context:
The conjecture links a qualitative restriction on graph structure to quantitative preservation of every distance. Removing one fixed graph from the set of permitted minors is predicted to prevent any distortion that grows with graph size, despite arbitrary edge lengths.

Finite \(\ell_1\) metrics are exactly nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric has value one on pairs separated by a vertex subset and zero on other pairs. This connects distance representation to weighted separation of vertices and hence to graph partitioning.

In the equivalent routing formulation, capacities are attached to graph edges and demands to arbitrary vertex pairs. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every demand, allowing a demand to split among paths. The flow-cut gap compares the best achievable fraction to the upper bound imposed by the sparsest cut. The conjecture predicts a constant gap on every fixed-minor-free family.

Demands in this correspondence may join any pairs; they need not themselves form a planar or minor-free graph. The multiflow/multicut optimization studied in recent work has a different objective and gap, so its constant bounds do not resolve the conjecture.

The planar case is already unresolved in the checked 2026 account: the upper bound grows as the square root of the logarithm of the number of vertices, while no superconstant lower bound is known there. Trees and several other restricted families do have constant bounds.

Lee and Sidiropoulos establish a constant bound on every minor-closed family excluding a fixed tree. Their stronger random-tree result applies to bounded pathwidth, a restriction stronger than bounded treewidth.

A constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs is known using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. The authors explicitly distinguish its stronger relaxation from the ordinary concurrent-flow relaxation, whose gap is the relevant one here.

For planar graphs with a selected terminal set covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a drawing, Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log(\gamma+1)})\). The added one handles the single-face boundary case in asymptotic notation. The number of covering faces is unbounded in the general conjecture.

Mori’s February 2026 preprint states that the worst distortion over edge lengths of \(K_{2,n}\) is \((3k-2)/(2k-1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\) and \(n\ge1\). Here \(K_{2,n}\) has two independent parts of sizes two and \(n\), with all edges between them. These values tend to \(3/2\), so this is progress within a bounded-distortion family.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
cards.definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

cards.context:
A linear program optimizes a linear function over a polyhedron. Moving between adjacent vertices is the geometric operation behind simplex pivots. The conjecture asks whether every pair of feasible vertices is joined by a short sequence of these moves, before any navigation rule or objective is chosen.

The facet count measures the number of essential inequalities. It can be much smaller than the number of vertices: the cube \([0,1]^d\) has \(2d\) facets and \(2^d\) vertices, but diameter only \(d\). Merely bounding distance by the number of vertices therefore does not give the desired polynomial.

A bound such as \(n^d\) allows the exponent to increase with the dimension. The conjecture demands one fixed exponent, and allows neither the multiplicative constant nor that exponent to depend on the particular polyhedron.

Santos’s 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets has diameter greater than 43, refuting the original Hirsch bound \(n-d\) for bounded polytopes. This leaves open all sufficiently large polynomial bounds. The bounded counterexample does not itself show superpolynomial growth.

Todd proves the general bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the single-vertex boundary cases treated separately. The earlier Kalai–Kleitman bound was \(n^{2+\log_2 d}\). These estimates are quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.

Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has exponent \(\log_2 d-\log_2\log d+O(1)\) for large \(d\). The exponent still grows without bound, so this improvement does not establish the conjecture.

The length of the best available path is different from the length of a path selected by a particular pivot rule. A positive answer would give geometric existence, without supplying a fast procedure for choosing the next edge or guaranteeing objective improvement.

Wulf proves that computing diameter is \(\Pi_2^p\)-hard even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, the convex hulls of incidence vectors of perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. This is a hardness classification at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It concerns finding the value, and is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on that value.

Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a circuit-diameter bound \(O(r^2\log r)\) for standard-form polyhedra \(\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank \(r\ge2\). A circuit direction is a nonzero kernel vector whose set of nonzero coordinates contains no smaller support of another nonzero kernel vector. A circuit step moves maximally in a feasible circuit direction and may pass through a higher-dimensional face. Such a walk need not follow graph edges.

A monotone path increases a chosen linear objective. A coherent monotone path is more restricted: it traces optimizers as a second linear objective varies along a line in objective space. Black and Xue’s July 2026 preprint gives polytopes for which every coherent monotone path for the chosen orientation is long. Their restriction is absent from ordinary graph distance.

More precisely, their Theorem 1.1 gives, for each \(q\ge3\), a polytope of dimension \(q+1\) with \((2q+1)(q+1)+1\) facets and an objective for which every coherent monotone path has length at least \(2^{q-1}-1\). The paper continues to list the unrestricted polynomial Hirsch question as open.

cards.title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) with the following property? For every finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\), encoded by its facets as below and promised to be a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold, \(M\) halts and outputs a bit satisfying
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(K))=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}\partial\Delta^5.
\]
Here \(\partial\Delta^5\) is the standard PL \(4\)-sphere. Output zero is required on every promised input that is not PL homeomorphic to it. There is no running-time or space bound, and connectedness is not part of the promise.
cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a finite family of finite subsets of a finite vertex set \(V\), containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its members are faces; inclusion-maximal faces are facets. The dimension of a nonempty face \(\sigma\) is \(|\sigma|-1\). Pure dimension four means that all facets have exactly five vertices.

Vertex labels are distinct nonnegative integers. The input lists each facet once, sorting labels increasingly within facets and sorting the facet lists lexicographically. Each label is written in binary with no leading zero except for the label zero itself. A fixed separator between labels and a second separator between facets make this a finite string over a fixed alphabet. The full complex is the family of all subsets of the listed facets, and its vertex set is their union. Renaming vertices does not affect the correct answer.

The geometric realization \(|K|\) is the subset of \(\mathbb R^V\) consisting of vectors \((t_v)_{v\in V}\) with \(t_v\ge0\), \(\sum_vt_v=1\), and \(\{v:t_v>0\}\in K\). Each face is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite simplicial subdivision is a finite triangulation of this realization by simplices contained in old simplices, whose union on each old simplex equals that simplex.

Two finite complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic, written \(K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}L\), when they admit finite subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection on vertices taking faces to faces in both directions. Equivalently, their realizations have a homeomorphism that is affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions.

The simplex \(\Delta^q\) is the complex of all subsets of a set of \(q+1\) vertices. Its boundary \(\partial\Delta^q\) consists of all proper subsets of that vertex set. The standard PL \(j\)-sphere is \(\partial\Delta^{j+1}\), up to PL homeomorphism.

The link of a vertex \(v\) is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
In this card, a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold means a finite pure four-dimensional complex for which every vertex link is PL homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^4\). Multiple connected components are allowed. No orientation, simple-connectivity, homology-sphere or prior topological-sphere promise is imposed.

A deterministic Turing machine has a finite transition rule, finite tape alphabet and finitely many tapes; it starts with the encoded complex on its input tape. Halting with output one means acceptance, and halting with output zero means rejection. Termination and correctness are required on all and only promised inputs; behavior on malformed strings or complexes outside the promise is unrestricted. The same finite machine must work for complexes of every size.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the stated machine or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish termination and the exact PL classification on every promised input, without additional unproved hypotheses. A negative answer must establish that every deterministic Turing machine has a promised input on which it either fails to halt with a bit or gives the wrong bit. A lower bound ruling out only polynomial time, a procedure that can return “unknown,” or a classifier proved correct only on a finite census does not settle this target. This is a binary decidability statement with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.

cards.context:
Finite input does not guarantee algorithmic decidability of a global geometric property. The question concerns existence of any always-terminating decision procedure, even one whose resource use is far beyond practical computation.

The PL sphere-recognition problem is decidable through dimension three and undecidable in dimensions at least five. The four-dimensional case is the exceptional gap in the checked account. This card fixes that dimension and promises a manifold rather than asking for manifold recognition itself.

The promise is local: links of vertices have the standard three-sphere type. The output concerns the entire four-dimensional space. Local manifold structure alone does not force the global space to be a sphere.

The topology category matters. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, whereas PL equivalence adds finite piecewise-affine structure. The standard PL sphere cannot be replaced silently by a merely topological sphere.

Pachner’s theorem characterizes PL equivalence of closed triangulated manifolds by finite sequences of bistellar moves, local replacements that preserve PL type. Such finite certificates are useful for individual positive instances. Existence of a certificate does not ensure a recognition procedure terminates on negative instances.

The 2022 computational study explicitly allows an inconclusive outcome. Its successful classifications establish properties of those tested triangulations, without proving that every permitted input will eventually be classified.

The 2026 census work examines closed orientable four-manifolds with at most six four-dimensional simplices. Among triangulations topologically equivalent to the four-sphere, it leaves at most four potentially distinct PL types and conjectures that all are standard. These are unresolved classifications, not a proof that four distinct structures exist.

That census uses generalised triangulations, permitting identifications among faces of a simplex. The card instead uses abstract simplicial complexes with the explicit vertex-set encoding. Neither the finite census limit nor its orientability restriction is added to the benchmark promise.

An algorithm here must reject disconnected promised manifolds as well as connected non-spheres. It must also answer correctly for any PL structures that actually exist, without assuming a conjectural classification of four-manifolds.

cards.title: Weak \(\varepsilon\)-net size exponent
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:f_d(\varepsilon)=O_d(\varepsilon^{-a})\text{ as }\varepsilon\downarrow0\}.\] The function \(f_d(\varepsilon)\), defined below, is the worst-case minimum cardinality of a weak \(\varepsilon\)-net hitting all convex sets that contain at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\). Net points may lie outside the input set. The requested answer concerns the exponent, with no requirement to determine logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time. For each fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1/2]\ \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0],\ f_d(\varepsilon)\le C\varepsilon^{-a}\}.\] Constants may depend on \(d\) and \(a\), but not on the accuracy or point set. The classical polynomial upper bound and inverse-accuracy lower bound give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le d\), so every requested value is a finite real number. The infimum need not be attained; a polylogarithmic factor in \(1/\varepsilon\) does not change the exponent. Different fixed dimensions may use different constants, with no uniform bound on their growth requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge2\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). The weak-net asymptotics take \(\varepsilon\) to zero at each fixed dimension.
cards.why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.

cards.context:
The source asks for the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension. the benchmark convention selects its polynomial exponent in inverse accuracy, rather than matching the entire function within constant factors.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.

cards.title: Dürer’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
cards.definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.
cards.why: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.

references.title: Overlapping Unfoldings of Cones and Convex Polyhedra
references.authors: MIT CompGeom Group; Hugo A. Akitaya; Erik D. Demaine; Fabian Frei; Stefan Langerman; Anna Lubiw; Joseph O’Rourke
references.locator: 10 July 2026 preprint; abstract, arbitrary overlap thickness for selected unfoldings, not impossibility of all unfoldings.

cards.context:
A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.

The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.

cards.title: Klee’s measure running-time exponent
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(d\ge3\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the optimal deterministic running-time exponent \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\text{some uniform exact algorithm has worst-case time }O_d(n^a)\}.\] The task is to compute the exact \(d\)-dimensional volume of the union of \(n\) explicitly given axis-aligned boxes in the real-RAM model below. Programs and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on the coordinates or input size. Logarithmic factors in running time are not part of the numerical answer.
cards.definitions: An input is a list of \(n\ge 0\) closed boxes \(B_i=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_{ij},b_{ij}]\), specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with \(a_{ij}\le b_{ij}\). Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of \(\bigcup_i B_i\), returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied. For a correct uniform deterministic program \(A\) in fixed dimension \(d\), let \(t_{A,d}(n)\) be its worst-case time on \(n\) boxes. Define \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ t_{A,d}(n)\le Cn^a\}.\] A different uniform program may be selected for each fixed dimension and each exponent bound, but not for each input length. Elementary input access and the cited algorithm give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le d/2\). The infimum need not be attained; in particular a value does not prescribe matching logarithmic factors. A lower bound must concern every permitted exact program, without an unproved complexity assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge3\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the specified exact real-RAM model at each fixed dimension. Lower bounds must cover all permitted uniform exact algorithms for that dimension.
cards.why: A basic measure-computation problem underlying geometric union and coverage algorithms.

references.authors: Sujoy Bhore; Subhash Suri; Jie Xue; Xiongxin Yang; Jiumu Zhu
references.locator: ICALP 2026, article 34. Full abstract and Introduction including Theorems 1–2 read, plus §7. Maintains exact volume dynamically with amortized update guarantees; recalls the O(n^(d/2)) static bound and states conditional, rather than unconditional, optimality claims.

cards.context:
Two boxes may cover the same region, so adding their individual volumes overcounts their intersection. In three dimensions, \([0,2]^{3}\) and \([1,3]\times [0,2]^{2}\) each have volume 8, but their union has volume 12. The task requests this single total volume; it does not request a full description of the union boundary. In higher dimensions a box is simply a product of intervals.

Chan’s 2013 algorithm computes exact union volume in \(O(n^{d/2})\) time for every fixed \(d\ge3\). This gives the finite upper bound \(x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le d/2\). Connections with clique problems provide conditional evidence, not an unconditional lower bound for all algorithms.

The real-RAM question counts an arithmetic operation on a coordinate as one step even when the coordinate would require many bits to encode. Chan also obtains logarithmic improvements for integer coordinates in a word-RAM setting. Those improvements do not automatically transfer to unrestricted real inputs, and the source explicitly discusses this distinction. The detailed primitive and worst-case conventions above make the inherited real-RAM target explicit.

The SoCG 2025 work speeds up approximation of union volume and proves a lower bound for algorithms restricted to certain object queries. A small relative error is permitted there. The ICALP 2026 work maintains exact volume under insertions and deletions and measures amortized update time. Both are significant results, but neither determines the unconditional optimal time of a single exact static computation in this card’s model.

cards.title: Logarithmic \(\ell_1\) distortion lower bound for planar Earth Mover Distance
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?\] Here \(D(n)\), defined below, is the least bi-Lipschitz distortion into \(\ell_1\) of the space of all probability measures on \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^2\), equipped with Earth Mover Distance using Euclidean ground distances.
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), a probability measure is a vector \(\mu:X_n	o[0,1]\) with \(\sum_x\mu(x)=1\); all real weights are allowed. For two such vectors put \[W_n(\mu,
u)=\min_\pi\sum_{x,y\in X_n}\|x-y\|_2\pi(x,y),\] where \(\pi(x,y)\geq0\), \(\sum_y\pi(x,y)=\mu(x)\) for each \(x\), and \(\sum_x\pi(x,y)=
u(y)\) for each \(y\). The minimum exists because the set of transport plans is a nonempty compact polytope. Thus unit total mass is transported, with cost equal to distance rather than squared distance. The space \(\ell_1\) consists of real sequences \(z=(z_i)_{i\geq1}\) with \(\sum_i|z_i|<\infty\), and norm \(\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|\). Define \(D(n)\) to be the infimum of all \(D\geq1\) for which a single map \(F\) from the whole probability simplex on \(X_n\) into \(\ell_1\) satisfies \(W_n(\mu,
u)\leq\|F(\mu)-F(
u)\|_1\leq D W_n(\mu,
u)\) for every pair \(\mu,
u\). Allow arbitrary nonlinear maps; the lower inequality normalizes scale and ensures injectivity. No restriction to distributions of bounded support size, uniform weights or a fixed denominator is imposed. No linearity, sketch length, algorithmic runtime or finite output dimension is required. Finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) maps remain admissible by padding with zeros. The infimum need not be attained; matching constant-factor bounds do not require an optimum-achieving map. If no finite-distortion map exists, the infimum is infinity, although the cited upper bound rules this out for each finite grid.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof that \(D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\) at every sufficiently large grid size for one \(c>0\). The matching logarithmic lower bound is recorded below among the dated results.
cards.why: The result identifies the optimal loss when representing planar transport by coordinatewise absolute differences. It closes a longstanding metric-embedding gap relevant to image comparison and nearest-neighbor methods, and shows that the logarithmic loss of classical representations is inherent. The completed result belongs in the historical archive rather than the active open benchmark.

references.authors: Chris Gartland; Mikhail Ostrovskii; Yuval Rabani; Robert Young
references.locator: Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2, and the paragraph attributing dimension two to Gartland–Ostrovskii.

cards.context:
Naor and Schechtman establish the historical gap between an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})\) lower bound and an \(O(\log n)\) upper bound. The binary target selects the logarithmic lower endpoint that was open at the benchmark cutoff; constant distortion was already ruled out earlier.

Gartland and Ostrovskii’s STOC 2026 paper closes that gap: Theorem 1.1 gives \(\Theta(\log n)\) distortion for the transportation-cost space of the planar grid. Their reduction to linear maps identifies its distortion with that of the Earth Mover space of probability measures.

The 2026 grid theorem uses the shortest-path grid metric, which is the planar Manhattan metric. On the same vertices, Euclidean distance is between \(1/\sqrt2\) times that metric and that metric. The corresponding transport distances satisfy the same comparison, so the logarithmic order transfers to the Euclidean ground metric here.

The lower bound is proved even for embeddings into the larger Lebesgue space \(L_1\), so it also applies to \(\ell_1\). The historical upper-bound constructions can be realized with finitely many \(\ell_1\) coordinates for each finite grid. The target-space notation therefore does not leave an asymptotic gap in this card.

A separate 2026 paper by Gartland, Ostrovskii, Rabani and Young extends the sharp dependence to higher-dimensional grids with dimension-uniform constants. Its planar case explicitly relies on the Gartland–Ostrovskii theorem. It is supporting later context, not the sole basis for identifying a planar resolution.

Grid side length and the number of grid vertices differ by a square, which changes a logarithm only by a constant factor. The number of support points of an individual distribution is a different parameter and is not substituted for grid size. Sketching independently represented point sets is likewise a separate computational question.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

cards.context:
The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.
cards.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

cards.context:
Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.

The rate-dependent polynomial convention, classical independent samples and exact every-secret recovery target are retained. cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.
cards.why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.

references.title: DNF formulas are efficiently testable with relative error
references.authors: Xi Chen; William Pires; Toniann Pitassi; Rocco A. Servedio
references.locator: Version 1, 22 January; primary author/arXiv abstracts and history read for scope only. The author page lists FOCS 2026; no publication date or full-proof verification is inferred. The stated result is query-based property testing, not a PAC learner

cards.context:
A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

source_formulation.text: The inherited question comes from the first paragraph of Feldman’s 2012 introduction: polynomial-time PAC learning of polynomial-size DNFs from random examples under an arbitrary unknown distribution. The retained size-sensitive statement permits improper learning. The integer learning parameters, explicit circuit syntax and charged example-access convention specify that target rather than adding query access or restricting the hypothesis to DNF.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 survey retains the distribution-free computational gap. The 2016 and 2021 improper-learning lower bounds retain random-SAT or local-PRG assumptions. Current 2025/2026 exact-query, property-testing and PQ-learning results have different access, output, distribution or runtime guarantees. No verified unconditional solution of the retained target was found in bounded primary-source checks; recent proofs were not independently certified.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

cards.context:
A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.
