cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.

cards.context:
Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

cards.title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
cards.formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.
cards.definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.
cards.why: One-way functions provide the basic computational ingredient for much of classical private-key cryptography. The question asks whether failure of a general-purpose circuit learner is already enough to supply that ingredient, without assuming that hard target functions can be efficiently generated at random.

cards.context:
The forward evaluation of a hidden target circuit is easy when its description is known. Learning is different: from observed input-output examples the learner must build a predictor that works on future draws. The challenge is computational, since a polynomial-size description and enough noiseless examples already give a finite statistical learning problem.

One-way functions are known to yield pseudorandom functions and thereby hard circuit-learning tasks. The reverse direction in this card starts with only failure of a worst-case learner. The source contrasts that question with classical equivalences based on average-case learning hardness, where an efficient process chooses the hidden target from a distribution.

The source proves a worst-case/average-case robustness theorem for learning the stronger concept classes EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. The corresponding decision-complexity consequences concern those stronger classes. They do not establish that every worst-case obstruction for ordinary polynomial-size circuits contains cryptographic average-case hardness.

FOCS 2023 Hirahara–Nanashima extends learning under nonexistence of one-way functions to richer agnostic and distribution-learning models. Its average-case guarantees sample the hidden advice or target distribution. Its worst-case guarantees have runtime exponential in the computational depth of the hidden description, where depth compares a time-bounded shortest description with an unbounded shortest description. That depth need not be logarithmic for arbitrary target descriptions.

ITCS 2025 Liu–Mazor–Pass Theorem 6 gives a worst-case characterization using black-box PAC learning under an explicit computational-shallowness promise on the joint sampler and predictor description. It also uses failure of infinitely-often polynomial-time learning for ordinary one-way functions. The theorem is stronger than an average-case-only analogy, but its promise and length quantifiers do not supply the unrestricted antecedent of this card.

STOC 2026 Hirahara–Nanashima studies approximation of the minimum program description needed for agnostic learning. Its Theorem 1.5 connects average-case hardness of the GapLearn decision problem to infinitely-often one-way functions, with an approximation factor governed by advice complexity of sampling. A minimum-description decision problem, average-case input choice and infinitely-often security are each distinct from this card’s exact implication.

The 2021 full source expressly retains the question. The 2025 journal version’s metadata and abstract were checked, but its subscription full text was not available. The checked 2023–2026 theorems clarify important partial connections without a matching resolution; the card therefore records uncertain current status rather than treating a bounded literature search as proof of openness.

cards.title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.
cards.why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.

cards.title: Square-root multiclass regret from Littlestone dimension
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty sets \(X,Y\), every nonempty class \(H\subseteq Y^X\) of Littlestone dimension at most \(d\), and all integers \(T\ge d\ge1\), the minimax expected regret satisfies \[R_T(H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Infinite instance and label sets are allowed, and no regularity or computability restriction on the class is added. For the prediction game defined below, \[R_T(H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in X\times Y}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T(1-p_t(y_t))-\min_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\}.\] Here \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\) is a probability distribution on labels. The infimum ranges over all causal prediction rules, without computational restrictions.
cards.definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) assigns a label from \(Y\) to each instance in \(X\). A depth-\(r\) Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels from \(Y\) on that node's outgoing edges; the pair of labels may vary by node. The tree is shattered if every root-to-leaf path has one fixed hypothesis agreeing with all its edge labels on its instance points. The dimension \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\) is the largest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. On each round the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner supplies \(p_t\), and the adversary then reveals \(y_t\). The learner observes the actual label before the next round and is charged expected zero-one loss \(1-p_t(y_t)\). It does not observe future instances. The adversary may react to \(p_t\); loss is the displayed expectation, not a reaction to a sampled label. The sequence need not be realizable by any hypothesis. The comparator is one fixed hypothesis chosen in hindsight, whose minimum loss exists since the possible losses are integers from zero to \(T\). A distribution here is a function \(p:Y\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{y\in Y}p(y)=1\), with this sum defined as the supremum of sums over finite subsets. It automatically has at most countable positive support. This atomic convention does not increase the best possible regret relative to arbitrary probability measures with measurable singletons: any missing atom mass can be assigned to one fixed label, increasing no zero-one loss. All histories and rules are arbitrary set functions, so no topology or measurability structure on \(X,H\) is required. Rules may know \(H\) and \(T\), need not be proper, and have no runtime, memory, computability or finite-description bound. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Dimension zero means all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The range \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime because cumulative regret cannot exceed \(T\). All requested comparison constants must be independent of the instance and label spaces, class, dimension and horizon.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that \(R_T(H)/\sqrt{dT}\) has a universal upper bound over the classes and horizons specified above, or prove that this ratio is unbounded on that domain.
cards.why: Would determine whether Littlestone dimension alone controls the exact minimax cost of multiclass sequential prediction, beyond the already known learnability characterization.

cards.context:
The learner sees the current instance and then receives the correct label after predicting. It can distribute its prediction among labels, and is scored by expected mistakes relative to the best fixed hypothesis. Labels can contradict every member of the class. The regret target is therefore different from a realizable mistake bound.

The 2023 paper proves that finite Littlestone dimension characterizes agnostic multiclass online learnability even for unbounded label spaces. This general learnability theorem does not require the separate minimax regularity assumption used in its sharper finite-label result. The remaining rate question asks how far a learner must fall behind the best fixed concept.

The unrestricted argument in §3 gives regret at most \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)+\sqrt{(T/2)\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\ln(eT/\operatorname{Ldim}(H))}\) for positive dimension. In the stated horizon range this yields \(R(d,T)=O(\sqrt{dT\log(eT/d)})\). A universal lower scale is \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\). The logarithm is part of the unresolved gap and cannot be suppressed when asking for constant factors.

For a finite label set, Theorem 9 gives \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{Ldim}(H)T\log|Y|})\) under the additional minimax regularity condition explicitly stated in p. 9 footnote 4 for those results. Under that condition a fixed label count yields the square-root scale, but the coefficient grows with the count. Even for two labels, removing the condition for unrestricted classes is a separate open issue recorded by the source and by the 2025 thesis.

The binary question restores the source’s square-root upper-bound conjecture. It retains arbitrary instance and label sets and does not add the regularity condition used in some sharper special-case theorems. The known lower scale motivates this endpoint; a complete determination of an alternative rate is not required.

The checked May 2026 oracle-complexity paper concerns binary classification and retains logarithmic factors in its dimension-dependent regret statement. It improves resource use within an online algorithm and does not resolve the unrestricted multiclass constant-factor rate.

cards.title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
cards.formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
cards.definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.
cards.why: The symmetric binary perceptron is a basic random constraint model in which many solutions can exist while known algorithms reach much smaller densities. Locating the small-margin search scale tests whether the observed computational obstruction captures all efficient algorithms or only particular algorithm families. Its links to discrepancy, random solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness make the threshold a substantial average-case complexity question.

cards.title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
cards.definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.
cards.why: A universal linear bound would connect sample-based combinatorial complexity with the number of examples needed for structured teaching. It asks whether recursive teaching can always be controlled at the same scale as VC dimension.

cards.context:
Simon’s 2023 Open Problem 3 asks for precisely this universal linear relationship. The earlier Simon–Zilles open-problem paper is retained as provenance from the already consolidated duplicate; there is a single active target.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Recursive teaching measures the hardest easiest-to-teach concept that remains after restricting the candidate class; it is not the maximum ordinary teaching dimension of the original class.

Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.

Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

Compton, Pabbaraju and Zhivotovskiy give lower bounds for particular greedy teaching-set constructions in 2025. They describe the universal conjecture as unresolved; limitations of those constructions are not counterexamples to the existence of small teaching sets.

The conjecture permits any universal constant, so examples separating the two dimensions by a fixed factor are compatible with it. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.

cards.title: Existence of one-way functions
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to \{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

cards.context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

One-way functions would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) nor any candidate’s hardness.

Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

cards.context:
Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.status_note: The full implication is explicitly open in the checked 2017 survey and Fall 2023 MIT lecture, but Li–Ni–Zan ePrint 2023/1260 explicitly claims a positive solution. This audit found the claim on 14 September 2026 and has not independently verified it or located a conclusive later verification or refutation. Status is therefore uncertain and the card remains active. The May 2026 MinRank result assumes a specific planted problem; oracle separations do not refute the unrelativized target.

The corrected Barak–Mahmoody author version proves the quadratic random-oracle query bound with explicit success loss; it withdraws the same quadratic claim for random permutations from the earlier manuscript.

Public-key encryption requires that anyone can encrypt with public information while a receiver can decrypt with a related secret key.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
cards.why: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.

cards.context:
Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.

cards.title: Exponential share-size lower bounds for perfect secret sharing
cards.formal:
An access structure specifies which groups of participants may recover a secret; a perfect scheme gives exact recovery to those groups and no information to all other groups. Precise definitions appear in Model & notation. Is the following proposition true?
\[
\exists c>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \exists\Gamma_n\subseteq 2^{[n]}:
\quad\forall\text{ perfect schemes for }\Gamma_n,\qquad
\max_{i\in[n]}\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the secret is one uniform bit, \(\Gamma_n\) is a monotone access structure with \(\varnothing\notin\Gamma_n\) and \([n]\in\Gamma_n\), and \(\mathcal S_i\) is participant \(i\)'s finite share alphabet. Here \(n_0\) is an integer, and the constants are universal. Sharing and reconstruction may be nonlinear and computationally unbounded.
cards.definitions:
A monotone access structure \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is a collection of authorized subsets such that \(A\in\Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) imply \(B\in\Gamma\).

A perfect scheme is a joint probability distribution of a uniform secret \(B\in\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_i\in\mathcal S_i\), where every \(\mathcal S_i\) is finite and nonempty. For each authorized \(A\), a deterministic map from \(\prod_{i\in A}\mathcal S_i\) to \(\{0,1\}\) recovers \(B\) with probability one. For every unauthorized \(A\), the distributions of \((X_i)_{i\in A}\) conditioned on \(B=0\) and on \(B=1\) are identical. Arbitrary joint distributions are allowed; there is no field or linearity restriction.

The cost of a share is \(\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\) bits, and the scheme's cost is the largest of these costs. This measures alphabet size, not Shannon entropy. Rounding to an integer encoding length does not change the exponential-existence question. The access structures need not be efficiently recognizable, and the schemes need not be uniformly constructible. The statement concerns all sufficiently large integer participant counts, with one positive constant \(c\) chosen first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified exponential lower bound, or a complete proof of its logical negation. A lower bound restricted to linear schemes or to bounded-complexity reconstruction does not meet the universal scheme quantifier. A merely superpolynomial lower bound does not establish the stated exponential bound.
cards.why: This asks whether some access-control policies inherently require exponentially large pieces of a one-bit secret, even with unlimited computation. It would distinguish an intrinsic information cost from limitations of the constructions currently available.

cards.context:
For a threshold policy, any sufficiently large group can recover a secret and smaller groups learn nothing. General policies can specify much less regular combinations of participants. The conjecture asks whether that freedom forces an exponential storage cost in the worst case.

Larsen and Simkin study the exponential lower-bound conjecture attributed to Beimel. Their theorem forces either large shares or a large description of reconstruction; it does not remove the reconstruction restriction needed for an unconditional share-size lower bound.

Recent linear and multilinear lower bounds concern schemes whose algebraic structure restricts the sharing or reconstruction maps. Such restrictions are absent here. The September 2026 multislices paper proves exponential lower bounds for a broad family covering known general constructions, rather than for all perfect schemes.

The upper-bound question TCS-0465 asks whether every policy admits shares with an exponent below one half. This lower-bound question asks whether some positive exponential exponent is unavoidable. Both propositions can hold simultaneously; they express different sides of the storage gap.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic communication for two-server private information retrieval
cards.formal:
Private information retrieval lets a user recover a selected database bit without revealing its index to either server. Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), a classical one-round two-server protocol with perfect correctness and perfect privacy has total communication at most
\[
C(\log_2 n)^k
\]
bits for every database \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), requested index \(i\in[n]\), and outcome of the user's randomness? The two servers each hold the entire database and do not communicate or collude. Model & notation specifies the protocol and exact privacy requirement. There is no computational hardness assumption or bound on local computation.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(n\), a protocol specifies a nonempty finite randomness set \(\mathcal R_n\), query maps \(Q_{1,n},Q_{2,n}\), deterministic answer maps \(A_{1,n},A_{2,n}\), and a deterministic recovery map \(D_n\). Queries and answers are finite binary strings. The user samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\mathcal R_n\), independently of the database, and sends \(q_j=Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) to server \(j\). The server sends back \(a_j=A_{j,n}(x,q_j)\). There is one query and one answer per server. The user starts with only \(n,i,r\), with no database-dependent advice or shared secret.

Perfect correctness means \(D_n(i,r,a_1,a_2)=x_i\) for every \(x,i,r\). Perfect privacy means that for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and all \(i,i'\in[n]\), the random strings \(Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) and \(Q_{j,n}(i',r)\) have identical distributions. Since answers are deterministic functions of a server's database and query, this also protects its entire view. The servers follow the protocol; robustness to false answers and confidentiality of the rest of the database from the user are not required.

The cost is the maximum of \(|q_1|+|q_2|+|a_1|+|a_2|\) over all \(x,i,r\), where \(|w|\) is the bit length of a string \(w\). Protocol descriptions may depend on \(n\) but not on \(x\) or \(i\). There is no uniformity or local-running-time restriction. The same constants \(C,k\) must work for every database size; they cannot grow with \(n\). Answers may contain more than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a protocol family and universal constants exist, or prove the logical negation. Privacy must be exact against each computationally unbounded individual server. The bound includes both queries and both answers in the worst case. Computational privacy, database-dependent client preprocessing, or a growing number of servers changes the target.
cards.why: Can keeping the address of a requested bit completely secret cost only a polynomial in the address length? This isolates the information cost of privacy from encryption assumptions, server computation and implementation details.

Dvir and Gopi give a one-round protocol with communication \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n}))\). This grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\), but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their Definition 1.1 supplies the exact correctness and privacy model used here.

Ghasemi and Kopparty explicitly identify polylogarithmic two-server communication as consistent with known lower bounds in their ITCS 2026 paper. Their lower bounds constrain a particular algebraic framework, not all protocols.

The October 2026 revision of Gupte and Ragavan improves communication for several fixed server counts. Its displayed bound at two servers still has the square-root logarithmic exponent above and does not reach the present polylogarithmic target.

TCS-7459 instead concerns computational privacy at a single server and the cost of preprocessing and answering queries. These are different models and objectives; neither card is merely a parameter change in the other.

context_blocks.text: With one server, perfect private retrieval of an arbitrary bit requires sending the whole database in the standard model. Two noncommunicating copies permit much smaller communication. The user can correlate the two queries while each query separately hides the requested index.

Dvir and Gopi give a one-round protocol with communication \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n}))\). This grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\), but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their Definition 1.1 supplies the exact correctness and privacy model used here.

Ghasemi and Kopparty explicitly identify polylogarithmic two-server communication as consistent with known lower bounds in their ITCS 2026 paper. Their lower bounds constrain a particular algebraic framework, not all protocols.

The October 2026 revision of Gupte and Ragavan improves communication for several fixed server counts. Its displayed bound at two servers still has the square-root logarithmic exponent above and does not reach the present polylogarithmic target.

TCS-7459 instead concerns computational privacy at a single server and the cost of preprocessing and answering queries. These are different models and objectives; neither card is merely a parameter change in the other.

cards.status_note: Targeted literature check on 6 November 2026 found no matching protocol or impossibility theorem. The October 2026 fewer-server result was checked separately. Computational PIR and protocols with client preprocessing do not resolve this unconditional, fresh-client model.

sentences: A user wants one bit from a database replicated at two servers that do not communicate.
Each individual server must learn nothing about which bit was requested.
The question asks whether one round can use only a fixed power of the logarithm of the database size in total bits.
Correctness and privacy are perfect, while local computation is unrestricted.
The known subpolynomial protocols leave a substantial gap to this communication target.
