cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal:
Does ordinary polynomial-hard decisional Learning With Errors imply indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, circular-security or leakage-resilience hypothesis?

Precisely, let \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) be the fixed classical nonuniform decisional-LWE assumption below, with prime modulus \(q(n)\ge n^4\) and Gaussian width \(n\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) assert the existence of the uniform classical probabilistic obfuscator defined below, with security against all classical polynomial-size circuit families. The proposition to establish or refute is the implication
\[H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\ \Longrightarrow\ I_{\mathrm{circ}}.\]
All modulus, error, sample, correctness and security quantifiers are fixed in the definitions. Neither subexponential hardness nor additional information supplied about the LWE secret or errors is part of the premise.
cards.definitions:
LWE assumption. For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(q(n)\) be the least prime at least \(n^4\), and let \(\mathbb Z_q\) mean integers modulo \(q=q(n)\). Define the probability distribution \(\chi_n\) on the integers by
\[\Pr_{e\leftarrow\chi_n}[e=t]=\frac{\exp(-\pi t^2/n^2)}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi j^2/n^2)}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).\]
The positive normalizing sum converges. This specifies an exact mathematical distribution; it is not an input consisting of real-number samples or a unit-cost real-arithmetic oracle.

For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(m=m(n)\), compare the following distributions:
\[X_n=(A,As+e\bmod q),\qquad Y_n=(A,u),\]
where \(A\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times n}\), \(s\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\), the \(m\) entries of \(e\) are independent samples of \(\chi_n\), and \(u\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). All these choices are mutually independent before forming \(As+e\); the same secret \(s\) is used in every row. Reduce each integer error modulo \(q\). Each residue is encoded as its canonical representative in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), using \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil\) bits, and the matrix and vector are fully listed. Public parameters \(n,m,q\) accompany the encoding. No leakage or other secret-dependent hint is given.

An ensemble pair is computationally indistinguishable if, for every family \((D_n)\) of classical Boolean circuits with description length bounded by some polynomial in \(n\),
\[\left|\Pr[D_n(X_n)=1]-\Pr[D_n(Y_n)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(n\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in the security parameter of each experiment. Circuit families need not be uniformly computable and may hardwire polynomially many advice bits. Deterministic distinguishers suffice here; private random coins can equivalently be allowed. The assertion \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) is indistinguishability for every such sample count and every such distinguisher family. This is asymptotic polynomial security, not a bound on the cost of attacks at a single numerical parameter.

Circuit model. A circuit has \(a\ge0\) labelled input bits, \(g\ge0\) gates in topological order, and \(b\ge1\) designated output wires. Gates are binary AND or OR, unary NOT, or constants 0 and 1. Wires may be reused. Gate predecessors must be inputs or earlier gates; each output names an existing input or gate. This defines a total deterministic function \(C:\{0,1\}^a\to\{0,1\}^b\). Constant gates are allowed as part of the conventional Boolean basis.

Use the explicit encoding \(1^a0\), then length-delimited counts \(U(g),U(b)\), followed by every gate and every output index. Here \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\). Each gate has a fixed three-bit type tag and the appropriate zero, one or two \(U\)-encoded predecessor indices. Input nodes come first, then gate nodes; unused tags and out-of-range indices are invalid. Each output is a \(U\)-encoded index, and trailing bits are forbidden. Define \(|C|\) to be the total description length. Thus every input, gate and output is explicitly counted; exponentially many undeclared inputs or succinctly generated gate lists are not allowed. Two circuits are equivalent when their input/output arities coincide and their outputs agree on every input, exactly.

Obfuscator. There is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(O\) and positive integers \(K,d\). On \((1^\lambda,C)\), for every integer \(\lambda\ge2\), it halts within \(K(\lambda+|C|+1)^d\) bit steps on every sequence of independent fair random bits. On a valid circuit it always returns a valid circuit with the same input/output arities, of description length at most the same polynomial bound. Malformed descriptions may be rejected, within the clock. All input reading, randomness, arithmetic and output writing are charged. There is no advice, quantum state, oracle, trusted setup or free preprocessing.

Functionality requires a uniform error bound over all circuits at each size scale. For every positive integer polynomial bound \(p\), there exists a negligible function \(\mu_p\) such that for every \(\lambda\ge2\) and valid \(|C|\le p(\lambda)\),
\[\Pr_r[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^a:\ O(1^\lambda,C;r)(x)=C(x)]\ge1-\mu_p(\lambda).\]
One successful output must be correct on all inputs simultaneously; a separate high success probability for each input is insufficient.

Indistinguishability requires that for every pair of circuit sequences \((C_{0,\lambda},C_{1,\lambda})\) of polynomially bounded description length, with equal description lengths, matching arities and equivalent functions for each \(\lambda\), and every classical polynomial-size distinguisher family \((D_\lambda)\), the advantage
\[\left|\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{0,\lambda};r))=1]-\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{1,\lambda};r))=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). The sequences themselves need not be efficiently generated. Distinguishers can hardwire the circuit pair and arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information. Variable-length outputs are presented with their length and zero padding to a common polynomial bound determined by the pair's size bound and the clock; actual length remains visible. Probabilities use fresh independent obfuscator coins. No efficiently verifiable certificate of circuit equivalence is supplied or required. The assertion \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) is existence of one machine and clock meeting both functionality and security for every polynomial size scale.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{circ}}\), or of its full logical negation. A positive construction must prove the stated uniform efficiency, simultaneous all-input functionality, and security against all nonuniform polynomial-size classical distinguishers using only the specified LWE premise and proved mathematical facts. Any parameter changes used inside a construction must be justified from that premise. The literal negation is \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\land\neg I_{\mathrm{circ}}\). Refuting one candidate, excluding only black-box reductions, or separating the notions in an oracle world does not establish this unrelativized negation. A construction needing stronger quantitative hardness, circular security or auxiliary-leakage resilience does not prove the specified implication unless those properties are themselves derived from the fixed premise.
cards.why: General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

cards.context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of the same function. It requires their obfuscations to be computationally indistinguishable when the original descriptions have equal size. It does not promise that a function hides information already revealed by its outputs, nor does it equate functionally different programs. These distinctions separate the mathematical notion from an informal claim that code is unreadable.

Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement: whatever can be learned from the code should be reproducible from oracle access to the function. Their revised full paper explicitly introduces the weaker indistinguishability comparison. Its impossibility result therefore does not supply a negative answer to this card.

LWE describes noisy linear equations over a finite residue field. The same hidden vector is used in all rows, while fresh independent errors perturb the products. Regev connects suitable LWE distributions to worst-case lattice problems by a quantum reduction. That historical foundation is evidence for studying LWE, not a proof of the exact classical nonuniform hardness hypothesis selected here. In particular, its rounded-Gaussian notation should not be silently identified with this card’s integer-Gaussian convention.

Jain, Lin and Sahai construct iO using four well-studied assumptions. The February 2026 journal theorem lists LWE, sparse-noise LPN over large prime fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and DLIN in bilinear groups. It requires subexponential security guarantees and a subexponential LWE modulus-to-noise ratio. Both the extra assumptions and the quantitative regime exceed the premise here. The journal publication follows earlier work; it is not a new LWE-only construction.

Their follow-up removes LWE from the sufficient set, leaving the other three assumptions. Its introduction explicitly raises the possibility that LWE alone might suffice. Removing one assumption from a conjunction does not show that the removed assumption implies the conclusion. The distinction between subexponential security for its iO theorem and polynomial security for its functional-encryption consequence also remains substantive.

The circular-security construction eliminates factoring and pairing assumptions, but its theorem still assumes subexponential LWE hardness together with a key-randomness circular form of shielded randomness-leakage security. The latter experiment provides structured information involving encryption keys and ciphertext randomness. Its Definition 7 is an additional security premise; plain noisy LWE samples do not contain these hints. The paper also repairs a gap in an earlier efficiency transformation.

Later lattice proposals continue to separate ordinary LWE from strengthened assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin explicitly introduce Circular Security with Random Opening, an LWE-with-hints assumption. Their abstract discusses attacks on earlier hint assumptions and presents the new proposal as a different target for cryptanalysis. No reduction from this card’s ordinary LWE premise is asserted in the inspected abstract.

Cini, Lai and Woo instead use NTRU and a new Equivocal LWE assumption alongside other lattice assumptions. Their abstract qualifies the post-quantum construction and identifies possible cryptanalytic targets. A construction based on lattice assumptions can be an important advance without establishing that plain LWE alone suffices.

The April 2026 authentication preprint, revised in June, likewise distinguishes several claims. Its lattice tool assumes decomposed LWE; its pseudorandom-obfuscation result additionally assumes subexponentially secure iO. A separate general-iO proposal is expressly labelled heuristic. Neither the extra-premise theorem nor that heuristic is a proof of the implication posed here.

The September 2026 trapdoor-function preprint assumes both iO and LWE for copy protection. Its separate LWE-only key-leasing result concerns another primitive. This recent application uses general iO as an input assumption rather than deriving it, so it does not close the source question.

This card retains the explicit editorial variant selected on 10 September: least-prime modulus at least n^4, integer Gaussian width n, polynomial sample counts, ordinary negligible-advantage security against classical nonuniform polynomial-size circuits, and a uniform classical obfuscator with negligible probability of any functionality error. cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(
u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le
u_s(\lambda)\). The probability includes key generation, fresh encryption coins for each bit, and evaluation coins. Eval’s time is polynomial in the entire supplied circuit and ciphertext encoding, with one algorithm for all C. There is one polynomial q, independent of C,t and s, bounding every evaluated ciphertext length and its decryption time by \(q(\lambda )\); keys also have polynomial length. The scheme must also correctly decrypt fresh encryptions. Multiple output bits mean separate output ciphertexts, so compactness scales linearly with output length. Only the usual one-evaluation correctness contract is required; no circuit privacy or additional guarantee for arbitrary malformed or previously evaluated ciphertexts is imposed. The assertion is an existence implication between these two primitives in the classical standard model; it permits non-black-box constructions and supplies no extra setup, ideal oracle, circular-security or number-theoretic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the existence implication, including the specified correctness, security and circuit-independent compactness bounds, or a Lean refutation of that implication. The target uses no supplied depth bound at key generation. An extra cryptographic premise or a separation restricted to black-box constructions does not settle this unrestricted implication.
cards.why: Determine whether computation over encrypted data requires fundamentally more than public-key confidentiality.

cards.context:
Public-key encryption permits confidential communication; fully homomorphic encryption additionally permits computation over ciphertexts. A general implication would make the stronger capability follow from the existence of the basic public-key primitive.

The cited black-box separation rules out deriving fully homomorphic encryption from even hierarchical identity-based encryption by that restricted type of construction. It therefore supplies a barrier and motivation, not a negative answer to an arbitrary non-black-box implication. The existing LWE-to-FHE card starts from a specific stronger assumption.

Key generation must work without a supplied circuit-depth bound, and decryption cost must remain independent of the evaluated circuit.
The scheme must remain secure with its evaluation key public.
Known black-box barriers and implications from additional primitives do not settle this unrestricted existence implication.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal:
In the ordinary classical computational model, is the following existence implication true?
\[\bigl(\exists f\;\operatorname{OWF}(f)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\operatorname{Gen},H\;\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\bigr).\]
The predicates are defined below. The honest functions and algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, and security is against every nonuniform family of polynomial-size classical Boolean circuits. The hash family has a freshly sampled public key \(k\) and maps \(H_k:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) for every positive integer security parameter \(\lambda\). Both members of a proposed collision may be chosen after the key is known. The implication permits unrestricted constructions and proof techniques, including use of a one-way function's implementation.
cards.definitions:
Parameters and computation. All strings are finite binary strings. The security parameters \(n,\lambda\) range over the positive integers, and \(1^n\) denotes the unary string of \(n\) ones. Honest algorithms are ordinary Turing machines with one fixed finite program, no advice and no oracles. Deterministic algorithms have polynomial bit running time in the total input length. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm additionally uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial running-time bound on every random tape; it therefore uses at most polynomially many random bits. The polynomial and its degree are fixed for each program, independent of the parameter and sampled inputs.

Adversaries. A nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) consists of finite acyclic Boolean circuits over AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with fan-in at most two and unrestricted fan-out. Size counts all gates and input and output wires, including random input wires. There are constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) such that each size is at most \(C(n+1)^d\). A randomized circuit receives independent uniform bits on its random wires. Circuit descriptions may be arbitrary functions of the parameter and the fixed public honest programs; no algorithm generating the family is required. They are fixed before the fresh challenge or hash key is sampled. Each family has its own polynomial bound.

Finite-string encoding. To supply a string \(z\) of length at most an integer bound \(P\) to a fixed-width circuit, use \(\operatorname{enc}_P(z)\): the binary representation of \(|z|\), padded to exactly \(\lceil\log_2(P+1)\rceil\) bits, followed by \(z\) and enough zero bits to fill a \(P\)-bit data field. Bounds used below are positive integer-valued polynomials. This encoding reveals the string and its length and adds only polynomial overhead. In particular, variable-length function outputs and public keys are not supplied as a length-regularity promise.

Negligibility. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in the security parameter of each experiment.
The threshold may depend on the exponent and the adversary, as well as on the fixed primitive. Security must hold eventually for every parameter, not merely on an infinite subsequence. No fixed inverse-polynomial or constant error is allowed.

One-way function. A candidate \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) is total and uniformly deterministic polynomial-time computable. Fix a positive integer-valued polynomial \(p\) bounding \(|f(x)|\) whenever \(|x|=n\). In its inversion experiment, sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), independently sample the circuit's random wires \(R\), and compute exactly once
\[Y=A_n(1^n,\operatorname{enc}_{p(n)}(f(X));R)\in\{0,1\}^n.\]
Define \(\operatorname{Inv}_{f,A}(n)=\Pr[f(Y)=f(X)]\). Then \(\operatorname{OWF}(f)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted family \(A\). Any preimage of the challenge of length \(n\) is accepted; recovery of the original \(X\) is not required. Restricting the circuit output to \(n\) bits only removes invalid answers, which could always be replaced by a fixed \(n\)-bit candidate. The choice of the polynomial padding bound does not change security because valid encodings with different bounds can be converted in polynomial time.

Publicly keyed hash family. A candidate consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time generator \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^\lambda,k,x)\). There is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial \(q\) such that every generated key has length at most \(q(\lambda)\). For every key in the support of the generator and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\), the evaluator outputs exactly \(\lambda\) bits. Write \(H_k(x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x)\) when the parameter is understood. No evaluator property is required for keys outside that support. The key need not be uniform over all strings; its actual distribution is the output of the generator. It is fully public, and evaluation needs no secret.

Collision experiment. Independently sample the generator's random tape \(S\) and the adversary's random wires \(R\), set \(k=\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda;S)\), and compute exactly once
\[(x,x')=B_\lambda(1^\lambda,\operatorname{enc}_{q(\lambda)}(k);R)\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\times\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}.\]
Define
\[\operatorname{Coll}_{\operatorname{Gen},H,B}(\lambda)=\Pr[x\ne x'\ \land\ H(1^\lambda,k,x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x')].\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted circuit family \(B\). The adversary can compute the public evaluator within its circuit budget and select both inputs as functions of the key. It does not receive the generator's private random tape. Fixed-width candidate outputs again lose no successful attacks.

Scope of the implication. Existence of any one-way function in this model is the only cryptographic hypothesis. The conclusion is existence of some secure hash family; it need not be a particular proposed transformation applied to every one-way function. There is no requirement that a single algorithm transform arbitrary program descriptions into hash-family descriptions. No random oracle, trusted setup, quantum computation, extra hardness assumption or stronger exponential-security requirement is supplied. The all-parameter, nonuniform security and exact factor-two compression conventions are retained from the inherited card.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the existence of the specified public-key generator and evaluator from the one-way-function hypothesis alone, including uniform polynomial-time computability, exact compression for every generated key, and negligible collision success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family. All transformations of parameters and security guarantees used in that proof must be justified. A proof may use function implementations and need not be black-box.

The logical negation requires proving both that a one-way function exists and that no hash family satisfying this model exists. For the latter assertion, every pair of uniform polynomial-time programs meeting the hash syntax must admit a permitted circuit family with nonnegligible collision probability. Equivalently, for each such pair there must be an adversary and a fixed \(c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) whose success exceeds \(\lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). Merely proving that a chosen construction fails, even for one secure one-way function, is insufficient.

An oracle world separating these primitives or an impossibility theorem restricted to black-box reductions establishes a barrier, not this ordinary-model negation. Target-collision resistance, resistance only to finding three or more colliding inputs, injective noncompressing functions, security only for uniform adversaries or only infinitely often, and constructions assuming quantitative product hardness do not meet the full conclusion. This is an exact yes-or-no implication, with no additive numerical tolerance on the security requirement.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

references.title: Black-Box Separation Between Multi-Collision Resistance and Collision Resistance
references.locator: ECCC TR26-046; manuscript 29 March, public record 5 April; full introduction, Theorems 1–2, §2.1 Definitions 6–7 and Theorem 15 checked; constant-K fully black-box hierarchy, not an unrelativized separation

cards.context:
A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing under stronger assumptions on simultaneously inverting independently sampled challenges. Their Theorem I.5 uses symmetric injective two-product functions whose batch inversion probability is at most \(2^{-n-\omega(\log n)}\) for polynomial-time attackers; a separate theorem treats noninjective functions under stronger quantitative hardness. Ordinary one-wayness only requires a negligible single-challenge inversion probability. The product assumption is therefore additional structure and security, not an established consequence of the hypothesis on this card.

Collision finding is also a total search problem: an explicitly represented shrinking circuit always has two distinct inputs with the same output, and a proposed pair can be checked efficiently. The published ITCS 2024 paper of Folwarczný and coauthors extends separation results to a restricted class of reductions for total NP search. Its main condition permits a single call to a total-search solver and no query to the one-way function before that call. The result includes semi-black-box reductions, but is still a limitation on a specified reduction model.

Mao and Zhang's March 2026 manuscript, published on ECCC in April, reports a further black-box hierarchy: for every fixed \(K\ge2\), \(K\)-collision resistance cannot be constructed fully black-box from \((K+1)\)-collision resistance in their model. Here an attacker seeks \(K\) distinct inputs with one common hash value. In particular, hardness of finding a triple does not give a black-box construction of hardness of finding a pair. The paper also separates distributional collision resistance from three-collision resistance. These are barriers among weaker primitives; the ordinary unrestricted implication from one-way functions remains open in the introduction.

Rothblum's July 2026 manuscript reports interactive arguments for deterministic computations taking time \(T\) and space \(S\), assuming one-way functions. The communication is \(S\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), the verifier time is \((S+n)\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), and the number of rounds is polylogarithmic in \(T\). Soundness loses a factor polynomial in \(T\) in the adversary-size bound. This weakens assumptions for an interactive application; its use of target-collision-resistant hashing does not supply full public-key collision resistance.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

source_formulation.text: Holmgren–Lombardi Question I.1 asks whether collision-resistant hashing can be based on an arbitrary one-way function. The inherited card selected the unrestricted ordinary-model existence implication, uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical security, fresh public keys and factor-two compression. These choices are preserved. The review specifies finite-string encodings, circuit randomness, negligibility and the exact logical negation; it does not replace the question by the already separated black-box construction problem.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The March/April 2026 primary multicollision paper explicitly leaves construction from general one-way functions open. It adds a fully black-box hierarchy, while the July interactive-argument result bypasses full collision resistance in a specific application. No unrestricted implication or ordinary-model refutation was found in the bounded primary-source search. Uniform honest programs, nonuniform classical adversaries, all-parameter negligible security and fresh public factor-two-compressing hashes remain the selected model; external proofs were not independently certified.

progress.text: Rompel obtains universal one-way hashing and secure signatures from arbitrary one-way functions; this uses the weaker target-before-key collision game.
Simon proves an oracle separation from one-way permutations, establishing the classical black-box obstacle.
Holmgren–Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing from quantitatively strong one-way product functions, an additional assumption.
Folwarczný and coauthors extend total-search barriers to specified single-query semi-black-box reductions; the preprint appears at ITCS 2024.

Mao–Zhang report a fully black-box separation between successive constant-multiplicity collision-resistance notions, including pair resistance from triple resistance. The unrestricted one-way-function implication remains open.
Rothblum constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions, without resolving the hashing implication.

sentences: The problem asks whether the existence of ordinary one-way functions implies a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family.
Honest algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, while security must hold against every polynomial-size nonuniform classical circuit family.
The hash compresses two security-parameter lengths to one, and an attacker chooses both colliding messages after seeing the freshly sampled public key.
A complete Lean proof must establish the unrestricted existence implication or prove its negation, including the existence of a one-way function and the failure of every eligible hash family.
Known oracle separations, stronger product-hardness constructions and the 2026 multicollision and interactive-argument results leave this ordinary-model implication unresolved.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
cards.why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.

cards.context:
A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
cards.definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.
cards.why: Public-key encryption protects a message from someone without its decryption key. Oblivious transfer must also protect a sender from a receiver who is entitled to learn one selected message, while hiding that selection from the sender. Determining whether the first capability already implies the second would clarify a basic boundary between secure communication and general private computation.

cards.context:
The two privacy obligations are different. The sender must not learn the receiver’s choice, and the receiver must not learn anything about the unselected message beyond what its allowed input and output already imply. Simulation expresses both requirements without assuming the messages themselves are random or secret from all prior information. Correctness is separate: a protocol that exchanges nothing may reveal nothing, but it does not deliver the selected bit.

Gertner and coauthors ask directly whether public-key encryption implies OT. Their positive results require additional oblivious-sampling properties of public keys or ciphertexts. Their negative result constructs an oracle relative to which encryption exists but even semi-honest OT does not. That theorem is a substantial restriction on relativizing construction methods; it is not an ordinary-world separation of the two existence statements.

The historical oracle theorem also has an explicit uniformity qualification. Its authors prove security and separation for probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries and state that extension to nonuniform circuit adversaries would require further work. The present card fixes nonuniform distinguishers, so the original theorem should not be presented as an exact separation for every quantifier in its definitions.

Allowing non-black-box techniques means a proof may use the actual finite descriptions of encryption algorithms. Replacing those algorithms by a freely chosen oracle can remove information that such a proof uses. An oracle barrier therefore cannot simply be reinterpreted as the negation of the unrestricted implication. The target also allows polynomially many rounds, so a barrier at a fixed small round count is insufficient.

Even passive-security OT is a powerful goal. Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box transformation from semi-honest OT to maliciously secure OT and then to general secure computation. Their formulation uses static corruption, standalone security and, for the stronger malicious task, simulators that may run in expected polynomial time. It does not promise fairness or delivery despite malicious abort. These are consequences in a specified model, not extra requirements silently added to this card.

Li, Zhang and Lin replace earlier oblivious-sampling conditions by public rerandomizability: given a public key, an algorithm can turn a ciphertext into a fresh one with the same plaintext. Their abstract gives OT constructions under this property. IND-CPA confidentiality by itself does not include such an algorithm, so the result covers an enriched encryption primitive.

The March 2026 updatable-encryption article likewise retains precise extra properties. Its two-round OT implication uses oblivious samplability of original ciphertexts and update tokens; its three-round implication uses oblivious samplability of updated ciphertexts. Updatable encryption is a structured symmetric encryption primitive with tokens for transforming ciphertexts across keys. The inspected theorem summaries do not start from an arbitrary IND-CPA public-key scheme.

The January 2026 Minicrypt preprint gives a particularly relevant distinction between a non-black-box implication and an oracle construction. Its abstract claims OT from a standard-model oblivious interactive hash function, and separately constructs that hash primitive in a random-oracle model. It explicitly says that these two statements cannot be composed into OT from a random oracle: the non-black-box step applies only to an ordinary finite implementation. No generic construction of that implementation from arbitrary PKE is claimed in the checked abstract.

The March 2026 stabilizer-decoding preprint gives another kind of progress: a new average-case hardness premise supports both PKE and OT. Having a common sufficient assumption does not show that either primitive follows from every implementation of the other. The additional algebraic structure of that decoding problem remains part of its construction’s foundation.

Fair coin tossing provides a related comparison. Maji and Wang prove limits on protocols that use PKE or key agreement as black boxes, whereas an OT resource supports the optimal fairness scale considered there. That result concerns a different functionality and a restricted construction model. It adds evidence about the hierarchy without resolving the unrestricted semi-honest OT implication.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

cards.context:
Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

source_formulation.text: The retained target is strict containment for total decision languages. In the inspected August 2019 edition of Wigderson, it is Conjecture 11.5, alongside Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2. Conjecture 11.4 in that edition concerns NP versus BQP; the older March 2018 numbering must not be carried over. The card keeps its finite H, T, CNOT basis and now gives explicit matrices, uniformity and measurement semantics.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

progress.text: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with the containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\); the inspected 2019 book states it as Theorem 11.2.
Shor’s polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms give major candidate advantages without an unconditional classical lower bound.
Boykin and coauthors prove universality of the finite Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT basis used here.
Raz–Tal establish a separation from the polynomial hierarchy relative to an oracle, preserving that oracle restriction.
Quantum publishes the shallow-circuit sampling separation, with explicit classical randomness/fan-in restrictions and a different output task.
A new oracle separates the promise-class comparison from the total-language comparison even when the language classes coincide.

sentences: BPP and BQP are classes of total decision languages with bounded error separately on every input, using classical randomness and quantum circuits respectively.
The quantum model uses one polynomial-time classical generator for finite H, T and CNOT circuits with auxiliary qubits initialized to zero and one final measured bit.
The question asks whether some quantum polynomial-time language has no classical randomized polynomial-time decider; the alternative is equality of the classes.
Factoring algorithms, oracle separations and shallow sampling lower bounds retain assumptions or output/resource differences that do not establish this full separation.
A September 2026 oracle result further distinguishes total-language equality from promise-class equality, while the ordinary total-language target remains unresolved in the inspected sources.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.

cards.context:
Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.
