cards.title: Weak automatability of Resolution
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?
cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. If a lower bound assumes a complexity separation, that separation must also be proved to settle the negative answer. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.
cards.why: Asks whether the existence of a short familiar refutation can make unsatisfiability efficiently recognizable even when finding a refutation in that same calculus is hard. This isolates an unresolved limitation of proof search and the theoretical analysis of SAT solvers.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

cards.context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and give each \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) probability \(2^{-n}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), with empty product one, and \[\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x),\qquad q_S=\widehat f(S)^2.\] These are real coefficients and \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}q_S=1\). Define \(\eta(0)=0\) and \(\eta(t)=t\log_2(1/t)\) for \(0<t\le1\), where \(\log_2 t=\ln t/\ln2\). Then \[H(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\eta(q_S).\] The sum includes the empty set and is not conditioned on nonempty spectral subsets or divided by the variance. For each \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) negate coordinate \(i\) and retain all other coordinates. Set \[I_i(f)=2^{-n}\bigl|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}\bigr|,\qquad I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n I_i(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|q_S.\] Influence uses an actual bit flip, with no additional probability of leaving that coordinate unchanged. All scalar Boolean functions are allowed; no balance, monotonicity, circuit-size, degree or efficient-computability promise is imposed. Constant functions satisfy \(H(f)=I(f)=0\). The inequality is non-strict, so it includes them.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal inequality for some positive finite constant, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must use the specified uniform measure, full squared spectrum, base-two Shannon entropy and total bit-flip influence for every \(n\) and every scalar Boolean function. A negative proof must establish \[\forall C>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\},\quad H(f)>C I(f).\] The dimension and function may depend on \(C\); equivalently, the entropy-to-influence ratios of nonconstant Boolean functions must be unbounded. Defeating one numerical constant or checking finitely many truth tables is insufficient. No optimal value of \(C\), algorithm for finding counterexamples or numerical approximation is required.
cards.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

cards.context:
A Fourier coefficient records correlation with a parity of selected input bits. Squaring these correlations gives a probability distribution on subsets of the coordinates. Its Shannon entropy measures dispersion among subsets; total influence is the expected cardinality of a subset from that distribution. The conjecture asks whether being the spectrum of a Boolean-valued function forces a universal linear relation between these two quantities.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

cards.title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Does there exist a positive integer \(C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(1\le d\le n\), and every real multilinear polynomial \(f\) in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\),
\[\bigl[\forall x\in\{-1,1\}^n,\ 0\le f(x)\le1\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists i\in[n]:\ \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)\ge\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C?\]
Variance and squared \(L_2\) influence use the uniform distribution on the entire Boolean cube, with the normalization below. The same exponent \(C\) must work for all dimensions, degrees, coefficients and variances.
cards.definitions:
Polynomials and domain. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\) for \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(\chi_{\varnothing}=1\). A real multilinear polynomial is a finite sum
\[f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\chi_S(x),\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R.\]
Multilinear means that each variable has exponent at most one in each monomial. Degree at most \(d\) means \(a_S=0\) whenever \(|S|>d\). The range restriction \(0\le f(x)\le1\) is required at every one of the \(2^n\) sign vectors. No range condition away from this cube is imposed.

Uniform averages and Fourier coefficients. For any real-valued function \(h\) on the cube, define \(\mathbb E h=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}h(x)\). The characters \(\chi_S\) give the unique multilinear representation on the cube, with
\[\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E[f(x)\chi_S(x)]=a_S.\]
In particular \(\widehat f(\varnothing)=\mathbb Ef\). Variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}(f)=\mathbb E[(f-\mathbb Ef)^2]=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
For the stated range, \(0\le\operatorname{Var}(f)\le1/4\).

Influence. Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be obtained from \(x\) by negating its \(i\)-th coordinate and leaving all others fixed. Set
\[D_if(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=\mathbb E[(D_if)^2]=\frac14\mathbb E[(f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i}))^2]=\sum_{S\ni i}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
This is a mean squared difference, not the probability that the two function values differ, their mean absolute difference, or the maximum change over inputs. All sums and expectations in the target use this same uniform measure.

Scope and quantifiers. Coefficients are arbitrary real numbers, without a rationality, description-length or computability restriction. The statement is an existence inequality, not a demand for an algorithm finding the coordinate. The coordinate may depend on the whole polynomial. No sparsity, block decomposition, common coefficient magnitude, Boolean-output, nonnegativity-of-coefficients or realizability-by-quantum-algorithms promise is present. There is no positive lower threshold on variance. Constant polynomials have zero variance and all influences zero, so every coordinate satisfies the inequality for them. The degree parameter is a positive upper bound, so division by zero never occurs.

Normalization of the exponent. Allowing any real \(C\ge1\) gives an equivalent assertion: for \(0\le v/d\le1/4\), increasing the exponent to a positive integer only decreases the right-hand side. A bound of the usual form \(c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^a/d^b\), with fixed positive constants \(c,a,b\), also yields this formulation after increasing \(C\). Thus the one-exponent statement records polynomial dependence without selecting a particular best exponent or a hidden constant depending on \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must prove one exponent works simultaneously for every allowed \(n,d,f\), including arbitrarily small positive variance. No optimal exponent or algorithm for computing an influential coordinate is required.

A negative answer must prove that for every positive integer \(C\) there exist integers \(n\ge1\), \(1\le d\le n\), and an admissible polynomial of positive variance such that
\[\forall i\in[n],\quad\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)<\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C.\]
The dimension, degree and polynomial may depend on \(C\). A rigorously specified family with those properties qualifies; a counterexample to just one proposed exponent does not negate the existence of another universal exponent. Numerical estimates must be certified strongly enough to establish the exact pointwise range and strict influence inequalities they assert.

A theorem only for Boolean-valued outputs, completely bounded forms, boundedly many quantum-query rounds, or a positive fraction of randomly restricted functions does not by itself cover the full polynomial class. An exponential dependence on degree is also weaker than the requested polynomial bound. This is a yes-or-no conjecture with an exact inequality, not a numerical target subject to additive 1/100 tolerance.
cards.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

cards.context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

A \(t\)-query quantum algorithm has acceptance probability represented on the Boolean cube by a real polynomial of degree at most \(2t\), with values in \([0,1]\). Aaronson and Ambainis prove that the influence conjecture would imply a classical estimate of this probability within additive \(\varepsilon\) on at least a \(1-\eta\) fraction of uniformly distributed inputs using \(\operatorname{poly}(t,1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)\) queries. The classical algorithm may depend on the quantum algorithm. This gives a concrete reason why a dimension-independent inequality for bounded polynomials matters to quantum computation.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

Complete boundedness imposes more than scalar boundedness. In a block-multilinear polynomial, each monomial contains at most one variable from each of several fixed blocks. Replace variables by square matrix contractions, meaning matrices whose Euclidean operator norm is at most one, and multiply factors in block order. The completely bounded norm is the supremum of the resulting operator norm over all such matrices and dimensions. Requiring this norm to be at most one can support influential-variable theorems, but it is an extra hypothesis not imposed on the polynomials in this card.

The published ITCS 2025 restriction theorem assumes \(d\ge2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\ge1/d\). Each coordinate is independently left free with probability \(\log(d)/(C_1d)\), and otherwise fixed to an independent uniform sign. For universal positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), the resulting function has a coordinate with influence at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)^2/d^{C_2}\) with probability at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\log(d)/(50C_1d)\). These are influences of the restricted function. The March 2026 revision retains both the restriction and original-variance assumptions; it does not establish the unrestricted claim.

Blanc, Docter, Strassle and Tan’s August 2026 theorem concerns quantum query rounds. A round applies parallel input queries between input-independent operations; the number \(r\) of rounds is distinct from the total \(t\) queries and from polynomial degree. Their classical query bound is \(2^{O(r^2)}(t\log(1/\eta)/\varepsilon)^{O(r)}\) for approximation error \(\varepsilon\) outside an \(\eta\) fraction of inputs. This is polynomial for fixed \(r\), but its exponent is not uniform over an unbounded number of rounds. The theorem neither treats every scalar bounded polynomial nor proves the full influential-variable conjecture.

The September 2026 theorem gives \(\sum_i\sqrt{\operatorname{Inf}_i(a)}\le t\|a\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\) for a polynomial with \(t\) blocks, summed over all variables. The constant is optimal, and the result permits nonadaptive classical queries in the associated restricted simulation. The authors expressly retain the unrestricted scalar conjecture as open. A small scalar norm does not supply the completely bounded norm hypothesis, so this sharper inequality is not a general resolution.

The 2019 Keller–Klein preprint once claimed a general proof, but the authors withdrew it on 2 December after a flaw in Lemma 5.3 invalidated the argument. The original abstract still contains the affirmative claim; its withdrawal notice is the controlling status information. It is not evidence that the conjecture has been established.

source_formulation.text: The inherited ITCS 2025 Conjecture 4 and Aaronson–Ambainis’s original Conjecture 6 ask for polynomially large influence in terms of variance and inverse degree. This card preserves its full scalar-polynomial scope, output interval [0,1], uniform sign cube, squared L2 influence, category and importance 96. The original source uses the bit cube and omits the factor 1/4 in its influence; changing cube coordinates preserves degree and this fixed normalization factor is absorbed by the unspecified exponent. Restricting the exponent to positive integers is equivalent, not an additional mathematical restriction.

cards.title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}\). A graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most \(|U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

cards.context:
Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width \(q\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected \(\varepsilon\). There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

references.locator: 12 July 2026 preprint, version 1; Theorem 1.1 concerns Unique-3-SAT and Corollary 1.2 general 3-SAT. The stated bounds are randomized; numerical certificates and imported analysis were not independently checked.

cards.context:
Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
cards.definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.
cards.why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every integer \(n\ge2\), every Boolean matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and every sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n\) supplied online, the algorithm outputs each \(Mv_t\) before receiving \(v_{t+1}\), and outputs \(Mv_n\) at the end, using at most
\[
 K n^{3-\varepsilon}
\]
word-RAM instructions in total on every execution, including preprocessing of \(M\), with probability at least \(2/3\) that all \(n\) output vectors are correct? Products are over the Boolean semiring:
\[
 (Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j\bigr).
\]
The OMv conjecture asserts a negative answer.
cards.definitions:
The input initially supplies \(n\) and all \(n^2\) entries of the fixed matrix \(M\), in row-major order. After the algorithm's initial preprocessing, vectors arrive one at a time in the order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Each vector is an arbitrary length-\(n\) bit string. The next vector is unavailable until the algorithm has finished returning the current vector's complete answer. The algorithm may preserve its computed state and earlier vectors, but cannot postpone an output to use future inputs. There is no per-query time bound beyond the total bound and these deadlines.

Both the matrix bit string and each input vector are explicitly packed into consecutive words with known zero padding. An output vector contains its \(n\) bits in coordinate order; an explicit array with one Boolean value per word is an allowed canonical output representation. Returning an implicit circuit, a pointer to uncomputed answers, a count of nonzero entries or just one queried coordinate is insufficient. All input access and output writes are charged. The matrix never changes. The operations \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) mean Boolean AND and OR; this is neither arithmetic multiplication over the reals nor multiplication over the field of two elements.

The computation is a sequential word RAM with
\[
 w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
\]
bits per word and one fixed finite program for all \(n\). Memory cells, registers and addresses are word-sized. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Multiword computations cost their component instructions. An independent uniform random \(w\)-bit word can be generated in one instruction. This permits deterministic algorithms as a special case. There are no quantum instructions, nonuniform advice, free precomputed tables or input-dependent oracles. Unused memory initially contains zero.

All instructions are counted, including construction of auxiliary tables, allocation or initialization performed by the program, preprocessing before the first vector, work between vectors, generation of random words, copying and output. There is no separate allowance for an arbitrary polynomial preprocessing phase. Space has no additional sublinear or near-linear restriction, but every address must fit in a word and writing any used state costs instructions. Only the currently supplied input is made available by the online interface; it supplies no information about a future vector.

For the success guarantee, the matrix and complete vector sequence are fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. The probability is over the program's random words, and the successful event requires every bit of every output to be correct. A separate success probability of \(2/3\) for each individual query is not the specified joint guarantee. The time bound holds for every random execution, including erroneous executions. Every output deadline and eventual termination must likewise be met on every execution.

The constants \(\varepsilon,K,B\) and the program are chosen once, independently of the input dimension and contents. Any fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) suffices. A merely logarithmic or subpolynomial improvement in total time is not a fixed exponent saving. No restriction to combinatorial algorithms is imposed: every algorithm implementable by the specified word-RAM instructions is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated algorithm exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist.

A positive answer must establish the fixed exponent saving after charging preprocessing and all input/output work, the online deadlines, and joint success for every fixed input. It refutes the OMv conjecture in this model. A negative answer must exclude every admissible uniform randomized program, every fixed word-size constant and every positive exponent saving. It proves the conjecture in this model and cannot assume the conjecture itself or another unproved hardness hypothesis.

An algorithm for structured matrices, an offline matrix product, a query bound after uncharged preprocessing, or a cell-probe bound with free computation does not meet the target without a proved extension. Neither does a speedup of the form \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), which supplies no fixed positive saving in the exponent.
cards.why: The conjecture supports many precise lower bounds for dynamic graph and data-structure problems. A general truly subcubic online algorithm would overturn these conditional barriers, while an unconditional lower bound would explain a shared obstacle to faster dynamic algorithms.

cards.title: Subexponential-time Circuit-SAT
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), an integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(\lim_{n\to\infty}g(n)/n=0\), such that \(A\) decides satisfiability of every explicitly given Boolean circuit with \(n\ge1\) input variables and \(s\ge0\) gates in at most
\[
K\,2^{g(n)}(N+1)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(N\) is the full binary encoding length, gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT, and depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The output must be correct on every circuit. The requested bound is abbreviated \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(N)\); its exponential parameter is the number of input variables, not the number of gates or encoding bits.
cards.definitions:
Use the [De Morgan circuit basis](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) with \(n\) input variables, free constants 0 and 1, and one designated output. A supplied circuit has size \(s\), the number of its operation gates. An input, constant or gate may serve as the output. Depth, fan-out and the growth of \(s\) with \(n\) are unrestricted. The polynomial overhead exponent \(d\) is fixed across all these sizes.

For an assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), evaluate gates in topological order using ordinary Boolean operations. Satisfiability means that at least one such assignment gives output 1. The algorithm returns exactly this yes/no answer; it need not count or enumerate satisfying assignments. All declared input nodes are explicitly listed and included in \(n\), even if some are unused.

Use the [self-delimiting integer code](definitions.html#sat-encoding). List the codes of \(n,s\), then \(n\) input-node markers, and then the \(s\) gates in a topological order. Number the constants 0 and 1 first, the inputs next and the gates last. Each gate has a two-bit type tag and coded predecessor indices, all smaller than its own index. Finish with the coded output-node index, with no trailing data. Invalid encodings are outside the domain. The total length \(N\) is \(O((n+s)\log(n+s+2))\); the polynomial factor pays for processing the entire explicit description.

The algorithm is one classical deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice, no oracle and no random bits. All input processing, intermediate bit computation and output are charged. The constants, function and program are chosen before the input: the quantifier order is \(\exists(A,d,K,g)\;\forall C\), subject to the displayed limit on \(g\). In particular, \(g\) depends only on \(n\), and \(d\) cannot grow with circuit size or an accuracy parameter. The limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an integer \(N\) such that \(g(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Thus one fixed saving \(2^{(1-\delta)n}\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\) does not by itself meet this target.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply a single deterministic algorithm, prove exact decision correctness on every encoded circuit, and prove the full charged running-time bound with fixed \(d,K\) and \(g(n)/n\to0\). A negative answer must unconditionally rule out every such algorithm and bound; a lower bound conditional on another conjecture establishes only that conditional statement.

An algorithm restricted to linear-size circuits, bounded depth, formulas or a fixed clause width does not establish this universal target. A running time subexponential only in \(N\) or \(n+s\), or a fixed positive saving in the coefficient of \(n\), also does not suffice. This is a genuine existence question, not a numerical request to approximate an infimum running-time exponent.
cards.why: Determining whether general circuit satisfiability admits a vanishing exponential rate would identify a fundamental boundary of exact algorithms, beyond fixed improvements to exhaustive search or restrictions to simple circuit families.

cards.context:
Circuit satisfiability asks whether a Boolean computation accepts any assignment to its inputs. The 2013 Dagstuhl report distinguishes its exponential-time behavior from that of formulas whose clauses have bounded width, despite their polynomial-time equivalence.

Williams proves conditional connections between satisfiability running times at different circuit sizes, including consequences giving subexponential algorithms for smaller circuits. These are implications from algorithmic assumptions, not an unconditional algorithm meeting this card.

This target implies the positive answer to TCS-7270, which asks only for a fixed exponential saving at each fixed linear gate density. The converse is not asserted: the present question requires a vanishing exponential rate and covers general gate counts.

An October 2026 OpenAI preprint claims subexponential counting for each fixed clause width. That theorem is stated for formulas in conjunctive normal form, meaning conjunctions of clauses that are disjunctions of literals (variables or their negations). It is not stated for general circuits measured by their original input variables. Introducing a variable for each gate can increase the variable count to \(n+s\), so that conversion alone does not establish the bound requested here. The preprint is recorded as a claim; its proof and formalization were not independently audited in this addition.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm{P}.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). The deterministic program and its fixed time bound may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or length. All input access, arithmetic and output count in the [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model).

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm{P}.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

cards.context:
A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm{P}\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm{L}?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
cards.definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{L}\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm{L}.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.

cards.context:
Logarithmic memory is enough for a constant number of input-position counters but not for storing an arbitrary long random history. Fresh coins can guide the computation without remaining available afterward. Allowing the machine to freely revisit an entire random string changes the resource model, which is why the random-access convention is part of the question.

Saks and Zhou obtained deterministic simulation in \(O((\log n)^{3/2})\) space. Hoza’s Theorem 1.6 improves this to
\[O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\). This remains larger than \(O(\log n)\). These are space bounds; they do not assert that the improved-space simulation also runs in polynomial time.

A read-once branching program is a finite layered computation: each newly read random symbol selects a transition to the next layer, and a designated final state determines the answer. Its width is the number of states per layer and its length is the number of symbols read. This represents the random part of a bounded-space computation after the ordinary input is fixed. Restricted transition structures or unusually short programs need not capture every BPL computation.

An ordinary pseudorandom generator approximates acceptance probabilities using a genuine distribution generated from a short uniform seed. A weighted generator instead associates possibly negative real weights with seeds and approximates acceptance through a signed weighted average. Such estimates can be useful for derandomization, but they are not themselves sampling probabilities. Improving weighted generators does not automatically supply an ordinary generator with identical parameters.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.
cards.why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

cards.context:
A branching program models a stream computation that remembers only its current state. Its width \(w\) permits roughly \(\log_2 w\) memory bits, while its length \(n\) counts inspected input bits. The quantifiers require one distribution that works simultaneously for every allowed transition table. Computing a favorable distribution after seeing a particular table would answer a different question.

Short-seed distributions exist nonconstructively; in particular, seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) is known for width-\(n\), length-\(n\) programs. The unresolved issue is explicit computation with the required space bound. An optimal ordinary generator of the kind requested here would imply \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\), the equality of deterministic and bounded-error randomized logarithmic-space decision classes. The card does not assert the converse implication.

The classical general bound is \(O(\log n\cdot\log(nw/\varepsilon))\) seed bits. For polynomial width and constant error, this becomes \(O(\log^2 n)\), whereas the requested bound is \(O(\log n)\). The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.
