cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
cards.definitions:
Write \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) for all binary strings of length \(n\). A probability distribution on this finite set is any function \(p:S_n\to[0,1]\) with real values and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\). Its min-entropy is
\[
H_\infty(p)=-\log_2\!\left(\max_{x\in S_n}p(x)\right).
\]
Thus the required entropy condition means \(p(x)\le 1/(2^C n)\) for every string \(x\). Distributions need not be uniform on their support, rational, computable or efficiently samplable. Independence means that the joint distribution is \(\Pr[X=x,Y=y]=p(x)q(y)\). The output probability in the question is the finite sum
\[
\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]=\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\,\mathbf1_{\{E_n(x,y)=1\}}.
\]
The indicator is one when its subscripted condition holds and zero otherwise. For a single output bit, the displayed bias is its statistical distance from the uniform bit, where statistical distance between distributions \(r,s\) on a finite set is \(\frac12\sum_z|r(z)-s(z)|\). There is no conditioning on either source in this guarantee.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and fixed finite tape alphabet. Its read-only input is \(1^n\#x\#y\), where \(|x|=|y|=n\), and its work tapes initially contain blanks. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol on each tape and moves each tape head by at most one cell, costing one step. There are no random coins, oracle calls, auxiliary seed, advice or length-dependent precomputed tables. The machine must halt and output exactly one bit on every such input. There must be integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that this takes at most \(K(n+1)^d\) transitions for all \(n,x,y\), including inputs at lengths with no eligible sources. The input contains no distribution description or samples other than \(x,y\); \(C,K,d\) and the machine are fixed existential choices, independent of both distributions and of \(n\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be the class of all machines meeting this total polynomial-time evaluation condition, and write \(E^A_n\) for the function computed by a member \(A\).

Only the probability bound concerns the random choice of the two input strings; the evaluator itself is deterministic. When \(\log_2n+C>n\), no eligible distribution exists, so the extraction requirement at that length is vacuous. Using a nonnegative integer for the existential additive constant fixes a harmless convention: any fixed real constant can be increased to such an integer. The task has one output bit and fixed error \(1/100\); it does not demand arbitrarily small error, more output bits or resilience to tampering.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence proposition, including one finite machine, its uniform polynomial-time bound and the probability guarantee for all eligible distributions. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: for every integer \(C\ge0\) and every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there exist \(n\ge1\) and distributions \(p,q\) on \(S_n\), each having min-entropy at least \(\log_2n+C\), for which
\[
\left|\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\mathbf1_{\{E^A_n(x,y)=1\}}-\frac12\right|>\frac1{100}.
\]
In this negation the length and distributions may depend on the machine and additive constant. A construction requiring \(c\log_2n\) entropy for an unspecified constant \(c>1\), nonuniform existence alone, or a conditional implication does not establish the displayed unconditional target.
cards.why: The additive threshold asks whether polynomial-time evaluation can match the entropy scale available without an efficiency restriction, including its leading coefficient. It is a basic question about converting two independent imperfect sources into a nearly unbiased bit and has consequences for explicit Ramsey constructions.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. Use [FPT and FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized). Here the parameter is the requested clique size \(k\). The languages reducible to this parameterized Clique problem form \(\mathrm{W}[1]\). Hence an FPT algorithm for Clique is equivalent to \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

cards.context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from \(\varepsilon\) to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

references.title: Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness Under ETH!
references.authors: Divesh Aggarwal; Rishav Gupta; Aditya Morolia; Chuanqi Zhang
references.locator: ICALP 2026, Article 8, published 1 July 2026; Definition 2.10 distinguishes deterministic/randomized ETH, Definition 2.11 separates Gap-ETH, and Theorems 1.1–1.2 specify the different lattice consequences.

cards.context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi define the exponential rates of bounded-width satisfiability and relate positive rate at width three to positive rates at other fixed widths. These are structural results about the hypothesis, not a proof of it.
The authors’ IPEC survey explicitly defines ETH by a positive infimum and distinguishes the number of variables from the complete input length.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook retains the positive-infimum definition, explains its distinction from ruling out a single subexponential algorithm, and gives consequences for parameterized complexity.

Liu gives a deterministic \(1.32793^n\) upper bound for 3-SAT up to polynomial factors, recorded in the checked March 2020 revision of the ICALP 2018 work. This leaves the positivity of the optimal rate unresolved.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia and Zhang derive new lattice approximation hardness under ETH or randomized ETH, with different assumptions for their closest-vector and shortest-vector results. The paper still treats these as assumptions and distinguishes Gap-ETH.

sentences: ETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rate for 3-SAT is strictly positive.
The exponential parameter is the number of distinct variables, while polynomial factors account for the complete encoded input.
One positive rate must obstruct every algorithm, and refutation permits different algorithms for arbitrarily small positive rates.
Known exponential-time algorithms provide upper bounds but no positive lower bound on the optimum.
The hypothesis supports quantitative lower bounds throughout exact and parameterized algorithms without being established by those conditional consequences.

cards.title: Strictness of the W-hierarchy
cards.formal:
Is the \(W\)-hierarchy strict at every positive level?
\[
\forall\,t\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad
W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1].
\]
The classes use uniform deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions and exact-weight satisfiability of bounded-depth Boolean circuits, as defined below. Equivalently, for every \(t\ge1\), is there a parameterized decision problem in \(W[t+1]\) that does not belong to \(W[t]\)?
cards.definitions:
A parameterized decision problem is a set \(P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\mathbb N\). An input is a finite binary string \(x\) together with a nonnegative integer \(k\), its parameter. The input length \(L\) includes both \(x\) and the binary encoding of \(k\), with delimiters. Membership is an exact yes/no question.

Use [FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized) in the deterministic [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model). Both the input and output parameters belong to the encoded pairs. Time includes writing the target instance.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with at least one input node and a designated output node of outdegree zero. Nodes of indegree zero are distinct Boolean input variables. Each other node is either a NOT gate of indegree one or an AND or OR gate of indegree at least two, with the usual Boolean semantics. Gates have unrestricted fan-out. A gate is large if its indegree exceeds two. The depth of the circuit is the maximum number of edges on a path from an input node to the designated output. Its weft is the maximum number of large gates on such a path. Unused input nodes are allowed and still count among the input variables.

For an explicit encoding, order all \(N\) nodes topologically, put the \(n\) input nodes first, and give the integers \(n,N\) and the output-node index, followed by each remaining gate's type, indegree and list of distinct predecessor indices. Predecessors must have smaller indices. Encode each integer \(u\ge0\) by \(1^{h}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary representation of \(u+1\) and \(h=|w|\); encode gate types NOT, AND, OR by integers \(1,2,3\). All listed integers use this code, and there are no trailing bits. Invalid encodings are no-instances in the circuit problems below.

For fixed integers \(t,d\ge1\), let \(\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\) be the parameterized problem consisting of pairs \((C,k)\) where \(C\) is an encoded circuit of weft at most \(t\) and depth at most \(d\), and some assignment to its input nodes has exactly \(k\) ones and makes its output one. The parameter is \(k\) alone. Circuits exceeding either structural bound, or having fewer than \(k\) input nodes, are no-instances.

Define
\[
W[t]=\{P:\ \exists\,d\ge1\text{ such that }P
\text{ has a fixed-parameter many-one reduction to }
\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\}.
\]
The integer \(d\) may depend on the problem \(P\) and level \(t\), but it is a fixed constant independent of the input and its parameter. The reduction may also depend on \(P,t,d\). This quantifier does not allow depth growing as a function of \(k\).

The inclusions \(W[t]\subseteq W[t+1]\) follow directly from the weft bounds. Strict inclusion means that at least one problem belongs to the larger class and not the smaller one. The formal target quantifies over all fixed positive integers \(t\); it does not require an algorithm that constructs witnesses from \(t\).

Separating \(\mathrm{FPT}\) from \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) would leave the requested adjacent-level separations to be proved.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1]\) for every integer \(t\ge1\), with the classes and reductions above; or supply a complete Lean-checked refutation, proving \(W[t]=W[t+1]\) for at least one particular \(t\ge1\). A proof for just finitely many strict inclusions does not establish the universal positive answer. Completeness or hardness for one of these classes, an oracle-relative separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle the target. No claim about collapse of all other levels is required for a negative answer.
cards.why: Parameterized completeness places many natural problems into different levels of a common hierarchy, but a level label alone does not prove a difference in computational power. Establishing strictness would show that these levels capture distinct forms of parameterized intractability. An equality would instead identify a new general reduction principle connecting problems currently treated as having different complexity.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
cards.definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

cards.context:
Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
cards.definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation for this card.

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph asks whether a prescribed number of vertices can capture a constant fraction of the greatest possible internal connectivity. Its approximation landscape is a central gap between available algorithms, conditional hardness and what follows from the usual P-versus-NP assumption. The answer also matters for several graph optimization objectives linked to its approximability.

cards.context:
The exact cardinality makes the objective distinctive. A large region of moderate density can be an excellent answer when size is unrestricted or only bounded below, yet it need not contain a k-vertex region with a comparable fraction of the optimum for exactly k. The card asks for the actual selected vertices, so evaluating a continuous objective or estimating an optimum is insufficient.

Bhaskara and coauthors give an \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Their paper includes a deterministic combinatorial algorithm. Its title’s \(O(n^{1/4})\) endpoint requires quasipolynomial \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time in that analysis. The 2026 AAAI paper still describes the quarter-power-plus-epsilon bound as the general polynomial-time benchmark; neither bound is a universal constant.

Manurangsi proves that the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out polynomial-time approximation within \(n^{1/(\log\log n)^c}\) for some universal \(c>0\). The paper states ETH as the absence of a deterministic \(2^{o(m)}\)-time algorithm for 3SAT with \(m\) clauses. Its hard YES instances contain a \(k\)-clique, a property called perfect completeness. The result already excludes every fixed approximation constant if ETH holds, but ETH is an unproved assumption stronger than \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

The corresponding conclusion under only P≠NP remains a different issue. The May 2026 at-least-k paper explicitly says that even NP-hardness of a 1.001 approximation for Densest k-Subgraph is not known. This is consistent with the ETH lower bound: different hypotheses support different conclusions. A proof of conditional hardness is significant evidence, but does not establish the unconditional negative answer required by the card.

Chuzhoy and coauthors propose a Low-Degree CSP conjecture. Together with \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), it would exclude a polynomial-time \(2^{(\log n)^\varepsilon}\)-approximation for some \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Their stated consequence uses Cook-type reductions, which may make multiple oracle queries. The work also connects graph partitioning, dense coloring and other graph objectives, sometimes with quasipolynomial reductions. These are qualified conditional relationships rather than constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences.

The 2012 integrality gaps demonstrate limitations of specified strong semidefinite relaxations. They exhibit a separation between what a relaxation permits and the objective attained by genuine selected vertices. Such a separation constrains approximation arguments based on that relaxation; it does not rule out every polynomial-time algorithm.

Jones and coauthors give further Sum-of-Squares lower bounds in a planted-subgraph distinction model for \(k\le\sqrt n\). Their Theorem 1.1 constructs high-degree pseudoexpectations on random graphs, with approximately correct first-moment cardinality and normalization. These are the theorem’s particular relaxation constraints; they should not be silently replaced by all exact cardinality identities. This adds evidence about a broad algorithmic framework without proving unrestricted constant-factor hardness.

The AAAI 2026 continuous formulation is exact in a different sense. Under a sufficient penalty, its global optima correspond to the combinatorial problem, with an additional local-optimum correspondence. The accompanying convergence result controls a criticality residual under its stated algorithmic conditions. It does not guarantee a global optimum or a fixed approximation ratio on every input. Practical optimization progress can therefore coexist with the unresolved worst-case target.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi show that the absence of every constant-factor DkS approximation would rule out a \((3/2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for the at-least-k density problem, for each \(\varepsilon>0\). Their latter objective is edges per selected vertex and permits more than \(k\) vertices. Its known constant-factor algorithms do not solve the exactly-k problem.

The August 2026 preprint of Grigorescu and Taziki claims a linear-time approximation scheme for the unrestricted density objective. It also gives a near-linear-time at-least-k result with value at least \((1/2-\varepsilon)\) of that objective’s optimum. Both statements permit a different feasible cardinality from this card. They are relevant recent progress, but neither is a claimed resolution of its constant-factor question.

cards.title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).
cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in L\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin L\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

cards.context:
Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

cards.title: Four-thirds approximation for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every symmetric rational metric TSP instance \(I\) defined below, always returns a feasible tour and satisfies \[\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le\frac43\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] Running time must be polynomial in the full distance-matrix encoding length on every random execution. The guarantee is against the optimum integral tour, with no restriction to a particular linear relaxation or rounding method.
cards.definitions:
An input \(I\) consists of an integer \(n\ge3\) and the full explicitly listed matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), with
\[
 d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)=d(j,i)>0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad
 d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}).
\]
Integers are binary encoded, and a rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L(I)\) be the full binary encoding length, including all entries and their delimiters. There is no promise of an embedding, a graph representation, bounded aspect ratio or a restricted metric family.

A feasible output is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its tour cost includes the closing edge:
\[
 \operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)),
 \qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).
\]
The positive number \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum of this cost over all permutations.

An algorithm is one uniform classical randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. For some polynomial \(p\), on every valid input and every random tape it halts within \(p(L(I))\) steps and outputs a feasible tour. Its program is finite and independent of the input length; no input-length advice, external oracle or uncharged real arithmetic is available. The runtime bound is worst-case over the coins, although approximation quality is measured in expectation over those coins. Deterministic algorithms are included.

A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and polynomial bound \(p\) with
\[
 \mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)
 \quad\text{for every valid }I.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial may depend on the fixed value \(r\), but not on the particular input or its unknown optimal tour. There is no requirement of an effective procedure that takes \(r\) and produces the algorithm. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty by known constant-factor algorithms, so its infimum is a finite number at least one. The infimum need not itself be achievable.

This quantity compares efficient algorithms with the integral tour optimum. It is distinct from the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the optimum of the subtour linear program. An integrality-gap example is not by itself a lower bound against every algorithm. A result for one rounding method, a bounded number of vertices, graph metrics, Euclidean metrics or a special class of fractional solutions does not determine this unrestricted algorithmic infimum.

For the context, put \(\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}=\inf\mathcal R\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the set of achievable factors defined above. No complexity assumption is imposed. A hardness argument conditional on an unproved assumption does not by itself refute the algorithmic assertion.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm always outputs a feasible tour and has expected cost at most \(4\operatorname{OPT}/3\) on each input, or refute the existence of such an algorithm.
cards.why: Determine the fundamental efficient-approximation limit of the canonical routing problem, beyond the guarantees of any one linear relaxation or rounding algorithm.

cards.context:
The 2021 breakthrough establishes a universal expected approximation strictly below \(3/2\), after decades at that threshold. Its theorem compares the returned tour with the optimal integral tour, matching this card’s denominator.

The later derandomization gives a deterministic guarantee below \(3/2\). Thus the current progress is not confined to algorithms with only an expected runtime bound.

The 2024 analysis records the explicit ratio \(3/2-2.18\cdot10^{-34}\). This improves a universal upper bound, but does not determine the best achievable ratio to absolute precision \(1/100\).

Approximating within any fixed factor strictly below \(123/122\) is NP-hard in the cited theorem. Such a hardness statement does not itself prove an unconditional numerical lower bound on the infimum over randomized polynomial-time algorithms.

The July 2026 \(10/7\) guarantee applies to half-integral cycle-cut instances. It does not give that ratio for every metric in this card.

A September 2026 preprint claims a larger universal saving above \(2.05522\cdot10^{-30}\) below \(3/2\). Its statement was checked, but its proof and numerical certificate were not independently audited. Even the claimed upper bound is far from a two-sided determination within \(1/100\).

cards.title: Deterministic k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite or infinite metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points, and every initial configuration \(C_0\in M^k\), do there exist a deterministic online rule \(A\) and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) such that \[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma;C_0)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\] for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)? Both parties have exactly \(k\) servers and start at \(C_0\); movement cost is the sum of distances in the model below. The rule and additive constant may depend on the metric and initial placement, but not on the future requests.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), define the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. 

A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(k\), metric and initial configuration, a deterministic online rule and a finite additive constant give the stated \(k\)-competitive bound on every sequence. To refute it, fix one such setting and defeat every rule and additive constant.
cards.why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

cards.context:
On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The selected target is the classical conjecture asserting an actual \(k\)-competitive rule. It implies \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\), but an infimum value alone need not give endpoint attainment. The September 2026 preprint claims the actual competitiveness statement; its proof-review caveat is retained below.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. cards.title: Matroid secretary conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), there is a randomized online selection strategy \(\mathcal A_M\) satisfying
\[\forall w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0},\qquad
\mathbb E_{\pi,U}\!\left[\sum_{e\in S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)}w(e)\right]
\ge\frac1C\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)?\]
The element weights are fixed adversarially before a uniformly random arrival permutation \(\pi\) and the strategy's independent randomness \(U\) are chosen. Each acceptance decision is irrevocable and must preserve independence. The same \(C\) must work for all matroids and all weights.
cards.definitions:
A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set \(E\) and a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) of independent sets with two properties. First, \(B\subseteq A\in\mathcal I\) implies \(B\in\mathcal I\). Second, if \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). In particular, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\). Loops, zero weights, ties and the empty ground set are allowed. The matroid rank is \(\max_{I\in\mathcal I}|I|\).

The strategy knows \(E\) and \(\mathcal I\) in advance, including all element identities and \(n=|E|\), but has no information about the weights of unarrived elements. At step \(t\), it sees the identity \(\pi(t)\) and its finite real weight \(w(\pi(t))\). Before the next arrival, it chooses to accept or reject that element. Its decision may use only the known matroid, the revealed prefix, its previous decisions and its random seed. An accepted element cannot subsequently be discarded, and a rejected element cannot subsequently be accepted. Every accepted prefix must belong to \(\mathcal I\), for every input, arrival order and seed. The notation \(S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)\) denotes the final accepted set.

A randomized strategy is a measurable nonanticipating decision rule; one may model its private randomness by \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), independent of \(\pi\). The permutation is uniform among the \(n!\) permutations of \(E\) and independent of the fixed weight assignment. Expectations include these two sources of randomness. For every fixed assignment the optimum is finite, so the expected reward is well-defined and finite. If all feasible weights are zero, the inequality still applies with a zero right-hand side.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C\;\forall M\;\exists\mathcal A_M\;\forall w\). A strategy cannot be selected after seeing the weight assignment. The guarantee has no additive loss, no dependence of \(C\) on size or rank, and no high-probability requirement beyond the stated expectation. There is no restriction on computation, preprocessing or independence queries. This is the competitive-existence question in the known-matroid model, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights; no finite encoding or polynomial running time is appended.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed constant-competitiveness proposition, or of its full logical negation. A positive proof must give a finite universal constant and admissible strategies with the expected guarantee for every matroid and weight assignment. A negative proof must show that for every proposed finite constant some matroid defeats every admissible strategy on some fixed nonnegative weight assignment. A result for a restricted matroid family, randomly assigned weights, or a constant depending on rank does not settle this target. A newly posted proof claim is not itself a Lean-checked answer.
cards.why: This is a central question about the power of random arrival order in online selection under general independence constraints. A universal bound would apply across all matroids and is equivalent, through established reductions, to a general random-order contention-resolution guarantee.

cards.context:
The classical secretary task chooses one item whose unknown value is revealed on arrival. Matroids extend the feasibility rule to collections of items. For example, a uniform matroid permits any set up to a prescribed size, while a graphic matroid permits sets of edges containing no cycle. The offline optimum knows every weight; the online strategy sees only a random prefix at each decision.

Random arrival order and random assignment of weights are distinct sources of information. In the random-assignment variant, a multiset of weights is distributed uniformly among ground-set elements. Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen obtain a constant guarantee for that variant even without advance knowledge of the matroid. Their May 2023 preprint explicitly leaves the adversarial-assignment conjecture open. Its theorem cannot by itself justify the general claim here.

Before the new September claim, the cited general guarantee was \(O(\log\log r)\), with the small-rank cases treated separately, where \(r\) is the matroid rank. A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, this card's advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.

cards.title: Breaking factor two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every valid unrelated-machine scheduling instance \(I\) defined below, outputs a feasible schedule \(\sigma\) with \[C_{\max}(\sigma)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] The machine count is part of the input, and \(\varepsilon\) is independent of it and of all processing times. No complexity assumption is included.
cards.definitions:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, define the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(N(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(N(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. 

An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(N(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm attains factor \(2-\varepsilon\) for one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) on all unrelated-machine instances, or refute the existence of every such algorithm and improvement.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.
