cards.context:
The selected target restores the original source question: a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for one fixed universal \(\varepsilon>0\). It does not request a numerical determination of the full approximation-ratio infimum.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. cards.title: Square-root-dimensional Euclidean convex body chasing
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), some deterministic online strategy \(A_d\) for convex body chasing in \(\mathbb R^d\) satisfies \[\operatorname{cost}_{A_d}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le C\sqrt d\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\] for every finite sequence of nonempty compact convex request sets? The strategy starts at the origin, sees each set before choosing its next point in that set, and pays Euclidean movement. The same strategy must work for every horizon; requests need not be nested, and no additive cost is allowed.
cards.definitions:
An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]


The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) bounds the competitive ratio by \(C\sqrt d\) for a deterministic strategy in each dimension, starting at the origin, for every horizon. A refutation rules out every proposed \(C\) on some dimension.
cards.why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.

cards.context:
The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

cards.context:
The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

The final gradient-descent preprint proves recovery at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt n\) from full-graph initialization, for each fixed desired error probability.
Nagda and Raghavendra’s revised paper derives optimal efficient distinguishing advantages under a hypothesis in the independent-vertex planting model.
COLT 2026 presents robust algorithms for overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs above the stated \(\sqrt{n\log n}\) scale. This is a different distribution.

A new preprint reports conditional average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation from fixed-size planted-clique detection, with a separate quantum hypothesis. This review did not independently verify its reduction.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
cards.definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
cards.why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.

cards.context:
Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the card’s single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

cards.title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
cards.formal: Is the following computational impossibility statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), rational \(0<\varepsilon<(k-2)/4\), and rational \(0<c<1\), no uniform randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm can, for all sufficiently large \(n\), recover a vector with absolute correlation at least \(c\) with a uniformly random hidden unit direction from the single rounded tensor observation \[Y=\lambda_n v^{\otimes k}+Z,\qquad \lambda_n=n^{k/4-\varepsilon},\qquad v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{n-1}),\] where all \(n^k\) ordered entries of \(Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables. Recovery must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\), averaged over the hidden direction, noise and algorithm coins. Rounding, output normalization and the uniform bit-cost model are defined below. The fixed power saving \(n^\varepsilon\) and the spherical prior are parts of the existing target, not replaced by a threshold for one algorithm family.
cards.definitions:
\(S^{n-1}=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i v_i^2=1\}\), with its rotation-invariant probability measure. A tensor is an array indexed by all ordered tuples \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in[n]^k\), including repeated indices. Its rank-one signal has entry \(\lambda_n v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_k}\). The Gaussian noise entries, the direction and learner coins are independent. In particular the noise is not symmetrized: entries indexed by different permutations remain independent. The learner has exactly one tensor observation, with no labeled coordinates, informative starting vector, auxiliary graph or additional independent noise samples. The fixed constants \(k,\varepsilon,c\) are known to its program, but \(v\) and \(Z\) are hidden.

For \(n\ge2\), put \[b_n=\lceil10k\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad Q_b(x)=2^{-b}\left\lfloor2^b\max\{-2^b,\min\{x,2^b\}\}\right\rfloor.\] The actual input is \(n\) and the complete list \((Q_{b_n}(Y_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}))_{[n]^k}\) in lexicographic tuple order. Each entry is encoded by its signed integer numerator with the common denominator \(2^{b_n}\); the numerator has at most \(2b_n+2\) bits. The clipping interval and rounding direction are fixed, not chosen adaptively by the algorithm. The exact real tensor exists only in the sampling experiment; the machine receives no oracle for its discarded digits. The input length is \(O(n^k\log n)\) at fixed \(k\). This is the previously adopted explicit finite-precision version of the Gaussian question, not a theorem asserting equivalence to every exact-real formulation.

An allowed algorithm is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. There exist constants \(B,a\ge1\), possibly depending on the fixed triple, such that it terminates within \(Bn^a\) bit operations on every encoded input of this dimension and every random tape. Reading, storage operations, arithmetic, writing the output and its rational encodings are included. The single program and polynomial work for all \(n\), with no advice depending on dimension. Since \(k\) is fixed, this is polynomial in the complete input length. There are no exact-real or quantum operations.

The output is a list of \(n\) rational coordinates \(w_i\), each a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. A malformed vector or \(w=0\) fails. Otherwise interpret \(u=w/\|w\|_2\), where \(\langle w,v\rangle=\sum_i w_i v_i\) and \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). The success event is the mathematically defined inequality \[|\langle w,v\rangle|\ge c\|w\|_2.\] The learner need not compute that event, since it does not know the planted direction. Absolute correlation permits a global sign flip, including the inherent even-order ambiguity. The output need not encode the irrational normalized vector exactly; its rational representative determines the direction.

Write \(p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)\) for the probability of this event in the specified experiment. The target is \[\forall(k,\varepsilon,c)\ \forall A\text{ of polynomial bit cost}\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:\quad p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)<2/3.\] Thus the conjecture rules out eventual success on all dimensions; it does not claim that every algorithm fails at every large dimension, or that its success probability must tend to zero. Conversely, a refutation needs one fixed triple and one machine with eventual success at least \(2/3\). The range of \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(\lambda_n/\sqrt n=n^{(k-2)/4-\varepsilon}\to\infty\), placing the signal above the usual statistical scale in the unrounded model.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the full quantified impossibility statement, or a Lean-verified counterexample consisting of one fixed triple, a single algorithm, polynomial worst-case bit/output bounds and an \(N\) for which \(p_A(n)\ge2/3\) for every \(n\ge N\). A lower bound against low-degree estimators, one iterative method, or a different prior is not the universal statement. Detection and recovery must not be interchanged without a proved reduction. Any normalization, symmetrization, multiple-sample or precision transfer must be justified in the same success and resource model. A conditional hardness reduction is partial progress until its premise is proved. Logarithmic threshold improvements or a constant-prefactor improvement at \(n^{k/4}\) do not supply the fixed exponent saving. The desired output quality is a fixed absolute correlation, not coordinatewise numerical recovery.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

cards.context:
Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Randomly initialized power iteration has a different benchmark from the best known general methods: Wu–Zhou analyze its scale \(n^{(k-1)/2}\) and improve it by a polylogarithmic factor. For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Randomly initialized power iteration has a different benchmark from the best known general methods: Wu–Zhou analyze its scale \(n^{(k-1)/2}\) and improve it by a polylogarithmic factor. For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.

cards.title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
cards.formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\geq6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that \(A\) never outputs \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) on any satisfiable \(3\)-CNF formula, and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{F\sim R_3(n,Cn),\,\rho}
 [A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]=1?
\]
The distribution \(R_3\), exact soundness, and worst-case time bound are defined below. The constant \(C\), machine and its time polynomial must be fixed before \(n\); the probability includes the algorithm’s independent random bits \(\rho\).
cards.definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. General inputs are explicitly listed \(3\)-CNF formulas, with at most three literals in each clause; repeated clauses, repeated literals and empty clauses are allowed. The empty clause is false. The number \(n\) of named variables and the list length are encoded in binary, followed by binary indices and sign bits with delimiters. Valid indices lie in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); unused variables are allowed. Let \(N\) be the complete encoded length. Malformed encodings receive \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\) in polynomial time.

For \(n\geq3\), the random distribution \(R_3(n,m)\) is an ordered list of \(m\) independent clauses sampled with replacement. For each clause choose a uniformly random three-element subset of \([n]\), and independently negate each selected variable with probability \(1/2\). Write its three variables in index order. Thus each random clause has three distinct variables, duplicate clauses may occur, and signs in all clauses are independent. This fixed-size distribution is not a planted distribution or a distribution conditioned on unsatisfiability.

The algorithm always outputs either \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) or \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). Exact soundness means that for every satisfiable input formula \(F\) and every sequence \(\rho\) of its random bits, \(A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). On an unsatisfiable formula it may also return \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\); the required frequency of success applies only to the stated random distribution. Even on exceptional input formulas or random choices there is no allowed false assertion of unsatisfiability.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine with independent fair bits and no advice or external oracle. There must be integers \(K,d\geq1\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence, including adversarial formulas. Reading random bits and producing the answer are charged, so only polynomially many bits may be used. This is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time bound on random formulas. Deterministic machines are included.

The probability limit requires that for every real \(\eta>0\) there is an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n\geq\max\{3,n_0\}\), the probability of \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) is at least \(1-\eta\). The rate of convergence need not be supplied as an algorithm. The density \(C\) is an absolute constant, not a function tending to infinity with \(n\). Choosing integer \(C\geq6\) loses no successful smaller constant-density regime: on a denser input the algorithm can run a lower-density refuter on the appropriate clause prefix, whose distribution is exactly the lower-density model. Unsatisfiability of a prefix implies unsatisfiability of the full formula, preserving soundness.

No named proof system or explicit derivation format is imposed. The output \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) must be justified by the proven soundness of the algorithm; the machine need not print a resolution or sum-of-squares proof. Existence of short unsatisfiability certificates without an efficient way of finding them does not meet this definition.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply one constant \(C\), one uniform algorithm, its worst-case polynomial time bound, exact soundness for every satisfiable input and every random-bit sequence, and the success limit for \(R_3(n,Cn)\).

A negative answer must rule out every such constant and every such algorithm. Equivalently, for every proposed sound polynomial-time \(A\) and every integer \(C\geq6\), there must be some \(\eta>0\) such that failure probability is at least \(\eta\) for arbitrarily large \(n\). Showing failure for a single algorithm, proof system or finite set of inputs is insufficient. A conditional theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. Algorithms requiring a growing clause density, allowing erroneous refutations on rare satisfiable inputs, or merely distinguishing a planted distribution do not satisfy the criterion.
cards.why: This problem isolates the gap between knowing that a typical sparse formula is unsatisfiable and efficiently proving unsatisfiability without ever making a false claim. A resolution would identify a major limit of average-case certification or produce an algorithm beyond the methods underlying existing refutation barriers.

cards.context:
Typical unsatisfiability has a short counting proof. For any fixed assignment, a random clause is satisfied with probability \(7/8\), so the expected number of satisfying assignments in \(R_3(n,Cn)\) is \(2^n(7/8)^{Cn}\). For \(C\geq6\), this tends to zero exponentially. Markov’s inequality therefore shows that the formula is unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Always printing UNSAT would exploit that statistical fact but would violate soundness on satisfiable inputs.

The task asks for a certificate on a particular input while exploiting its typical structure. Search and proof existence are separate: a family of short refutations does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds one. The 2015 source explicitly separates these possibilities in its comparison of efficient refutation algorithms and nondeterministically available certificates.

Spectral and semidefinite methods give efficient refutation at much higher clause counts, around \(n^{3/2}\) for random \(3\)-SAT in the source’s historical account. The relevant density is the number of clauses divided by \(n\), so this regime grows like \(\sqrt n\), in contrast to the constant required here. A bound for other predicates, such as not-all-equal clauses, cannot be substituted for ordinary disjunction clauses.

Gap refutation proves that every assignment violates a positive fraction of clauses. It must therefore remain silent even on suitable nearly satisfiable formulas. Barak’s cited formulation of Feige’s hypothesis uses this stronger soundness requirement. The present target retains the previously approved requirement of soundness only on satisfiable formulas, so consequences of a gap hypothesis must be checked separately.

The 2026 work extends the density, relaxation degree and refutation-strength tradeoff to more general random CSP distributions without uniformly random literals. Its sum-of-squares lower bounds restrict a particular family of algebraic relaxations; its generalization of the upper bounds does not supply the unrestricted constant-density algorithm asked for here. The paper treats binomial random-instance models in its displayed theorems, another reason to avoid identifying them verbatim with this fixed-size target.

The August 2026 ECCC report states stronger lower bounds for resolution extended to bounded-width disjunctions of conjunctions. Such a result blocks algorithms restricted to those refutations, but it does not rule out a different sound polynomial-time computation. The claim is recorded at the abstract level rather than as an independent full-proof audit.

If \(\mathsf P=\mathrm{NP}\), a deterministic polynomial-time SAT decision algorithm can refute every unsatisfiable input, and the elementary counting argument gives the required average-case success. Consequently an unconditional negative answer here would imply \(\mathsf P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer would be a distribution-specific algorithm and would not itself decide worst-case SAT.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every proper initial colouring. Denote it by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\). The chain is ergodic in the stated range.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: This tests whether the simplest local update rule samples proper colourings efficiently throughout the full range where it is guaranteed to move between all solutions. It connects random sampling, approximate counting and antiferromagnetic spin systems at a longstanding boundary for general graphs.

cards.context:
The source poses polynomial mixing at the degree-plus-two threshold. This card retains the already adopted heat-bath update rule and the explicit requirement of one polynomial for all degrees and palettes. The source’s initial update description uses proposal-and-rejection; that clock is stated separately rather than silently identifying its transition matrix with this one.

At one fewer colour, a clique on Δ+1 vertices can be frozen: every vertex already sees every other colour. Thus ergodicity itself can fail at q=Δ+1. At q≥Δ+2 the basic chain is ergodic, but eventual convergence alone supplies no polynomial bound on how long it takes.

The2020 source proves polynomial mixing for bounded-treewidth graphs at the additive threshold and for chordal graphs with fixed multiplicative slack. Its treewidth-dependent exponent and the extra hypotheses do not establish the all-graph uniform statement.

The2024 flip-dynamics theorem applies for Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ. Its comparison gives polynomial Glauber mixing in that range; the sharper O(n log n) corollary permits a constant depending on degree and palette. Neither the larger palette ratio nor that parameter dependence is the selected degree-plus-two theorem.

The August2026 girth-seven revision treats Metropolis updates with q≥(1+δ)Δ, for fixed δ and degree sufficiently large in terms of δ. The separate girth-five preprint gives a heat-bath theorem under analogous fixed-slack and large-degree conditions. The latter’s general bound is Oδ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); its optimal-order corollary has further bounded-degree qualifications. Both retain structural assumptions absent here.

The ICALP2026 paper repeats the ordinary colouring-sampling conjecture before studying prescribed colour-class sizes. Fixing class sizes changes the stationary state space and the allowed moves, so those refined sampling results do not settle the chain defined here.

cards.title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
cards.formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
cards.definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\) for \(P_L\) with law \(\pi_L\), from every initial spin configuration. One step is one site update. A continuous-time clock of rate one per site has a different normalization. The target concerns the defined transition law with its exact probabilities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.
cards.why: This is a basic question about whether a standard local sampling dynamics remains efficient at a phase transition in three dimensions. The equilibrium system has correlations on many scales, so high-temperature mixing guarantees do not directly apply. A polynomial bound or a superpolynomial obstruction would clarify the computational cost of critical fluctuations in one of the central lattice models.

cards.context:
Bauerschmidt and Dagallier relate functional inequalities for Ising dynamics to susceptibility bounds. Their critical finite-volume application uses mean-field susceptibility behavior and yields polynomial control on free-boundary lattice boxes in dimensions at least five. The checked result does not establish the needed hypothesis or conclusion in dimension three.

The source also distinguishes the earlier two-dimensional critical theorem from the higher-dimensional argument. Having polynomial mixing in dimension two and in dimensions at least five leaves the three-dimensional target separate; interpolation between dimensions is not a stated theorem.

The 2024 Prodromidis–Sly note proves polynomial mixing at the uniqueness threshold of the infinite regular tree for bounded-degree graphs. At degree six its parameter is \(\operatorname{arctanh}(1/5)\). The word critical in that title refers to the tree threshold, not to the infinite cubic lattice threshold defined in this card.

Boundary conditions materially affect low-temperature dynamics. The source contrasts slow mixing with free boundaries and a different conjecture under all-plus boundaries. Keeping the free-boundary convention is necessary to preserve this card’s specific critical-lattice question.

cards.title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.
cards.why: A general guarantee for a basic sampler that preserves individual degrees, with applications to network and fixed-margin statistical models. The reported solution would close the gap between eventual convergence and a uniform polynomial sampling bound.

cards.context:
Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: Cutoff for bounded-degree transitive expanders
cards.formal:
Does every sequence of bounded-degree vertex-transitive expander graphs exhibit total-variation cutoff for lazy simple random walk? More precisely, consider any sequence \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) of finite connected undirected simple graphs, with \(N_k=|V(G_k)|\to\infty\). Assume each \(G_k\) is vertex-transitive, that there is a fixed integer \(D\ge3\) with \(3\le d_k\le D\) for its vertex degree \(d_k\), and that the lazy-walk spectral gaps satisfy \(\gamma_k\ge\delta\) for some constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). Must
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{t_k(\varepsilon)}{t_k(1-\varepsilon)}=1?\]
The transition rule and worst-start mixing times \(t_k\) are defined below. The constants \(D\) and \(\delta\) may depend on the sequence. No quantitative cutoff window or common leading constant for different sequences is demanded.
cards.definitions:
A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. Vertex-transitive means that for any vertices \(x,y\) there is a bijection of the vertex set preserving adjacency in both directions and mapping \(x\) to \(y\). Consequently all its vertices have the same degree \(d_k\). The graph sequence is deterministic and need not come from a particular construction or a random-graph model.

One lazy-walk step stays at the current vertex with probability \(1/2\), and otherwise chooses a neighbor uniformly and moves there. Its transition matrix is
\[P_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2&y=x,\\1/(2d_k)&\{x,y\}\in E(G_k),\\0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The stationary probability is \(\pi_k(y)=1/N_k\). List the real eigenvalues in decreasing order as \(1=\lambda_{1,k}>\lambda_{2,k}\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_{N_k,k}\ge0\), and set \(\gamma_k=1-\lambda_{2,k}\). A uniformly positive lower bound on \(\gamma_k\), together with bounded degree, is the expander assumption used here. Laziness includes bipartite graphs without periodicity problems.

At an integer time \(t\ge0\), let
\[d_k(t)=\max_{x\in V(G_k)}\frac12\sum_{y\in V(G_k)}\left|P_k^t(x,y)-\frac1{N_k}\right|,\qquad t_k(\eta)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_k(t)\le\eta\}\quad(0<\eta<1).\]
The maximum is over every starting vertex. Times count discrete lazy steps, including steps that stay put. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the denominator \(t_k(1-\varepsilon)\) is positive for all sufficiently large \(k\); the limit uses this eventual tail. The displayed ratio condition defines total-variation cutoff. It asks that the transition between distance near one and distance near zero occupy a vanishing fraction of the mixing time.

The source first states the question with one fixed degree. Allowing degree to vary in a fixed finite range is equivalent at the level of this universal conjecture: each degree occurring infinitely often gives a fixed-degree subsequence. Neither degrees growing without bound nor expansion constants tending to zero are admitted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every sequence satisfying the hypotheses has the displayed cutoff property, or a Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must establish a sequence satisfying every hypothesis for which the ratio limit fails for at least one fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\). A single finite graph cannot refute an asymptotic cutoff statement. Logarithmic mixing-time bounds alone, cutoff in a different distance, or a result only for a special class of expanders do not meet the criterion.
cards.why: Expanders combine sparse connectivity with fast random-walk mixing and are central objects in algorithms and pseudorandomness. This conjecture asks whether spatial symmetry forces their approach to equilibrium to be abrupt. A resolution would separate the role of expansion in the speed of mixing from the role of symmetry in the shape of convergence.

cards.context:
The textbook asks this question for a fixed degree and explicitly chooses lazy random walk. The card retains that walk and the total-variation meaning of cutoff, while making the graph-sequence and uniform-gap quantifiers explicit.

Salez’s 2025 notes state the vertex-transitive expander conjecture as Problem 2.3. The notes explain that expansion already gives mixing time of logarithmic order in the graph size; cutoff asks for substantially finer asymptotic information.

Lubetzky and Peres prove cutoff for simple random walk on non-bipartite \(d\)-regular Ramanujan graphs, where all adjacency eigenvalues other than \(d\) have absolute value at most \(2\sqrt{d-1}\). This is a much stronger spectral condition than an arbitrary fixed positive gap. Their result supplies a major special case, not a proof for every transitive expander.

cards.title: FP versus #P
cards.formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). Use the shared definition of [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.
cards.why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.

cards.context:
A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

A polynomial-space computation can enumerate all witnesses while keeping only a polynomial-length counter. The textbook therefore notes that P = PSPACE would imply a positive answer. This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.
