cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_a\), integers \(B_a\ge a+3\), \(k_a\ge0\) and \(C_a\ge1\) with the following property? On every explicitly represented directed graph \(G\) with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integer arc capacities
\[0\le u_e\le n^a,\]
the algorithm uses words of \(w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, halts on every random execution within
\[C_a(m+n)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{k_a}\]
word operations, and outputs an exact integral maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with probability at least \(2/3\)?
The output must give a flow value on every original arc. The algorithm, constants and logarithmic exponent may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its capacities, its terminal choices or its input ordering. The complete graph, flow and machine conventions are specified below.
cards.definitions:
Graph and representation. The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An ordered arc list \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) consists of distinct ordered pairs \(e_j=(x_j,y_j)\in[n]^2\) with \(x_j\ne y_j\), so \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\). Opposite arcs may both occur and have independent capacities; parallel copies of the same ordered pair and loops are excluded. The graph may be disconnected and may contain isolated vertices and zero-capacity arcs. The terminals \(s,t\in[n]\) are distinct. The input is an array of machine words containing the header \((n,m,s,t)\), the list \(1,\ldots,n\) of vertices, and the triples \((x_j,y_j,u_{e_j})\) in the given arc order. Correctness and time bounds hold for every ordering. Capacities and labels are unsigned integers, each in one word. The explicit vertex list fixes the \(m+n\) convention even when \(m=0\). There is no succinct representation, adjacency oracle or precomputed index.

Feasible flow and optimum. A flow is a list \(f=(f_{e_1},\ldots,f_{e_m})\) of integers with \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) on every arc and
\[\sum_{e=(x,v)}f_e=\sum_{e=(v,y)}f_e\qquad\text{for every }v\in[n]\setminus\{s,t\}.\]
Each sum ranges over the arcs actually present. Its value is the net flow leaving the source,
\[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{e=(s,y)}f_e-\sum_{e=(x,s)}f_e.\]
Incoming arcs at \(s\), outgoing arcs at \(t\), and circulations are allowed. Conservation implies that this equals the net flow entering \(t\). Define \(F(G,u,s,t)\) as the largest value among the feasible integral flows. The set of such flows is finite and nonempty because the all-zero list is feasible, so the maximum is attained and nonnegative. Also \(F\le(n-1)n^a\). The usual integral-flow theorem identifies this optimum with the real-valued maximum flow for integral capacities. A successful output is the list of exactly \(m\) integers in original arc order that forms a feasible flow with value \(F\). No prescribed tie-breaking between different optimal flows is required. If \(m=0\), the empty list is the correct output.

Machine model. Put \(L_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), so each word contains \(w=B_aL_n\) bits. A word stores an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The random-access machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite set of registers and word-addressed memory; input words occupy the initial array and other memory is initially zero. Each executed instruction costs one operation. Allowed instructions are word reads and writes, moves, conditional branches, comparisons, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer division with a nonzero divisor. A logical shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A memory address must fit in one word. Input, output and all memory used must fit within the address space, with \(B_a\) chosen as part of the algorithm's fixed constants. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented using these operations and charged accordingly. Exact real arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

Randomness and resources. A random-word instruction returns a fresh independent uniform element of \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\) at cost one; equivalently its bits are independent fair bits. The success probability is over this sequence for each fixed valid input. A run outside the successful event may return a failure marker or an incorrect result, but must obey the same time bound. All graph preprocessing, memory accesses, random generation and writing of output words are charged. The bound is on the total running time of every run of this one static computation, not merely on expected time or on typical executions. An amortized analysis of internal operations is permitted if it establishes this total bound. There are no oracles, quantum operations, input-dependent advice or free preprocessing. Behavior outside the stated input promises is unrestricted.

Uniformity and quantifiers. For each fixed \(a\), one finite program works for all \(n,m,G,u,s,t\); it cannot contain a table or different advice indexed by \(n\). The quantifier order is
\[\forall a\ge1\ \exists A_a,B_a,k_a,C_a\ \forall(G,u,s,t).\]
The selected target does not additionally require an effective procedure that constructs \(A_a\) from \(a\), a common logarithmic exponent for all \(a\), or a bound polynomial in \(a\). For each fixed \(a\), however, \(k_a\) is a single integer independent of input size. The explicit running-time expression is precisely the meaning of the title's \(O((m+n)\operatorname{polylog}n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, for each fixed capacity exponent \(a\), one program and fixed constants satisfying both the every-run time bound and the per-input success probability, including exact integral feasibility and optimality of all output arc values. A deterministic algorithm with that bound also qualifies. A negative proof must establish a fixed \(a\ge1\) for which every uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm in this model having any such fixed-polylogarithmic worst-case bound has some valid instance with success probability strictly below \(2/3\). A lower bound for one flow framework, an oracle-only algorithm, or a conditional conjecture does not prove that universal negation. A \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate flow, the optimum value alone, an algorithm for a restricted graph class, or a bound of \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) without the required fixed logarithmic overhead is insufficient. The algorithmic exact-flow requirement is retained; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace its output specification.
cards.why: Maximum flow is a central primitive for routing, cuts and combinatorial optimization. Almost-linear algorithms have already removed a polynomial overhead. This question asks whether exact directed flow can be computed with only a fixed power of a logarithm beyond explicit input size, on all polynomial-capacity instances and with a complete flow as output.

cards.context:
Capacity constraints bound how much can travel along each arc, while conservation couples choices throughout the network. Exactness asks for the largest transferable amount, not merely a feasible routing. Because capacities are integral, an integral optimum exists, but the algorithm still has to find an optimal routing among many interacting possibilities.

The logarithmic overhead is the unresolved guarantee. For example, \(h(n)=2^{\sqrt{\log_2(n+2)}}\) satisfies \(h(n)=n^{o(1)}\), yet exceeds \((\log_2(n+2))^k\) for every fixed \(k\) once \(n\) is sufficiently large. Thus almost-linear and fixed-polylogarithmic time bounds are different. In this simple directed-graph format, \(n\le m+n\le n^2\), so logarithms of input word count and vertex count differ by only a constant factor.

Chen and coauthors’ 2022 breakthrough computes exact maximum flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\log U\) time with high probability for integral capacities bounded by \(U\). For \(U\le n^a\), the capacity term is logarithmic, while the subpolynomial graph-size overhead remains. Their analysis uses fixed-point quantities with polynomially many logarithmic bits; charging multiword arithmetic does not turn that overhead into a fixed logarithmic power.

The 2023 deterministic algorithm of van den Brand and coauthors also obtains exact almost-linear flow. The 2024 duality paper further improves the stated static bounds: its Theorem 6.17 gives randomized \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{3/4}\log\log m)}\) time and deterministic \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{5/6}\log\log m)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral minimum-cost flow. These are still guarantees with subpolynomial overhead, rather than the fixed logarithmic bound requested here.

Li and Wice’s August 2026 manuscript removes the outer interior-point loop from another almost-linear maximum-flow framework. Its deterministic pseudo-circulation subroutine is combined with a randomized balanced-graph flow routine, and the stated final result remains almost-linear. The deterministic nature of an intermediate step does not make the full reduction deterministic, and removing the outer loop does not itself establish fixed-polylogarithmic overhead.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm of Fleischmann, George Z. Li and Jason Li has fixed-polylogarithmic overhead for constant-accuracy approximate flow on undirected graphs. Both qualifications matter: the present task concerns arbitrary directed graphs and exact integral output, and that approximation theorem has additional inverse-error dependence. It does not directly establish the target here.

An approximation with a fixed relative error need not determine an integer optimum whose magnitude grows with the input. Likewise, finding only an optimal value does not fulfill the requested output list. Polynomially bounded capacities ensure each input capacity and output arc value fits in a logarithmic number of bits; the question does not hide arbitrarily long integers behind unit-cost input access.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.

cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t_F^\star(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t_F^\star(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}\), a query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t_F^\star(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t_F^\star(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t_F^\star(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

cards.context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
cards.definitions: The universe is \(U_w=\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo \(2^w\), multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

cards.context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Polynomial lower bounds for adaptive dynamic data structures
cards.formal: Is there an explicit dynamic Boolean problem for which adaptive randomized polynomial-space cell-probe data structures require polynomial amortized cost? Precisely, seek one problem family for which, for every fixed space exponent s, there is \(\eta_s>0\) such that every structure using at most \(n^s\) cells incurs expected \(\Omega(n^{\eta_s})\) probes per operation on some polynomial-length operation sequence, for infinitely many n.
cards.definitions:
Editorial explicitness convention: a problem has a state of at most \(n^a\) bits, an initial all-zero state, updates, and Boolean queries, for one fixed constant a. Each operation type and argument has at most \(a\log_2(n+2)\) bits. State transitions and answers are specified by uniform deterministic algorithms running in polynomial time in n; they are independent of any data structure being lower-bounded. Queries do not change the abstract state.

A structure stores at most \(n^s\) addressable cells of \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with fixed constants s,c; constants must permit addressing the memory. Within each operation arbitrary computation is free, and each cell read or write costs one probe. The next address may depend on earlier read contents, hence adaptivity is allowed. All information retained between operations, including registers, counts toward storage. Preprocessing may depend on n and the initial state but not future operations; its probes are not charged to the online sequence. Randomness is independent of the sequence. Each query must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every fixed legal sequence; a simultaneous all-queries success guarantee is not assumed.

The lower bound is on total expected probes divided by the number of operations in a fixed sequence chosen independently of the random coins. The sequence length is polynomial in n, with exponent permitted to depend on the structure and space exponent, and must include a query. This total-cost convention forces high amortized cost for at least one of updates and queries. The exponent eta may depend on the fixed space and word constants; it must be positive and independent of n. No external computational hardness assumption is part of the requested result.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit the explicit problem family and prove the stated lower bound in Lean against all adaptive bounded-error structures in this model. A bound only for nonadaptive probes, deterministic structures, restricted update/query tradeoffs, or superpolynomially long histories does not suffice. A negative resolution must prove that every problem in the specified explicit class admits structures excluding the asserted polynomial lower bound.
cards.why: A polynomial unconditional barrier would change the known limits of dynamic data structures beyond polylogarithmic lower bounds.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

cards.context:
Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon,a}\) and constants \(K,d,B\ge1\) with the following guarantees?

For every \(n\ge2\) and every valid oblivious sequence of \(T\le n^a\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty graph on \([n]\), the expected total initialization and update cost is at most
\[
K\left[n+T\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\right].
\]
With probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\), after every update the algorithm maintains an explicit matching \(M\) in the current graph \(G\) such that
\[
|M|\ge\frac{\nu(G)}{1+\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality. The same constants apply to every \(n,T\) and sequence for the fixed \(\varepsilon,a\).
cards.definitions:
At all times the graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, with the fixed vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Initially there are no edges. One update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge; only valid update sequences are required to be handled. The graph need not be bipartite or have bounded degree.

A matching is a subset of the current edges in which no vertex belongs to more than one edge. The integer \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum possible number of edges in a matching, and it is zero for an edgeless graph. The algorithm stores a mate array \(\operatorname{mate}[1..n]\): zero means unmatched, while a nonzero value \(\operatorname{mate}[v]=u\) must have \(u\ne v\), \(\operatorname{mate}[u]=v\) and \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Together with its stored cardinality, this explicitly represents \(M\). A size estimate or a fractional assignment to edges is not this representation.

After each completed update, reading the mate of any specified vertex or reading \(|M|\) takes at most a fixed constant number of word operations. Listing the full matching may scan the array in \(O(n)\) time, and need not be performed after every update. All work needed to modify the representation, including every changed array entry and the cardinality, counts toward update cost. External requests to read or list the maintained matching are charged their stated query costs separately; they do not excuse extra update work.

The update sequence is oblivious: for each guarantee it is any fixed sequence independent of the algorithm’s random bits. Updates are delivered one at a time, and the algorithm must finish processing one before seeing the next. It knows \(n\) and has the fixed parameters \(\varepsilon,a\), but the future sequence and its actual length are not supplied in advance. This is distinct from a computation receiving all updates at once, and it makes no guarantee against an adversary choosing updates from observed random-dependent outputs.

Use a word-RAM with word length \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with \(B\) a fixed positive integer for the algorithm. Memory cells have word addresses and initially contain zero; every access or write costs an operation, and untouched cells require no initialization work. The instruction set consists of word reads and writes, indirect addressing, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one operation. Stored random words and intermediate values use ordinary memory. Larger integers must use multiple words, with all operations charged; no arbitrary-precision operation, graph oracle or precomputed instance advice is available. No additional linear-space restriction is imposed.

Expectation is over the algorithm’s private randomness on each fixed sequence and includes the entire initialization and all \(T\) updates. The bound is amortized over that sequence, not a worst-case bound on each individual update. The required finite expectation includes termination with probability one. Separately, one event of probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\) must ensure the valid mate representation and approximation inequality after every update in the sequence simultaneously. A separate probability bound at each time without this joint guarantee is insufficient.

The parameters \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\) are fixed independently of \(n\). The machine and constants may depend on both; no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) and no uniform compiler taking \(\varepsilon,a\) as inputs is required. Integer \(a\) covers every polynomial sequence-length regime. There is no demand for an infinite update sequence with one global success event. This is an exact existence proposition for the stated approximation scheme and resources, not a numerical question about \(\nu(G)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply algorithms and a complete Lean-checked proof covering every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\), every fixed polynomial horizon, every \(n\), and every valid oblivious sequence, including the expected total cost, representation-access costs and simultaneous success event. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation of these quantified guarantees; failure for one fixed accuracy and one fixed horizon exponent, for every admissible algorithm and constants, suffices.

An estimator without explicit matching edges, a fixed approximation factor bounded away from one, a partially dynamic algorithm, an algorithm receiving future updates, or an update bound larger than every fixed power of \(\log n\) does not prove the proposition. A lower bound requiring accuracy to shrink with \(n\), polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), or an adaptive adversary does not by itself refute this weaker stated target. Conditional lower bounds require their hypotheses and are not unconditional negative answers.
cards.why: A single insertion or deletion can change which edges should be used together in a large matching. The question asks whether a near-optimal explicit solution can be kept current at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically with graph size, combining approximation quality with efficient dynamic maintenance.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist integers \(a,d\ge1\) and \(B\ge c+3\), a real constant \(K\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic word-RAM data structure with the following guarantees for every \(n\ge2\) and supplied integer capacity \(n\le m\le n^2\)?

The data structure maintains a simple directed graph on the fixed vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with at most \(m\) live edges and edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots,n^c\}\), under online single-edge insertions, deletions and weight changes. It returns the exact current distance for every queried ordered vertex pair. Write \(\ell=\log_2(n+2)\). Preprocessing an arbitrary initial graph uses at most \(Kn^d\) instructions, and space is at most \(Kn^d\) words at every time. Every individual query uses at most \(K\ell^a\) instructions. After preprocessing, every finite valid sequence containing \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries uses at most
\[
K\bigl(Um\ell^a+Q\ell^a\bigr)
\]
instructions in total. The constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n,m\), the initial graph or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions:
The initial graph is explicitly given as a list of ordered endpoint pairs and integer weights, together with \(n\) and \(m\). There are no self-loops, and each ordered pair has at most one edge. An insertion supplies an absent edge and its allowed weight, a deletion names a present edge, and a weight change supplies a new allowed weight for a present edge. Every resulting graph must have at most the fixed supplied capacity \(m\) edges. The algorithm must support all such valid sequences, however long. The value \(m\) is neither the number of updates nor the current number of edges.

A query supplies \(s,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and requests the minimum sum of edge weights along a directed path from \(s\) to \(t\), with distance zero when \(s=t\) and a distinguished symbol \(\infty\) when no path exists. Positive weights imply that every finite distance is at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output is this one distance, not a shortest path or a full matrix. Every answer must be correct. Operations arrive one at a time, and each must finish before the next is supplied; future operations are unavailable.

For a given \(n\), a machine word has exactly \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Memory is indexed by unsigned words, and \(B\) must also be large enough to address the allowed \(Kn^d\) words. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, unsigned comparisons and conditional branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Finite distances and the infinity marker must have an unambiguous constant-word encoding. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented and charged through these operations. The program is finite and independent of \(n,m\); it receives no advice or uncharged precomputed tables.

Preprocessing includes reading and constructing all initial data. After it finishes, the displayed total bound applies to every finite prefix, including prefixes with no updates or no queries. There is no extra additive \(n^d\) allowance in that post-preprocessing bound. Individual updates may exceed their amortized charge, but each query also satisfies the stated worst-case bound, regardless of the preceding operations. All instruction counts include maintenance work and any rebuilding performed during the operation sequence. The space bound applies throughout preprocessing and all operations.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic data structure for every fixed \(c\), prove all exact query answers and the capacity-sensitive bounds for every allowed graph and operation prefix, and account for word size and polynomial space.

A negative answer must disprove the existence proposition in the stated model; a result conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis remains a conditional obstruction and must identify that assumption. An update bound near \(n^2\) only has the requested dependence on \(m\) for sufficiently dense graphs. Approximate distances, offline sequences, planar graphs, insertion-only updates, or an amortized query bound alone do not establish the stated target. The fact that one edge change alters many pairwise distances is not by itself a lower bound on an implicit distance oracle.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized data structure maintaining the exact global minimum-cut value of a fully dynamic simple unweighted undirected graph with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time, polylogarithmic worst-case query time and polynomial space? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) and fixed integers \(b\ge1,c\ge0\) such that, for every fixed integer confidence parameter \(a\ge1\), there is a constant \(C_a\ge1\) for which the following holds? For every \(n\ge2\), initialize on the empty graph on \([n]\). For every legal operation sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the random bits, with \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries and \(U+Q\le n^a\), require all of:
\[\text{space on every execution}\le C_a n^b\text{ words},\qquad \mathbb E[T_{\rm init}+T_{\rm updates}]\le C_a\bigl(n^b+U L^c\bigr),\]
\[\text{each query takes at most }C_aL^c\text{ steps on every execution},\qquad \Pr[\text{all }Q\text{ answers equal the current }\lambda(G)]\ge1-n^{-3},\]
where \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the machine model and costs are defined below. The exponents \(b,c\) and program are independent of \(a,n,\sigma\) and all cut values; constants may depend on \(a\).
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), fixed throughout the sequence. Each edge is an unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) of distinct vertices and occurs at most once. A legal update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge. There are no loops, weights, parallel edges or vertex changes. For \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]\), put \(\delta_G(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E(G):|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and
\[\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]}|\delta_G(S)|.\]
Thus \(0\le\lambda(G)\le n-1\), and \(\lambda(G)=0\) precisely for disconnected graphs, including the initial empty graph. A query returns just this integer, not a minimizing vertex set, edge list or prescribed-terminal cut. Isolated vertices are not discarded. There is no upper bound on connectivity other than \(n-1\).

The algorithm receives \(n\) and \(a\) at initialization. It then receives one operation at a time, represented by a query tag or an insertion/deletion tag with the two vertex indices. It is not given future operations. The external sequence is fixed in advance independently of the algorithm’s randomness, including any answers or internal state; its prefixes are legal. Correctness is simultaneous over all queries in each fixed sequence, not simultaneous over all possible sequences for one random seed. No correctness obligation is imposed on invalid update sequences. Initialization and updates must finish almost surely before the next operation is provided; the finite expectation bound applies to every legal sequence and hence to each prefix. Queries have the stated worst-case bound for every choice of random bits. Expected cost includes unsuccessful executions, not only those with correct answers.

Use a uniform word-RAM. For each fixed \(a\), the word length is \(w=B(a)L\) bits, where \(B(a)\ge1\) is an integer determined by a fixed computable function chosen with the algorithm, independently of \(n\) and the operations. Words represent unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). One step may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare two words, branch, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. A random instruction returns one fresh independent uniformly distributed \(w\)-bit word in one step. Arithmetic requiring more than one word is charged for its word operations; there are no real-number, unbounded-integer or oracle primitives. The finite program and computable word-length rule are common to all inputs, with no nonuniform advice or free precomputed tables.

Space counts all stored words, including tables and temporary work. Initialization work, random choices, rebuilding and all other computation belong to the operation during which they occur; there is no uncharged background work. The expectation bound includes initialization once and all update work. Query work is separately bounded, so expected total time is also at most \(C_a(n^b+(U+Q)L^c)\). The additive initialization allowance is polynomial, not an allowance repeated at each update. Amortization concerns the total over the supplied sequence, with no average over random input graphs. A query answer that differs from the exact integer is an error. The fixed failure bound \(n^{-3}\) applies to the entire sequence of length at most \(n^a\); \(a\) is supplied to set the horizon and confidence, not to reveal the actual sequence.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a data structure satisfying every displayed requirement, or an unconditional proof of the negation in the same model. A positive answer must define one program and its computable word-length rule, establish fixed exponents, and prove the space, expected total update/initialization cost, worst-case query cost and joint correctness probability for every allowed parameter and oblivious sequence. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of program and exponents; a theorem conditional on a conjecture alone does not do so. An insertion-only algorithm, an approximation, a bounded-connectivity guarantee, superpolylogarithmic update time, or polylogarithmic updates accompanied by slower queries is insufficient. Lower bounds for weighted graphs or terminal cuts require a proved transfer preserving this exact model. The output is exact because the question asks for an exact-maintenance algorithm; there is no additive 1/100 approximation option.
cards.why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

cards.context:
The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. Stability of the value alone does not specify whether an update changes it. The all-input guarantee includes long sequences in which different vertex partitions attain the minimum.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup give a deterministic algorithm with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. Its permitted updates only insert edges. The present target permits both insertions and deletions, including repeated removal and reinsertion of the same edge.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors give a randomized exact algorithm with \(\widetilde O(n)\) worst-case update time and a deterministic algorithm with \(\widetilde O(m^{29/31}n^{1/31})\) amortized time. Their March 2024 revision corrects an expander-decomposition running time. These bounds are substantial improvements over recomputing from scratch, but do not give the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. Here \(m\) denotes the current edge count and \(\widetilde O\) hides logarithmic factors.

The final June 2026 Algorithmica article by de Vos and Christiansen gives the deterministic exact amortized bound \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple unweighted graphs. This is Theorem 6 in the journal version; the article distinguishes it from an erroneous earlier cited exponent. Returning a full cut has a separate output-sensitive bound. The theorem does not establish polylogarithmic maintenance for all graph densities.

The inherited SODA 2026 theorem of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li gives deterministic exact \(n^{o(1)}\) amortized update time within a cut-size range bounded by \(2^{\Theta((\log n)^{3/4-\eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta<3/4\) in its parameter regime. It extends the earlier small-connectivity range. Both restrictions matter: the theorem does not cover every value up to \(n-1\), and a subpolynomial time bound need not be a fixed power of \(\log n\).

The word “subpolynomial” permits bounds that are larger than every polylogarithm; for example, \(2^{\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{o(1)}\) eventually exceeds \((\log_2 n)^c\) for every fixed \(c\). Thus replacing “polylogarithmic” by “subpolynomial” would change the target even if exactness and the cut-size range were otherwise identical.

El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm instead maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. A multiplicative estimate with relative error \(\epsilon\) can have additive error \(\epsilon\lambda\). Integrality does not turn such a guarantee into exactness uniformly over large \(\lambda\); the approximation accuracy and its effect on running time remain essential.

Kenneth-Mordoch’s February 2026 preprint reports a canonical exact minimum-cut algorithm with polylogarithmic worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n)\) queries. Its query procedure constructs a sparse contracted graph and computes a cut on that graph before reporting the result. Consequently, its stated query bound is not just the cost of printing the cut’s vertices, and the theorem does not provide the polylogarithmic value query required here.

The SOSA 2026 paper by Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer gives another tradeoff: its publisher abstract states \(\widetilde O(n/\lambda)\) worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n^2/\lambda^2)\) worst-case queries for positive connectivity. This becomes efficient in the high-connectivity range, but it is not a polylogarithmic bound uniform over all positive values of \(\lambda\). Disconnected graphs are also part of the present target.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

source_formulation.text: Retains the polylogarithmic exact fully dynamic global-minimum-cut question from the OMv open-problem discussion, using the previously selected simple unweighted, expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention. Makes the inherited polynomial horizon, common exponents, polynomial initialization/space, worst-case value queries and oblivious-sequence joint correctness explicit. The specified RAM instructions and integer confidence parameter fix the model; no weighted, terminal-cut or small-connectivity variant is substituted.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No algorithm satisfying both polylogarithmic expected-amortized updates and worst-case value queries for unrestricted exact connectivity, or unconditional impossibility theorem in the chosen model, was found in the bounded primary-source review. The SODA2026 exact result restricts cut size; the final June2026 tree-packing bound is not polylogarithmic. The February2026 pseudo-deterministic result has nearly linear queries, and the SOSA2026 tradeoff depends on connectivity. These are distinct guarantees; new proofs were not independently certified.

progress.text: The OMv framework leaves polylogarithmic dynamic global minimum cut as an explicit open problem in §5.2.
Goranci–Henzinger–Thorup achieve exact polylogarithmic incremental maintenance, allowing insertions only.
Goranci and coauthors give exact fully dynamic algorithms for unrestricted edge connectivity; v2 corrects an expander-decomposition runtime.
El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain \((1+o(1))\)-approximate fully dynamic minimum cut in subpolynomial amortized time.
El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain deterministic exact subpolynomial amortized updates for superpolylogarithmic, but still restricted, cut sizes.
Kenneth-Mordoch–Krauthgamer’s SOSA paper gives simpler exact algorithms and a connectivity-dependent update/query tradeoff.
The revised pseudo-deterministic minimum-cut preprint gives polylogarithmic updates with nearly linear queries, a different resource guarantee.
The final Algorithmica Theorem 6 gives deterministic exact amortized update time \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple graphs.

sentences: The global minimum cut is the minimum number of edges crossing any nonempty proper vertex subset, with value zero for a disconnected graph.
The question asks for one randomized data structure returning that exact value while arbitrary legal edge insertions and deletions arrive online.
It requires polylogarithmic expected amortized updates, polylogarithmic worst-case queries and polynomial space, with explicit initialization cost and uniform exponents.
For each fixed oblivious polynomial-length operation sequence, all answers must be simultaneously correct with error probability at most \(n^{-3}\).
A complete Lean proof must establish the whole guarantee or its unconditional impossibility; approximate, small-cut, insertion-only and fast-update/slow-query results do not suffice.

cards.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed real deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), do there exist constants \(C_\delta>0\) and \(a_\delta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta n^{a_\delta}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge2?\] Here \(N_\delta(n)\), defined below, is the number of independent deletion traces needed to reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with success probability at least \(2/3\). Processing is unrestricted, and the length and deletion probability are known. Constants may depend on fixed \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each fixed deletion probability the worst-case trace count for exact reconstruction at success probability \(2/3\) is polynomial in the string length. A refutation requires one fixed deletion probability for which no polynomial bound suffices.
cards.why: Determine the intrinsic amount of information needed to recover an arbitrary string when repeated observations lose the positions of deleted symbols. This separates the statistical cost of hidden alignment from the computational cost of processing the observations.

cards.context:
The selected binary target asks whether a polynomial number of traces suffices for every fixed deletion rate. It does not require the optimal sample exponent or a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its bound is \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\), for retention probability \(p=1-\delta\) and an absolute constant \(c\). This dated theorem does not by itself give a polynomial bound.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant.
