Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

context_blocks.text: The selected binary target asks whether a polynomial number of traces suffices for every fixed deletion rate. It does not require the optimal sample exponent or a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its bound is \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\), for retention probability \(p=1-\delta\) and an absolute constant \(c\). This dated theorem does not by itself give a polynomial bound.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.
cards.why: This asks whether allowing one universal constant loss of alignment accuracy reduces worst-case sequence comparison to the cost of reading the input, apart from a fixed polylogarithmic overhead. The result would locate a basic computational boundary that remains beyond the known fast constant-factor algorithms. Even a large universal factor would resolve this existence question.

cards.context:
Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and explicitly supplied string \(s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), the algorithm outputs an acyclic grammar \(G\) generating exactly \(s\), with
\[
|G|\le C\,g^*(s),
\]
in at most \(K(L(s)+1)^d\) Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(|G|\) is the total number of terminal and nonterminal occurrences on all right-hand sides, \(g^*(s)\) is the minimum such size among grammars generating \(s\), and \(L(s)\) is the explicit binary input length.
cards.definitions:
A permitted grammar consists of ordered nonterminals \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), one production \(X_j\to\alpha_j\) per nonterminal, and start nonterminal \(X_r\). Each \(\alpha_j\) is a finite nonempty sequence whose entries are terminals from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) or references to \(X_i\) with \(i<j\). Every nonterminal is reachable from the start. The order makes the dependency graph acyclic, and each variable has exactly one expansion into terminals. The expansion of \(X_r\) must equal \(s\), symbol for symbol. There are no alternatives, cycles, empty productions, reversal instructions, iteration instructions or extra generated strings. Right-hand sides may have arbitrary positive length; they need not be binary concatenations.

The size is \(|G|=\sum_{j=1}^r|\alpha_j|\). Every occurrence of a terminal or a referenced nonterminal contributes one unit, even when the same entry occurs repeatedly. This counts neither just the number of productions nor the binary description length. A repeated block written many times on a right-hand side is charged for each occurrence; a run-length exponent is not a substitute. The optimum \(g^*(s)\) ranges over all permitted grammars, independently of the algorithm. It exists and satisfies \(1\le g^*(s)\le n\), since one production containing \(s\) is permitted. Ordering the acyclic dependencies and removing unreachable rules does not change the optimal value.

For definiteness, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), \(a\ge0\), consist of \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary representation of \(a+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). The input is \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), followed by the \(n\) symbols, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Its full length is \(L(s)\). The alphabet is not required to have a fixed size, and symbols not used by \(s\) are allowed in the ambient alphabet.

The output explicitly lists \(r\), then for each production its right-hand-side length and all its entries. Lengths and identifiers use the same self-delimiting code, and each entry has a one-bit terminal/nonterminal tag. The start is \(X_r\). Writing this entire binary output counts toward runtime. The approximation inequality still uses the stated symbol-occurrence size, not the number of output bits.

The computational model is a fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite tape alphabets, read-only binary input, initially blank work tapes and a binary output tape. Each step reads or writes the cells under its heads and moves each head at most one cell. All parsing, preprocessing, computation and output writing are charged. There is no advice, oracle, randomness, quantum computation or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. No separate workspace bound is imposed. Malformed inputs may be rejected in polynomial time.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(C,K,d,A)\,\forall n\,\forall s\). The approximation factor and runtime exponent cannot depend on string length, alphabet size, repetition pattern or optimum grammar size. The task is to produce a grammar, not only estimate its minimum size. Exact optimization and approximation arbitrarily close to one are stronger targets than required here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must construct one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and prove its grammar is valid and within one fixed factor of the optimum for every allowed string. A negative proof must rule out every fixed constant factor and polynomial-time algorithm unconditionally. A theorem under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or another unproved hypothesis must be identified as conditional and does not alone prove the logical negation.

Hardness of exact optimization, a PTAS, or some small approximation constants does not refute all constant factors. An empirical bound, a guarantee only for a restricted string family, or a lower bound for one particular compressor does not decide the proposition. A proof in a different grammar-size convention must justify its transfer to the convention stated here.
cards.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

cards.context:
A grammar names reusable pieces and combines them hierarchically. The optimum measures how economically this can be done, while the algorithm must find a comparably small representation from the explicit string.

The classical guarantee is \(O(1+\log(n/g^*(s)))\). The same work excludes ratios strictly below \(8569/8568\) unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). This leaves the possibility of a larger universal constant.

The fixed-alphabet paper proves APX-hardness for alphabet sizes at least 17 and separately retains constant-factor approximation as an open problem. Exact hardness and absence of a PTAS do not rule out every constant.

Recent assembly-index work evaluates compressors on finite datasets. Such comparisons can assess practical performance but do not establish the worst-case all-string guarantee required here.

cards.title: Factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, given any explicit finite list of strings over an explicitly given finite alphabet, outputs a common superstring of length at most twice the minimum possible length? All occurrences are forward contiguous substrings. The input, zero-optimum convention and full bit-cost model are defined below. The algorithm need not use the maximum-overlap greedy rule.
cards.definitions:
For context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of ratios achievable by the deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithms defined below, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\mathcal R\). 

An instance is an integer \(\sigma\ge1\) and a finite list of finite strings \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) over \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}\), where \(k\ge0\). Encode \(\sigma,k\), the length of each string and each symbol in binary with self-delimiting integer fields. For definiteness, encode \(z\ge0\) by a unary prefix giving the bit length of \(z+1\), a zero delimiter, then the binary expansion of \(z+1\). The list contains every symbol explicitly; neither grammar compression nor an oracle representation is allowed. Let \(L\) be the total number of input bits.

A feasible output is an explicit string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) such that, for each \(i\), there are strings \(u_i,v_i\) with \(w=u_i s_i v_i\). Occurrences are ordinary forward contiguous substrings; reversal, reverse complementation, subsequences and cyclic wraparound are not allowed. The objective \(|w|\) counts symbols, not bits. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) as the minimum feasible length. Concatenating the input strings proves feasibility and finiteness. Empty and repeated input strings are allowed. If the list is empty or every member is empty, the optimum is zero, and every finite-factor algorithm must return the empty string. Strings contained in other input strings may be removed by preprocessing, but that work is charged.

An admissible algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program. For its chosen ratio \(r\), some constants \(K>0\) and integer \(d\ge1\) bound its total steps by \(K(L+1)^d\) on every encoded input. It rejects malformed encodings within that bound. On valid inputs it always outputs a feasible string satisfying the claimed ratio. Reading, preprocessing, integer and symbol operations and writing the complete output all count as bit steps. The program has no advice, randomness or free oracle. Its program and polynomial may depend on \(r\), but not on input size or on the instance.

The infimum is over ratios achievable with one such global guarantee. It need not itself be achievable by a single algorithm. Known constant-factor algorithms make the set nonempty, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}\) is finite and at least one. A lower bound on this infimum concerns all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms; a bad input for one particular heuristic is insufficient. No separation assumption such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is built into this existence question. In particular, an algorithmic or hardness claim conditional on an assumption yields only a conditional bound unless that assumption is also proved.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that a uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm always outputs a superstring at most twice optimal in length, or rule out every such algorithm on the specified list encoding.
cards.why: A long-standing approximation threshold for a basic string-assembly problem with direct algorithmic genomics and compression motivation.

cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.
cards.why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.

cards.context:
Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
cards.definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.
cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

cards.context:
A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this card, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.

cards.title: Constant-factor truthful-in-expectation scheduling
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(K\ge1\) such that, for every machine count \(m\ge2\), some family of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms handles every finite job count \(n\ge1\) and every finite nonnegative real processing-time matrix \(t\) with \[\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]\le K\operatorname{OPT}(t)?\] Here \(C(\sigma,t)\) is the makespan of assignment \(\sigma\), as defined below. The factor is independent of \(m,n,t\); arbitrary correlated random assignments and payments are allowed, and computation is unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
\[R(m)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_m}\ \sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0}}
\frac{\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(t)}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_m\) consists of the families satisfying the incentive and zero-optimum conditions below. 

Jobs, machines and private costs. Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). There are \(m\ge2\) machines and \(n\ge1\) indivisible jobs. Machine \(i\) has a private type \(t_i=(t_{i1},\ldots,t_{in})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Executing a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). All entries are finite; zero is allowed. The times on different machines and jobs have no promised relation. Every job is assigned exactly once, and all jobs assigned to one machine are executed sequentially. There are no release times, precedences, eligibility restrictions, migration, preemption or interactions between different jobs' costs.

Direct mechanisms. Reports have the same domain as types. For each report matrix \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), a mechanism specifies numbers
\[q_\sigma(b)\ge0\quad(\sigma:[n]\to[m]),\qquad\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(b)=1,\]
and a finite real expected payment \(p_i(b)\in\mathbb R\) to each machine. Thus the outcome at each fixed report is a distribution on the finite set of \(m^n\) assignments. Define the marginal assignment probability
\[x_{ij}(b)=\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(j)=i}q_\sigma(b).\]
The numbers \(q_\sigma(b)\) may be arbitrary reals, and assignments of different jobs need not be independent. Payments can be deterministic amounts \(p_i(b)\): allowing random payments with finite expectations makes no difference to the risk-neutral utility or objective here. Positive payments are received by the machine. No individual rationality, budget balance, sign restriction, transfer bound, anonymity or task-independence condition is imposed.

Truthfulness in expectation. For every machine \(i\), true type \(t_i\), alternative report \(b_i\), and fixed reports \(b_{-i}\) of all other machines, require
\[p_i(t_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{-i})
\ \ge\ p_i(b_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{-i}).\]
This is the dominant-strategy condition for expected payment minus true processing cost. Only one agent's report changes in this comparison. There is no prior distribution on types, expectation over other players' reports, or assumption that those reports are honest. The expectation is over the mechanism's own allocation randomness. Truthfulness of each deterministic rule obtained by fixing a random seed is not required.

Performance. When the report matrix equals the true matrix \(t\), an assignment has makespan
\[C(\sigma,t)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}t_{ij},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min_{\sigma:[n]\to[m]}C(\sigma,t).\]
The expectation in the formal statement is the finite sum \(\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(t)C(\sigma,t)\). It is the expected maximum load, not the maximum of the expected loads. Payments do not enter the makespan. The optimum uses the same machines and jobs with full knowledge of the true processing times. For every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\), an admissible mechanism must have expected makespan zero; division by zero is omitted from the displayed supremum. All positive-optimum instances and all job counts are included, with no additive error term.

Optimization over mechanisms. For a fixed \(m\), a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_m\) precisely when each member has the stated domain and satisfies truthfulness and the zero-optimum condition at every report profile. Its supremum ratio may be infinite. The infimum is finite because a truthful minimum-total-cost allocation has ratio at most \(m\), so \(1\le R(m)\le m\). A single family must meet its ratio simultaneously for every \(n\) and \(t\); it cannot be chosen after the true instance is known. Different job counts and machine counts may have different rules, and no uniform finite program, computability, representation or time bound is required. The selected problem is an incentive-theoretic extremum over mathematical rules on real reports. A bit encoding or efficient sampling requirement would change that class.

Attainment and asymptotics. The infimum need not be attained. To establish \(R(m)\le u\), it is enough to have admissible families with ratios at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The constants in the requested asymptotic comparison must be independent of \(m\), \(n\), and all processing times. The finite distribution on assignments at each individual report must not be confused with a report-independent finite or countable distribution over entire deterministic truthful mechanisms; the latter is an additional restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one finite approximation factor works for every machine count through truthful-in-expectation mechanisms satisfying the stated bound on expected makespan. A refutation must rule out every finite universal factor.
cards.why: Quantifies how much load-balancing efficiency must be lost solely to multidimensional private costs when randomization and unrestricted payments are available. Matching asymptotic bounds would show whether expected-utility incentives can overcome the linear loss now known for deterministic truthful scheduling.

references.title: Universally truthful mechanisms for scheduling
references.authors: Georgios Anastasiadis; George Christodoulou; Elias Koutsoupias; Annamária Kovács; Conrad Schecker
references.locator: v1, 11 September 2026; §2.4 and §3.1, Theorem 3, Theorem 4 and Corollary 2; n denotes machines in the paper; lower bound restricts to countably supported mixtures of deterministic truthful rules; new preprint claim not independently certified

cards.context:
A machine can report a different processing-time vector to reduce the work it receives. Payments give the scheduler a way to counteract that incentive. Because a machine can be fast on one job and slow on another, its type is multidimensional; a single reported speed describes a substantially different model. The goal here measures the schedule at honest reports, while honesty must be optimal even when other machines report arbitrary vectors.

Total processing cost and makespan impose different objectives. A truthful minimum-total-cost allocation assigns each job to a cheapest machine, with appropriate payments. Its makespan is at most its total cost, which is at most the total cost of an optimal makespan assignment and hence at most \(m\operatorname{OPT}(t)\). This explains a universal factor \(m\). With complete information and unlimited computation, an optimal makespan assignment exists; the issue in this card is the additional incentive constraint.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that no deterministic truthful mechanism improves the worst-case factor \(m\). The result was posted in 2023 and published online in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It settles the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture without a computational hardness assumption. It does not give the same lower bound for truthfulness in expectation.

Universal truthfulness means that the mechanism samples a deterministic truthful rule from a report-independent distribution. Truthfulness in expectation asks only that honest reporting maximize expected utility and permits a larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\) for this larger class. Their theorem allows arbitrary finite processing times, including zero, and is independent of computational limitations.

Lu and Yu give the general truthful-in-expectation guarantee \((m+5)/2\). Together with the deterministic upper bound and the unrestricted randomized lower bound, the inspected literature gives
\[2-\frac1m\le R(m)\le\min\left\{m,\frac{m+5}{2}\right\}.\]
Thus the general gap remains between a constant and a linear function. The same WINE paper reports a linear lower bound under its task-independence restriction; that restricted conclusion cannot be transferred to the whole class defining \(R\).

Correlations matter even when every individual assignment probability is fixed. Take \(m\) unit jobs on \(m\) machines, with every processing time equal to one. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly chosen machine gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\) and makespan \(m\). Assigning the jobs by a uniformly chosen bijection also gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\), but makespan one. Both have expected load one on every machine. Expected utilities depend only on the marginal probabilities and expected payments, whereas expected makespan also depends on the joint assignment distribution.

The 11 September 2026 preprint of Anastasiadis and coauthors claims a lower bound \((3/2-\sqrt2)(m-1)\) for universally truthful mechanisms given by countably supported distributions over deterministic rules, and a universal upper bound \(m/2+o(m)\). The authors discuss extension to uncountable support as an expectation, not a proved theorem. These claims concern a stricter incentive model than this card. In particular, finitely many possible assignments at any fixed report do not imply a countably supported mixture of truthful rules over all reports. The new proof has not been independently certified here.

Small-instance bounds concern different extrema. Kuryatnikova and Vera place the optimal ratio for two machines and two jobs within their randomized monotone, task-independent, scale-free class between \(1.5059953\) and \(1.5059964\). Their scale-free restriction means that multiplying all processing times by one positive constant leaves an allocation rule unchanged. Their mechanisms permit correlated random choices; task independence of a fixed rule is not the same as statistical independence of job assignments. Neither that interval nor the selected restricted mechanism class determines the full \(R(m)\).

A bounded answer would show that randomization keeps the incentive cost of private processing times under control as the system grows. An unbounded answer would show a persistent efficiency loss even with risk-neutral agents and unrestricted transfers. Matching bounds would quantify that loss. Extra assumptions about independent types, Bayesian incentives, fractional execution or computational efficiency describe other questions and cannot be used silently in this one.

cards.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) and one uniform deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol which, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every profile of \(n\) nonatomic additive cake valuations, makes at most \(Cn^d\) queries and produces a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the entire cake satisfying
\[
 \mu_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_j)\qquad\text{for every }1\le i,j\le n?
\]
Every allocated piece may be a finite union of intervals. The allocation must be complete and exactly envy-free on every profile and for every valid choice of cut-query responses.
cards.definitions:
The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent \(i\)'s valuation \(\mu_i\) is an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure: it is nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu_i([0,1])=1\), and \(\mu_i(\{x\})=0\) for every point \(x\). A piece is a finite union of intervals, with endpoints assigned consistently to make the pieces disjoint. Endpoints have zero value for every agent. Measures need not have densities, and there is no bound on density, number of breakpoints or description complexity. No distribution over profiles is assumed.

The protocol receives \(n\) and accesses valuations only through these exact oracles:

\(\operatorname{Eval}(i,x,y)\), for known marks \(0\le x\le y\le1\), returns \(\mu_i([x,y])\).

\(\operatorname{Cut}(i,x,\alpha)\), for a known mark \(x\) and a requested real value \(0\le\alpha\le\mu_i([x,1])\), returns some \(y\in[x,1]\) such that \(\mu_i([x,y])=\alpha\). This returned coordinate becomes a known mark. Initially only \(0\) and \(1\) are known. Nonatomicity guarantees existence of an answer. If an interval has zero value, a cut may have several valid positions; every such response must preserve the guarantee. The protocol must issue only valid queries.

Each evaluation or cut call counts as one query. The protocol may combine interval values by additivity and use previously learned values without paying again. It may query one agent at a mark obtained from another. The final allocation must use endpoints among the known marks; arbitrary newly guessed endpoints are not available as free cuts.

Uniformity means one finite program for all \(n\). Between queries it may use integer computation, store and copy exact real answers, perform real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero number, and compare real numbers exactly. Its program has rational real constants and may perform arbitrary finite loops and finite searches. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; no time, memory or bit-precision bound is imposed on this local computation. It must nevertheless terminate after finitely many operations on every allowed execution. This specifies a query model with exact real arithmetic, not a Turing computation of the digits of arbitrary valuation reals.

The output lists, for each agent, finitely many intervals with known endpoints. Their union covers \([0,1]\), and no interior point belongs to two agents' pieces. Shared boundary points are assigned to one incident piece. Empty pieces are allowed, but no positive-length residue may be discarded, even if all agents value it at zero.

Envy-freeness compares all pieces using the evaluating agent's own measure. It requires every displayed inequality exactly, with no additive or multiplicative fairness error. It does not require a connected piece per agent or impose any incentive-compatibility condition. The query bound is worst-case over both valuation profiles and valid oracle responses. There is no randomization or favorable-profile exception.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one protocol and constants satisfying the statement, with proofs of query validity, termination, complete allocation, exact envy-freeness and the uniform polynomial query bound; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence claim in the specified model.

A protocol with an arbitrary finite bound depending on \(n\), a polynomial average-case or approximate-fairness guarantee, or a protocol leaving cake unallocated is insufficient. A lower bound for one particular procedure does not rule out all polynomial-query protocols. This is an existence question about an exact fairness property and an asymptotic resource bound, so numerical approximation of envy does not meet the answer criterion.
cards.why: The question asks how much preference information is necessary to divide a continuous resource exactly without anyone preferring another person’s share. A polynomial query bound would separate the information needed for fairness from the enormous bounds in existing general protocols.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent two
cards.formal: Does the matrix multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\) equal two? Precisely, writing \(s(n)\) for the minimum arithmetic gate count of an exact circuit multiplying two \(n\times n\) complex matrices, is it true that \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2},\qquad s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}?\] The circuit family and its constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\); an \(O(n^2)\) bound is not required.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required \(n^2\) outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). Use an [arithmetic circuit](definitions.html#arithmetic-circuits) over \(\mathbb C\), with input variables, arbitrary field constants, and binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The binary target is \(\omega=2\), with the positive-slack convention just stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an upper bound \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\) on the specified arithmetic-circuit size over \(\mathbb C\), or show that some positive \(\varepsilon\) admits no such bound.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

cards.context:
The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The selected target is the familiar conjecture \(\omega=2\). Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, a separate circuit family and constant are permitted for every positive slack in the exponent. This is weaker than requiring an \(O(n^2)\) circuit-size bound and is distinct from numerical approximation of the exponent.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An upper bound strictly above two does not by itself settle this binary question. Conversely, a negative answer must prove \(\omega>2\) for unrestricted circuits, rather than a barrier for one tensor framework.

cards.title: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing
cards.formal: Is polynomial identity testing for explicitly represented arithmetic circuits over the integers in deterministic polynomial time? More precisely, do a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, on every valid circuit encoding of bit length \(N\), \(A\) decides whether the output is the zero formal polynomial and halts within \(C(N+2)^k\) steps?
cards.definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Each input node is either one of the explicitly listed variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or a signed integer constant given in binary. Each internal gate has two ordered predecessors and computes addition, subtraction or multiplication over \(\mathbb Z\). Intermediate results may be used by several later gates; the graph need not be a formula. A topological list of all nodes, their labels, predecessor indices and the output index is supplied, with the full variable list and all bits of every constant included in the input length \(N\). Repeated use of a variable or predecessor is allowed. Gates compute in the commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and the zero polynomial means that every coefficient is exactly zero. No division, exponentiation, comparison, oracle or approximate-arithmetic gate is present. There is no depth restriction, multilinearity promise or bound on the number of nonzero monomials. No separate polynomial bound on total degree is promised: repeated multiplication can give a degree exponential in the circuit description length. The algorithm has access to the complete graph and labels, not only an oracle for evaluations. Its running time counts bit-level Turing-machine operations, including all work on constants and any integers it computes; unbounded-size integer operations are not free. Correctness is exact on every valid encoding, with no randomness or advice. Malformed encodings are rejected within the same polynomial bound. One fixed machine and one fixed polynomial bound must work for all numbers of variables, circuits, degrees and integer constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated bit model. A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm correct for every allowed circuit, including those of exponential degree. A negative answer must exclude every deterministic machine with any fixed polynomial time bound; a lower bound for one procedure does not suffice. Results only for formulas, restricted depth, bounded-read circuits, sparse polynomials or a restricted degree regime do not resolve the full target. An evaluation-only lower bound without the explicit circuit-description promise also does not refute it. Numerical agreement at sampled inputs does not establish a formal identity.
cards.why: Polynomial identity testing is a central concrete derandomization problem: a polynomial may be identically zero because of cancellations invisible in the circuit syntax. A deterministic polynomial-time test would affect symbolic computation and numerous algebraic algorithms, and is known to imply major circuit lower bounds. This places the question at the intersection of efficient verification of algebraic identities and fundamental complexity limitations.

cards.context:
Two very different circuit expressions can represent the same polynomial. For instance, \((x+y)^2-x^2-2xy-y^2\) is zero as a formal polynomial. Identity testing asks for this conclusion without first expanding an expression that may contain exponentially many monomials.

The circuit description is part of the input. Its reuse of intermediate values can compress a large polynomial into a small graph, but the algorithm may inspect that graph. This differs from access only to a polynomial’s values, without any representation-size promise.

Strozecki’s enumeration survey explicitly identifies deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for arithmetic-circuit representations as a major unresolved step. The discussion explains why identity tests arise in procedures that generate the monomials of an implicitly represented polynomial.

The card adopts the standard integer-circuit, bit-complexity version of that direction, as explicitly defined in the 2026 STACS paper. Binary integer constants are included with their encoding cost. The target neither gives free arbitrary field constants nor silently bounds the circuit’s degree.

Randomized polynomial-time identity testing is known with one-sided error: the zero polynomial is always recognized as zero, while a nonzero polynomial is rejected with a fixed probability bounded away from zero. The requested change is a fully deterministic, all-input guarantee in polynomial time.

Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove that a polynomial-time deterministic identity test would force a major lower bound for Boolean circuits or for arithmetic circuits computing the permanent. This implication explains why removing randomness here is consequential. It does not make the task identical to proving any one chosen arithmetic lower bound.

Černý and Seppelt’s 2026 work shows that the same general identity-testing problem governs certain equivalence questions for graphs and weighted tree automata. Their reductions retain identity testing as a derandomization condition; they do not supply the requested deterministic test.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives deterministic identity tests for special expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} f_i^d\), where the \(f_i\) are sparse low-degree polynomials and the common power \(d\) is sufficiently large relative to \(r\). The input structure and parameter conditions are essential, and its polynomial bounds in those degree parameters do not cover all circuits in time polynomial in their bit length.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit field representation \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\) and every dense polynomial \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\ge1\), the algorithm outputs the complete irreducible factorization of \(f\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\bigr)^d
\]
bit operations?

The input includes the prime \(p\), the supplied monic irreducible field modulus \(h\), and every coefficient of \(f\). The algorithm and the constants are independent of \(n,p,h\) and \(f\), and no unproved number-theoretic assumption is allowed.
cards.definitions:
Let \(p\ge2\) be a prime, let \(e\ge1\), and let \(h(t)\in\mathbb F_p[t]\) be a monic irreducible polynomial of degree \(e\). The field \(\mathbb F_p\) is the integers modulo \(p\), and \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\), where \(q=p^e\), is the field of residue classes modulo \(h\). Its elements are represented uniquely by polynomials of degree less than \(e\), with each coefficient in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). Addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication followed by reduction modulo \(p\) and \(h\).

The input writes \(p,e,n\) in binary, all coefficients of \(h\), and all \(n+1\) coefficients of \(f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jx^j\), with \(a_n\ne0\). Each field coefficient uses its full \(e\)-tuple of residues, each residue occupying \(\lceil\log_2p\rceil\) bits. Integer and array boundaries use a fixed unambiguous encoding. In particular, the polynomial is dense: zero coefficients are present, and neither a circuit nor an evaluation oracle substitutes for the coefficient list. The field representation is also part of the counted input, rather than fixed advice. Primality of \(p\) and irreducibility and degree of \(h\) are promises; constructing \(h\) from \(p,e\) is not an additional output task. No correctness condition is imposed on malformed or unpromised inputs.

A nonconstant polynomial \(g\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) is irreducible if it cannot be written as the product of two polynomials of positive degree over this same field. Monic means that its leading coefficient is one. A complete factorization consists of a nonzero field element \(u\), a list of pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) of positive degree, and positive binary integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), satisfying the exact polynomial identity
\[
f=u\prod_{i=1}^r g_i^{m_i}.
\]
All factors are written as dense coefficient lists in the supplied field representation. The order of factors is irrelevant. Multiplicities are required, including for repeated factors in positive characteristic; there is no square-free or separability promise. Merely deciding irreducibility, returning a proper factor, or finding roots when they exist is not the specified output.

Time is worst-case deterministic bit time on a standard multitape Turing machine. Reading, arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factorization all count. The full input length is polynomially related to \(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\), so the displayed bound is equivalent to a single polynomial bound in that length. It is not polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(p\) or \(q\). There is no random tape, oracle, uncharged field operation or family of field-specific algorithms. Extension degree and characteristic may both grow with the input.

The target is an existence proposition about an exact symbolic factorization algorithm. Absolute numerical approximation does not replace the polynomial identity or irreducibility conditions.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and a complete Lean-checked proof that it terminates with the specified complete factorization on every valid input and obeys one bound of the displayed form. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no deterministic algorithm with any such absolute polynomial bound exists.

An expected-time randomized algorithm, an average over inputs or primes, polynomial dependence on the field cardinality or characteristic, a restriction on degree or Galois group, or a bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle this proposition. The failure of a particular method is not a proof of the negative answer.
cards.why: Finite-field factorization is a basic operation in computer algebra and coding theory. Randomized polynomial-time algorithms are available, while a deterministic algorithm must handle every coefficient list and every characteristic without trying a number of possibilities proportional to the field size. The question isolates a central derandomization gap in an exact algebraic task.

cards.title: Sum-of-square-roots problem
cards.formal:
Does the sum-of-square-roots decision problem belong to deterministic polynomial time? An instance explicitly gives an integer \(n\ge1\), signed integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\), and positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), all in binary. The required answer is whether
\[
E(c,a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\sqrt{a_i}\ \ge0,
\]
where each square root is the nonnegative real square root. There is no promise that \(E\ne0\), that the radicands are distinct or square-free, or that their magnitudes are polynomial in \(n\). The target is one uniform deterministic algorithm with a polynomial bound in the total input bit length. This selects the standard algorithmic question explicitly stated in the newer sources; the original TOPP entry principally asks for tight separation bounds, a related quantitative question distinguished below.
cards.definitions:
For \(a>0\), \(\sqrt a\) denotes the unique real \(r\ge0\) with \(r^2=a\). Coefficients may be positive, negative or zero, and repeated terms are permitted. The comparison is exact: when \(E=0\) the answer is yes, however close a nonzero \(E\) is to zero. No approximate value of \(E\), promise of a numerical gap or factorization of the radicands is supplied.

Fix the following binary encoding. For an integer \(r\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\); its code is \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary expansion of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(c\) is encoded by the code of \(2c\) if \(c\ge0\), and of \(-2c-1\) otherwise. A valid instance is the code for \(n\ge1\), followed by the signed code for \(c_i\) and the code for \(a_i\ge1\), for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\) in order, with no trailing bits. Write \(L\) for the full encoded length. Define the language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) to consist exactly of valid encodings for which \(E(c,a)\ge0\); every malformed string is outside \(Q\).

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its fixed alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tapes have nonnegative integer cell indices, all heads start at zero, and the input tape holds the input bits followed by blanks. One transition reads all scanned symbols, updates the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at zero stays at zero. Two halting states output zero and one. Each transition costs one, including all parsing and arithmetic work. The program and number of tapes are independent of the instance. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, exact-real register or unit-cost square-root instruction.

The statement \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\) means
\[
\exists M\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:
\]
the single machine \(M\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions and outputs one exactly when \(x\in Q\). Thus the clock holds on every binary input, and all binary magnitudes contribute to the measured length. No running-time dependence exponential in \(n\), in the largest radicand or in its bit length is hidden in the polynomial constants.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\), or that \(Q\notin\mathrm{P}\), for the stated encoding and machine model. A positive answer must provide the one finite machine and polynomial constants and prove termination, the uniform time bound and both correctness directions on all inputs. A negative answer must show that for every such machine \(M\) and every \(C\ge1,d\ge0\), some binary input either is not answered within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions or is answered incorrectly.

A proof for equality testing alone, unary inputs, a fixed number of terms, inputs separated from zero by a promised gap, or a unit-cost real-arithmetic model does not meet the criterion. Nor does a lower bound against a particular numerical procedure prove the negative answer. This is an unconditional yes/no complexity question: a conditional separation of complexity classes or a merely conditional algorithm does not decide it.
cards.why: This is a basic barrier between exact geometric algorithms and computation on finite binary inputs. A general polynomial-time comparison procedure would remove a recurring obstacle to placing geometric decision and verification tasks in familiar discrete complexity classes. The problem also connects algebraic-number representation, exact numerical computation and the complexity of arithmetic circuits.

cards.context:
Euclidean distances between points with integer coordinates are square roots of integers. Comparing the lengths of two routes therefore leads to sums of these quantities. Binary input represents the integers compactly, while the comparison may depend on a very small difference between real numbers. Exact equality is part of the problem, rather than an excluded case.

TOPP Problem 33 primarily asks for tight upper and lower bounds on the minimum nonzero gap between two \(k\)-term square-root sums whose radicands are bounded by an integer \(B\). Its motivation asks whether the number of bits needed to separate the sums is polynomial in \(k\) and \(\log B\). This card explicitly chooses the standard polynomial-time decision question from the newer primary literature instead of presenting that separation problem as equivalent to it.

A sufficiently strong uniform separation bound would imply an efficient exact comparison algorithm. The converse is not asserted: TOPP explicitly allows that a polynomial-time comparison algorithm could exist even if its proposed precision bound fails. The algorithmic target places no requirement on how an algorithm represents its intermediate computation.

The signed-integer coefficient convention is the one used by Eisenbrand, Haeberle and Singer. The sign-list formulation in other references has the same polynomial-time decision status under polynomially related binary encodings. The card does not restrict to geometric instances, unary magnitudes or square-free radicands.

The 2024 separation theorem has a positive factor depending on the full tuple of radicands, without an explicit uniform bound on that dependence. Its improved dependence on the coefficients does not itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary binary instances. The unary result of Balaji and Datta instead supplies polynomial-size circuits, or polynomial-length advice depending on the input length; this is a different guarantee from one uniform algorithm.

Testing whether the sum is exactly zero is known to be polynomial-time decidable. Distinguishing a positive sum from a negative one remains the extra requirement. Recent work on succinct arithmetic-program encodings and on efficient practical exact comparison addresses other models or guarantees.

progress.text: The last listed TOPP revision records the separation problem and explicitly distinguishes a polynomial precision bound from the possibility of a polynomial-time sign algorithm.

Gaillard and Jindal distinguish the already polynomial-time equality problem for explicitly represented integers from generalized versions with arithmetic-program inputs. Their results for power series and succinct equality do not decide general sign comparison.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal restate the signed-root decision problem and its relation to positivity of straight-line-program outputs. Their sum-of-squares results concern arithmetic-program problems and do not settle this decision problem.
