cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.
cards.why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

cards.context:
One transmitter must convey two independent messages through a single stream of inputs. Each receiver sees its own noisy observations, so the possible pairs of reliable rates form a tradeoff region. Unlike an interference channel, there are no separately informed transmitters. This is a central network information theory question because even the general two-receiver case lacks a known evaluable capacity characterization in the checked sources.

The two individual capacities do not determine the joint region. If the same noiseless input bit reaches both receivers, either receiver alone can receive one bit per use, but the private rates satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le1\). If the input is instead a pair of bits and each receiver receives its designated bit, the region is \([0,1]^{2}\), although both individual capacities are still one. These examples distinguish the shared resource in the question from two independent point-to-point capacity calculations.

Marton’s 1979 region is a general achievable inner bound, and the original paper identifies channel classes for which capacity is known. Its two independent private messages match this card. The original separate average-error requirements and this card’s vanishing probability that either decoder fails are equivalent by elementary probability bounds; neither is the maximal-message error criterion.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite bounds on the auxiliary alphabet sizes in Marton’s inner region, making that region closed and computable. Their formulation permits a common message; setting its rate to zero gives the private-message slice relevant here. They also establish that this inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region can differ. This gap alone does not identify which bound is loose, and computability of an inner region does not establish its equality with capacity.

Geng and coauthors determine capacity for certain product-channel classes and prove that the UV outer bound is not always tight. Their full version also explains the multiletter sum-rate characterization: normalized Marton sum rates on successively longer repeated channels recover the operational sum capacity in the limit. This limiting equality supplies no general finite stopping guarantee for the numerical answer requested here. Nonadditivity of Marton’s inner bound must not be confused with a failure of the usual rate normalization for repeated uses of the channel itself.

Dou and coauthors give numerical methods for evaluating several inner and outer bounds. Their Theorems 5–7 prove convergence under explicit hypotheses: the initial distribution and a global maximizer must lie in a suitable connected superlevel set, and the objective must be concave there. These are conditional convergence results, not an unconditional global capacity evaluator. Even exact optimization of a bound would still leave the issue of its tightness. Their numerical conventions use natural logarithms unless otherwise specified; this card fixes bits throughout.

Gohari, Liu and Nair’s 2026 manuscript strengthens sum-rate outer bounds through two auxiliary receivers, with a full-region version in its appendix and numerical improvements for skew-symmetric examples. The auxiliary receivers are proof variables, not extra terminals available to a code. The reported improvements still leave inner/outer gaps and do not give the general function.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s preprint of 20 August 2026 claims strict suboptimality of the complete one-letter Marton region. A fixed-input-distribution example has ternary input; their separate constraint-removal theorem and explicit construction produce an unconstrained channel on a much larger finite alphabet. Section III.D specifies rational mixing probabilities and a rational joint channel, so that example is within this card’s domain. It should not be described as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample. The claim concerns a gap from an inner bound, not a matching capacity evaluation. Its full proof and interval-arithmetic certificates were not independently verified or rerun in this review.

The rational-table domain is the saved editorial specialization of the general capacity question. The absolute \(1/100\) acceptance rule follows the numerical formulation of 12 September 2026 and is retained here. It is not an assertion of exact equality with any proposed capacity curve. The checked literature discusses the underlying exact characterization; this review does not infer that a historical open-status statement alone proves that the fixed-tolerance benchmark remains unsolved.

cards.title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
cards.formal:
Do there exist an integer \(q\ge1\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\), such that for every integer message length \(k\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\) with \(k\le n\le Ck^d\), an injective encoding
\[
 E_k:\{0,1\}^k\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,
\]
and randomized local decoders \(D_{k,i}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), satisfying
\[
 \Pr[D_{k,i}^{\,z}=x_i]\ge\frac23
\]
for every message \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) and every received word \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) differing from \(E_k(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) coordinates, while each decoder reads at most \(q\) bits of \(z\) on every execution?
cards.definitions:
Here \(k\) counts message bits and \(n\) counts stored codeword bits. The Hamming distance between two length-\(n\) words is the number of coordinates where they differ. The allowed corruptions are precisely the words at Hamming distance strictly less than \(\delta n\), as in the source definition. In particular the uncorrupted codeword is included. The constants \(q,C,d,\delta\) are fixed before \(k\); they do not depend on the message, requested coordinate, corruption or code length. The blocklength \(n=n(k)\), encoding and decoder descriptions may depend on \(k\). Polynomial blocklength does not require constant rate or a polynomial of any prescribed degree.

This is an existence question in the classical randomized bit-query model. For fixed \(k,n,i,E_k\), a deterministic query procedure is a finite binary decision tree of depth at most \(q\). Each internal node is labelled by a coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\); the oracle returns the single bit \(z_j\), and this chooses the next child. Each leaf is labelled by the output bit zero or one. A randomized decoder is a probability distribution over such trees, fixed independently of \(x\) and \(z\). This describes adaptive queries: later coordinates may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries count toward the same bound, and early stopping is allowed. The tree distribution may depend on the requested index and the code, but the only information it learns about the actual received word is through the queried bits.

The probability in the statement is solely over that decoder's private randomness. The guarantee holds separately for every triple \((x,z,i)\); a single random choice need not decode all message coordinates at once. Corruptions may depend on the full encoding and message and are computationally unrestricted, but \(z\) is fixed before the decoder draws its randomness. There is no secret key or randomness shared with the channel. The output is one bit: an erasure symbol, a candidate list or success only averaged over requested indices does not meet the definition.

Encoding linearity, systematic form and local correction of every codeword coordinate are not required. There is no bound on encoding time, decoder computation between queries or description length, and no additional requirement that one efficient uniform program construct the family. The finite decision-tree formulation makes the query resource explicit without granting access to any unqueried received bits. Codes must be available for every message length under one set of constants; a finite catalogue or a query bound growing with \(k\) does not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this existence statement, specifying or proving the existence of the encodings and decoders and verifying the common constants, polynomial blocklength, worst-case query bound and all corruption/success quantifiers; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

An efficient explicit construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative proof must rule out every fixed query count and every polynomial degree, including nonlinear codes and the unrestricted decoder model. A lower bound only for two or three queries, only for matching-vector constructions, or only for locally correctable codes does not establish that negation. Relaxed, approximate, list or amortized decoding and growing-alphabet symbol queries require a proved conversion meeting the exact binary single-bit requirements. No approximation tolerance applies to the yes/no target.
cards.why: Determine whether a constant number of bit probes can recover any requested message bit despite a constant fraction of adversarial corruptions using only polynomial storage. This is a central locality-versus-redundancy question with connections to private information retrieval and complexity theory.

cards.context:
Local decoding retrieves one chosen message bit without scanning the stored codeword. The positive constant corruption fraction prevents a direct read of a systematically stored bit from meeting the requirement.

The textbook gives polynomial-length binary codes with polylogarithmic query complexity and asks whether the query count can be constant. Its cited constant-query constructions instead have superpolynomial blocklength.

The general odd-query lower bounds apply even to nonlinear binary codes. For each fixed query count their blocklength bounds are polynomial, so they leave open a sufficiently large polynomial exponent in this existence question.

The August 2026 matching-vector bound yields superpolynomial length within a particular three-query construction framework at fixed modulus. The target permits other encodings and any fixed query count.

The subsequent August preprint also bounds three-restricted matching-vector families, without claiming a lower bound for every binary locally decodable code.

Relaxed decoders may report failure on some corrupted inputs. Their shorter codes and theorems comparing relaxed and full decoding do not automatically give the required success on every requested message bit.

The September 2026 construction combines relaxed outputs with amortizing queries over a consecutive block of message symbols. Constant queries per recovered symbol in that model are different from a constant total number of probes to recover any one requested bit.

cards.title: Li–Li conjecture
cards.formal:
For every network instance \(I\) defined below, is
\[\mathcal C(I)=\mathcal R(I)?\]
Here \(\mathcal C(I)\) is the closure of the rate vectors supported by finite deterministic causal zero-error network codes, with an entropy capacity shared between the two directions of every undirected edge. The region \(\mathcal R(I)\) consists of all rates supported by fractional multicommodity routing. The quantification includes every finite network size, every positive rational capacity vector, every finite list of independent unicast sessions, every finite message and symbol alphabet, every causal schedule and every nonlinear local encoding function.
cards.definitions:
Network and sessions. An instance is \(I=(G,c,((s_i,t_i))_{i=1}^k)\). The supply graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, simple and undirected, with at least two vertices; an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Each edge \(e\) has a capacity \(c_e\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). The number of sessions \(k\) is a positive integer, and \(s_i,t_i\in V\) with \(s_i\ne t_i\). Different sessions may share either endpoint, have opposite directions, or have the same ordered endpoint pair. Such sessions still carry independent messages, each required at its own single destination.

Messages and initial knowledge. Choose a nonempty finite alphabet \(A_i\) for each session. The random variables \(M_i\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \(A_i\); singleton alphabets are allowed. Initially, a vertex \(v\) knows exactly the tuple of messages with \(s_i=v\), along with the fixed instance and code. Thus a destination can also know messages of other sessions for which it is itself a source. There is no additional message-dependent initial information and no private or shared random seed. Local computation and storage have no resource bound.

Causal finite code. Before messages are sampled, fix a nonnegative integer \(L\), a schedule \((u_\ell,v_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) with \(\{u_\ell,v_\ell\}\in E\), and nonempty finite transmitted-symbol alphabets \(\Sigma_\ell\). At step \(\ell\), the sender \(u_\ell\) sends \(Z_\ell\in\Sigma_\ell\) to \(v_\ell\). Its encoding function is an arbitrary deterministic function of all messages initially at \(u_\ell\) and the tuple of symbols received there at steps strictly less than \(\ell\). Previously sent symbols are already functions of that information. The schedule and alphabets do not depend on the messages; timing and unrecorded silence carry no extra information. For each \(i\), a deterministic decoder at \(t_i\), applied to its initially known messages and all symbols received there, must output \(M_i\) for every tuple in \(\prod_{j=1}^k A_j\). This is exact recovery with zero error. Linear encoding is not required.

Entropy and supported rates. All probabilities come from the uniform product distribution of the messages. For a finite random variable \(Z\), write
\[H(Z)=-\sum_{z:\Pr[Z=z]>0}\Pr[Z=z]\log_2\Pr[Z=z].\]
Entropy is measured in bits, so \(H(M_i)=\log_2|A_i|\). For each orientation \(u\to v\) of an edge, let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the ordered tuple of all symbols sent in that direction during the whole schedule; the empty tuple has entropy zero. For a real scale \(b>0\), a code supports \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) if
\[H(M_i)\ge b r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{\{u,v\}}\quad(\{u,v\}\in E).\]
Each directional transcript is measured jointly across its uses, and the two directional entropies are then added. This is not the entropy of their combined bidirectional tuple, nor a separate full-capacity allowance in each direction. The positive scale normalizes messages and edge budgets together. It may depend on the code and need not be an integer. No bound on the schedule length or on the alphabets is imposed in terms of this scale.

Coding region. Let \(\mathcal C_0(I)\) be the set of supported rate vectors over all such finite codes, alphabets and positive scales, and let \(\mathcal C(I)=\overline{\mathcal C_0(I)}\) in the ordinary topology of \(\mathbb R^k\). Explicitly, \(r\in\mathcal C(I)\) means \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(r'\in\mathcal C_0(I)\) with \(\max_i|r_i-r'_i|<\varepsilon\). The closure allows limiting rates; it does not allow decoding errors. This card fixes the inherited entropy-capacity model. Equivalence with a fixed-length bit-budget or vanishing-error definition is not assumed.

Routing region. Let \(\mathcal P_i\) be the finite set of simple paths from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) in \(G\). A vector \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) belongs to \(\mathcal R(I)\) exactly when there are real numbers \(f_{i,P}\ge0\), one for every \(i\) and \(P\in\mathcal P_i\), such that
\[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f_{i,P}\ge r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P_i\\e\in P}}f_{i,P}\le c_e\quad(e\in E).\]
A unit of flow consumes one unit of capacity on every edge of its path, regardless of the traversal direction. Each commodity may split among arbitrarily many of these paths. Flows need not be integral. The region is a closed bounded polytope, since the graph, path lists and capacities are finite and every source differs from its destination. Multicast delivery of one common message to several receivers and recovery of functions instead of messages are different tasks.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal equality or its negation. An affirmative proof must cover all the specified instances, independent finite messages, deterministic causal nonlinear codes and positive scales, and must justify passage to the closure. The familiar inclusion \(\mathcal R(I)\subseteq\mathcal C(I)\) is also part of the checked equality; the substantive conjecture is the reverse inclusion.

A negative answer may give one finite instance, a finite code, a positive scale and a supported rate vector outside \(\mathcal R(I)\). The checked proof must establish every encoder's causality, exact decoding on every message tuple, the transcript-entropy capacity inequalities, and infeasibility of the fractional routing constraints at that rate. This finite-code form loses no possible counterexample: a point of the coding closure outside the closed routing region has a neighborhood disjoint from that region and hence contains a supported finite-code rate.

Beating a particular routing algorithm, integral paths, or a cut bound does not establish a separation from the optimal fractional region. A result for directed edges, correlated messages or multicast does not refute this statement. An impossibility result only for linear encoders does not prove it. Any use of a different error or capacity convention requires a checked implication to the model above. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this exact yes-or-no equality.
cards.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

cards.context:
Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits \(x\) and \(y\), it may send \(x\oplus y\); a receiver that already knows \(y\) can recover \(x\). Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match coding for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide necessary information bounds, but meeting all of them need not make multiple demands fractionally routable. In the unit-capacity \(K_{3,2}\) example, put vertices \(a,b,c\) on one side and \(d,e\) on the other, and use sessions \((a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(d,e)\) at one common rate. The sparsity bound is one, while the maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\). Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval prove that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). Thus a cut–flow gap alone is not a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family whose gap grows as a positive power of \(\log |V|\). General cut–flow bounds give a logarithmic upper bound. Consequently a single strict separation would imply unbounded asymptotic improvements, rather than merely an isolated constant-factor gain.

Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that the conjecture implies an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for Boolean circuits multiplying two \(n\)-bit integers when both fan-in and fan-out are bounded by a constant. Their theorem is conditional on the network-coding conjecture; a multiplication lower bound has not already been obtained from ordinary cut constraints. The bounded-degree circuit model matters to the stated consequence.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

The other August 2026 manuscript reports a session-interaction characterization: universal validity is equivalent to an independence property of every irreducible core. It does not establish this property for every core. Its Definition 3.1 footnote corrects the conference wording so that one common optimal coding solution witnesses all the independence requirements, rather than allowing a separately chosen solution for each pair. The characterization and its restricted cases are recorded as reported progress, with that quantifier correction.

source_formulation.text: The inherited card selected independent uniform messages, deterministic causal zero-error codes, positive real scaling, directional transcript-entropy budgets and closure of the full rate region. These choices are retained. Appendix A of Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman supplies the causal exact-decoding and entropy-capacity framework, and Appendix B the fractional-routing comparison. The review makes initial knowledge at shared source vertices and the scope of every quantifier explicit without replacing the target by multicast, a restricted topology, or a different error convention.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The August 2026 primary manuscripts explicitly retain the general multiple-unicast conjecture. Their restricted topology theorems and session-interaction characterization do not establish it universally; multicast separations have a different demand model. The card retains its precise causal zero-error directional-entropy formulation. No matching general resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search, and external proofs were not independently certified.

progress.text: Li and Li formulate the undirected no-coding-advantage conjecture, as recorded in the subsequent primary literature.
Jain and coauthors prove that the four-session \(K_{3,2}\) example has coding rate equal to routing rate \(3/4\).
Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman show that any constant strict advantage amplifies to a polylogarithmically growing gap.
Afshani and coauthors derive conditional multiplication-circuit lower bounds from the conjecture.
Vamsi–Thakor analyze specified asymmetric demands in layered networks.
Braverman–He give superconstant undirected multicast gaps; the unicast conjecture is explicitly left open.
Liu–Que–Li–Li report metric-based proofs for further network classes, including at most five terminal locations.

A separate session-interaction framework reduces the conjecture to a property of all irreducible cores; it does not establish that property universally. Its manuscript corrects a quantifier in the conference definition to require one common witnessing solution.

sentences: An undirected network carries independent messages, each from one source to one destination, with a common capacity budget for both directions of every edge.
The Li–Li conjecture asks whether arbitrary causal zero-error network coding has exactly the same closed rate region as optimal fractional multicommodity routing.
The card fixes independent finite uniform messages, deterministic encoding, exact decoding and the sum of the two whole-transcript entropies on each edge.
A complete Lean proof must establish the universal equality or certify a finite coding instance whose supported rate is outside the fractional routing region.

Recent restricted topology results and a corrected session-interaction framework leave the general question open, while undirected multicast separations rely on shared messages with multiple receivers.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

cards.context:
Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

cards.context:
A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.
cards.why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.

cards.context:
For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.

cards.title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
cards.definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.
cards.why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.

cards.context:
A set function assigns a value to each possible subset of a ground set. Submodularity says that adding an element cannot become more valuable merely because the receiving set has grown. Equivalently, it satisfies the union/intersection inequality in the definitions. With \(n\) elements there are \(2^{n}\) values, so inspecting a polynomial number of them is a small fraction of the complete object.

Testing allows an unresolved band of nearby nonsubmodular inputs. The tester must accept genuinely submodular functions and reject functions that disagree with every submodular function on at least an \(\varepsilon\)-fraction of subsets. It is not required to reconstruct the closest submodular function or to decide exact membership for every oracle.

Hamming distance treats any changed entry as one disagreement. In contrast, an \(\ell_p\) distance for finite \(p\) averages the magnitudes of changes. Many tiny discrepancies can therefore contribute little to that norm while affecting a large fraction of the table. The published constant-query result for bounded functions in an \(\ell_p\) metric does not imply polynomial-query testing in the Hamming metric used here.

The saved problem asks both for optimal query complexity and, specifically, whether polynomially many queries suffice. This card selects that explicitly posed polynomial threshold as its single yes/no target. The one-sided-error convention is taken from Definition 1.2 of the cited foundational paper. The finite-program exact-real convention makes the value-oracle interpretation explicit; it is not a claim about bit complexity or noisy measurements.

The existing upper and lower bounds leave a substantial gap: known general testing uses a subexponential number of queries for fixed distance, while a nearly quadratic lower bound rules out much smaller sample budgets. Neither result decides whether some fixed polynomial suffices. Bounds on the frequency of a particular kind of local violation also have a narrower scope than a lower bound against every adaptive tester.

progress.text: Seshadhri's Bertinoro problem explicitly asks whether \(\operatorname{poly}(n/\varepsilon)\) queries suffice. The listed matroid-rank and coverage directions are separate special questions, not promises imposed on the general target.

Seshadhri–Vondrák give a one-sided tester with query complexity \((1/\varepsilon)^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) in the small-distance regime. Their Theorem 1.4 also gives examples with few violated squares; that obstruction to this particular local test is not a superpolynomial lower bound for all testers.

Hatami–Vondrák's author manuscript proves an \(\Omega(n^{2}/\log n)\) query lower bound for constant distance in Theorem 1.2. This is still compatible with a polynomial-query tester of larger degree. No later publication venue is inferred for this manuscript.

Blais–Bommireddi prove dimension-independent query bounds for testing \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1]\) under \(\ell_p\) distance for each fixed finite \(p\ge1\) and fixed positive proximity parameter. Theorem 1.1 uses a different distance metric from this card.

Haris–Palit's published k-submodularity paper records the remaining gap for ordinary submodularity. Its constant-query theorem concerns bounded functions in \(\ell_p\) distance; its Hamming-distance results test separate component properties with subexponential bounds. These results do not supply the polynomial Hamming tester asked for here.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

cards.context:
A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. cards.status_note: An open general classification question in the 2022 survey and the published July 2026 Krokhin–Vagnozzi article. The latter resolves a restricted three-element target family; the May 2026 Promise MMSNP preprint gives a logical correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full unconditional finite-pair dichotomy or counterexample. Individual theorem statements and scopes were checked, but their full proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Bulatov proves the ordinary finite-template CSP dichotomy, covering the special case \(A=B\).
Zhuk independently proves the same ordinary CSP dichotomy; the final arXiv revision is dated 2 October 2020.
Brakensiek and Guruswami give a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations; the checked revised manuscript is dated 6 May 2021.
Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz classify all symmetric Boolean promise CSPs without requiring negations.
Barto establishes a tractable finite promise pair whose every finite intermediate exact CSP is NP-complete.
Krokhin and Opršal survey the open general classification and distinguish decision from search.
The Banakh–Barsukov–Nakajima preprint proves the Promise MMSNP correspondence and states a monochromatic-clique dichotomy with conditional hardness; it subsequently appears at LICS 2026.

The published Krokhin–Vagnozzi theorem proves NP-hardness for \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) and completes the three-element symmetric ternary target classification for approximations of exactly-one satisfaction.

sentences: A finite promise CSP distinguishes inputs satisfying stronger local constraints from inputs failing even weaker constraints.
The question asks whether every fixed finite template pair has a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm or is NP-hard under promise-preserving many-one reductions.
The algorithm or reduction may depend on the pair, and no effective procedure for classifying input templates is required.
The ordinary CSP dichotomy and several promise subclasses are known, but relaxing the constraints changes the classification problem substantially.
The checked 2026 results concern restricted families and leave this full unconditional decision dichotomy open in the cited sources.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
cards.definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(N\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

cards.context:
The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.
