cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm{P}\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

Use the shared definition of [NP](definitions.html#p-np). A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.
cards.why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.

cards.context:
The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain. Homogeneity over a finite relational signature also gives quantifier elimination, so each fixed first-order reduct relation can be tested on that finite pattern by a fixed quantifier-free formula.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification. A model-complete core is a homomorphically equivalent template in which every endomorphism agrees, on each finite subset, with some automorphism; an endomorphism is a homomorphism from the template to itself.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open. Here first-order definability means that one fixed first-order sentence on finite inputs decides the CSP, and L denotes deterministic logarithmic work space.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card. The Ramsey condition says that for every pair of finite patterns P,Q and every finite number of colours, a larger finite pattern exists in which every colouring of embeddings of P has a copy of Q whose internal P-embeddings all receive one colour.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(N\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.
cards.why: Many applications need an assignment rather than recognition that an assignment must exist. A universal implication would connect tractability classifications of promise decision problems to actual construction across finite local constraint languages. A separation would identify a fixed finite promise problem whose decision gap is efficiently recognizable while its promised solutions resist every deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm.

cards.context:
The strong template A describes the constraints guaranteed to be simultaneously satisfiable; B describes the weaker constraints an answer must satisfy. The map from A to B proves that a weak answer exists whenever a strong one exists, but the input supplies only that existence promise. A decision algorithm recognizes the promised gap, whereas search must actually construct the weaker assignment.

For graph colouring, one may take A and B to be complete graphs on three and six vertices. Search then asks for a six-colouring of a graph promised to admit a three-colouring. Decision only separates three-colourable graphs from graphs admitting no six-colouring; it has no required behaviour on graphs with chromatic number four, five or six. This example illustrates the promise and does not assert tractability for that particular pair.

A polynomial-time search algorithm implies decision by returning a proposed weak assignment that can be checked. The reverse implication is known for ordinary fixed finite CSPs, where A=B. With two templates, fixing a variable to a weak-domain value can destroy the stronger promise, so ordinary decision self-reducibility does not automatically apply.

Known constructive cases include templates admitting a fixed finite intermediate structure C with A→C→B and tractable CSP(C). The survey also discusses tractable promise problems whose explanation requires more than such a finite intermediate problem, under the usual separation assumptions. Thus the ordinary CSP case does not supply the general statement.

Larrauri studies rounding for three standard decision relaxations: the basic linear program using consistent local distributions, an affine integer program, and their combination. Finding a weak assignment on every input accepted by one of these relaxations can encode arbitrary total NP search problems. A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.

cards.title: Dichotomy for consistent query answering under primary keys
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite relational schema with one designated nonempty primary key for each relation, and every fixed Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) over that schema, is the language \(\operatorname{CERTAINTY}(q)\) either in deterministic polynomial time or coNP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?

The input to this language is an explicitly represented finite database \(D\), possibly violating its keys. It is accepted exactly when \(q\) is true in every inclusion-maximal subdatabase of \(D\) that satisfies the keys. Repeated occurrences of a relation in \(q\), called self-joins, are allowed.
cards.definitions:
A schema lists relation names and their positive integer arities. Each relation has a fixed nonempty subset of its positions as its primary key. A database is a finite set of tuples for each relation, with values encoded as finite binary strings. A key is satisfied if any two tuples agreeing in all key positions also agree in every position. A subdatabase deletes tuples without inserting or changing values. A repair is such a subdatabase that satisfies all keys and cannot be enlarged by putting back any deleted tuple while still satisfying them. Thus, for each nonempty group of conflicting tuples with one key value, a repair chooses exactly one tuple; this is inclusion maximality, not an optimization over all possible edits.

A Boolean conjunctive query is a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms with all its variables existentially quantified; variables may repeat within and across atoms, and fixed constants are allowed. It contains no negation, disjunction, inequality, function symbol or aggregation. Truth means that some assignment of its variables makes every atom a stored tuple. Query and schema, including keys, are fixed separately for each language; only the database varies. Time is measured in the total bit length of its explicit encoding, with constants and polynomial degree allowed to depend on the fixed query/schema.

Use [P and coNP](definitions.html#p-np) and polynomial-time [many-one reductions](definitions.html#reductions) for coNP-completeness. The two-case classification is for each fixed query. It requires neither an effective classifier taking the query as input nor a separation of P from coNP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition. Results for a restricted query family do not settle its universal scope. A conditional negative result must retain its unproved assumptions and is not an unconditional refutation.
cards.why: Conflicting primary-key records are routine in integrated data. This question asks whether every fixed database query is either efficiently answerable with certainty across all repairs or computationally complete for a standard hard class.

Consistent answers retain only conclusions that survive every repair of inconsistent records. The difficulty comes from universal quantification over these alternative databases, even though evaluating the fixed query on one consistent database is easy.

The ICDT 2023 paper formulates the unrestricted primary-key dichotomy and gives a common polynomial-time method covering the known self-join-free and path-query tractable cases. It also explains why that method does not capture all tractable queries with self-joins.

For queries without repeated relation names, the 2019 result sharpens the tractable side to logarithmic space. That restricted classification leaves the universal self-join target stated here.

cards.title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total deterministic algorithm which, given any finite conjunctive query \(q\), decides whether all distinct answers to \(q\) can be enumerated on every finite database \(D\) with \(O_q(N)\) preprocessing time and \(O_q(1)\) worst-case delay?

Self-joins and projection are allowed. Here \(N\) is the database size defined below; the enumeration model is the specified deterministic word-RAM. The classifier has no prescribed running-time bound.
cards.definitions:
A conjunctive query is finite syntax
\[
q(\bar x)=\exists\bar y\;\bigwedge_{i=1}^{s}R_i(\bar z_i).
\]
The head \(\bar x\) is an ordered list of distinct variables, and \(\bar y\) lists the other variables. Each variable occurs in an atom. Each relation symbol has one fixed positive integer arity within the query, and the length of each argument list agrees with it. A symbol may occur in several atoms (a self-join); a variable may repeat within an atom. There are no constants, negation, disequalities, aggregation, or additional constraints on the database. All relation arities and the complete formula are part of the classifier input, not fixed globally. An empty conjunction has no variables and is the constantly true Boolean query.

A database for the query has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for any integer \(n\ge0\), and explicitly lists each relation \(R^D\subseteq[n]^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\). Each tuple occurs at most once in its relation list; list order is arbitrary. Domain elements outside all relations are permitted. Define the word size of the data by
\[
N=1+n+\sum_R\operatorname{arity}(R)\,|R^D|.
\]
All tuple entries and \(n\) are provided as binary integers. In particular, the domain-size contribution to the resource parameter is \(n\), not merely its binary encoding length. No succinct relation representation or data-access oracle is provided.

An assignment maps query variables to domain elements. It satisfies an atom exactly when the resulting tuple belongs to that relation. The answer set \(q(D)\) consists of head tuples having at least one satisfying extension to \(\bar y\). Different witnesses for the same head tuple give just one answer. An empty head gives either no answer or the one empty tuple, according to whether the query is false or true.

For a fixed query, an enumerator is a finite deterministic word-RAM program, with constants \(B,C\ge1\) independent of the database; \(B\) is an integer. Its word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits. The address universe contains \(2^w\) initially zero cells. Each read, write, indirect access, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient or remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or shift costs one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return results modulo \(2^w\); a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger values occupy multiple words with all operations charged. No random instruction, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, database-specific advice or oracle is available.

Every accessed cell and every output operation is charged. Unused addresses require no initialization. There is no further requirement that memory used in preprocessing be linear, or that enumeration use only constant additional memory. The fixed exponent implicit in the address universe may depend on the query and algorithm. Writing an answer writes its head coordinates, or one marker for the empty tuple; the output is append-only.

The program first finishes a preprocessing phase of at most \(CN\) operations, then enumerates exactly \(q(D)\) in any order without repetition and halts. After preprocessing, the time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to halting is at most \(C\). If there are no answers, it must halt within \(C\) operations after preprocessing. The same constants and program must work on every database for that query.

The classifier is a deterministic Turing machine on a full finite encoding of query syntax, with relation names, variable names and arities encoded by finite binary strings. It halts on every valid query and says yes exactly when an enumerator and constants as above exist; malformed encodings may be rejected. Its input is \(q\), not a database. It need not produce an enumerator or the constants, and its running time has no required bound. The property being classified is actual, unconditional existence of an enumerator. A classification under an unproved complexity hypothesis is not silently substituted for that property. This effective existence proposition is the previously selected precise version of the source’s broader classification request.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a total classifier and a complete Lean-checked proof of its correctness for every query in the stated syntax and enumeration model, or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such total classifier exists. A positive answer need not effectively construct the enumerators whose existence it classifies.

An algorithm for only a restricted query family, or sufficient and necessary conditions leaving other queries unclassified, is not complete. Exhibiting a query without efficient enumeration does not refute the existence of a classifier: a correct classifier may reject that query. Conditional exclusions must retain their hypotheses and do not by themselves establish an unconditional answer.
cards.why: Database queries can have far more answers than input tuples. Constant delay after linear preprocessing gives both output-sensitive total time and a bounded wait for each answer. A complete effective classification would identify exactly which query patterns allow this guarantee, including repeated uses of the same relation.

cards.title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every pair \((q_1,q_2)\) of finite conjunctive queries with the same output arity and correctly decides whether
\[
 \forall\text{ finite bag databases }D\quad
 \forall a\in U_D^r:\qquad q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a),
\]
with the unrestricted syntax and natural-number sum-product semantics defined below? Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions:
A relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified nonnegative integer arity. It is part of the query input, with no fixed bound on the number of symbols or their arities. Both queries use a common signature; unused relation symbols have no effect. They also use a finite set \(C\) of named constants. A finite bag database \(D\) consists of a finite domain \(U_D\), an injective interpretation \(\iota_D:C\to U_D\) of the constant names, and a function
\[
 D_R:U_D^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\to\mathbb N
 \quad\text{for every }R\in\tau,
\]
where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The value is the tuple's multiplicity; zero means absence. All natural multiplicities and all finite domain sizes are allowed, without a bound determined in advance. No key, dependency or other integrity constraint is imposed. The domain may be empty when there are no constants. A nullary relation has one possible tuple, the empty tuple.

A conjunctive query has syntax
\[
 q(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\;:\!-\;A_1,\ldots,A_m,
\]
where each \(A_j\) is a positive relational atom \(R_j(t_{j,1},\ldots,t_{j,a_j})\), \(a_j\) is the arity of \(R_j\), and each term is a variable or a named constant. Every variable occurs in at least one body atom. The head \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\) is a list of variables from the body; variables may repeat in the head. Body variables not in the head are existentially quantified. Distinct variable names may be assigned the same domain element, and a variable may be assigned the value of a constant. Different named constants denote distinct elements. The body is a list of atom occurrences: relation names, variables and entire atoms may repeat. There is no disjunction, negation, inequality, built-in comparison, aggregation syntax, recursion or duplicate-elimination operation. Identifying variables can enforce equality, but no additional predicate is interpreted specially.

Write \(\operatorname{Var}(q)\) for the finite set of variables in \(q\). For an assignment \(h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\), extend \(h\) to constants by \(h(c)=\iota_D(c)\), and write \(D(A_j[h])\) for \(D_{R_j}\) evaluated at the instantiated tuple. For every output tuple \(a\in U_D^r\), define
\[
 q(D)(a)=
 \sum_{\substack{h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\\
                  (h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_r))=a}}
       \prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h]).
\]
The arithmetic is ordinary exact addition and multiplication of nonnegative integers. The sum is finite; an empty sum is zero and an empty product is one. Each repeated occurrence contributes its own factor. For example, the bodies \(R(x)\) and \(R(x),R(x)\) give multiplicities \(D_R(a)\) and \(D_R(a)^2\), respectively. Output tuples that violate equalities forced by repeated head variables receive zero.

A Boolean query has \(r=0\) and returns a natural multiplicity at the unique empty tuple; it does not merely report whether a witness exists. An empty body is permitted only with no variables, hence has empty head and returns one. These conventions also define evaluation on empty domains.

Input queries, signatures, variable names and constant names have finite, effectively parseable binary encodings, for example length-prefixed symbol lists and atom lists. The machine receives only these two queries and their signature, not a database or a database-size bound. It must accept exactly when the displayed inequality holds for every database and every output tuple and reject otherwise. It can reject ill-formed encodings immediately. There is no required bound on its running time beyond halting on every input, and there is no noncomputable advice or external oracle. The inequality is exact and one-sided, with no input scale factor or additive slack.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total decision algorithm exists, with an implementation and proofs of termination and correctness on every input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists.

Enumerating finite counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment and does not establish decidability. A decision procedure for equivalence, set semantics, or a proper query subclass is insufficient on its own. A theorem about bag-set inputs may be used only together with a proved effective reduction covering the bag-valued input model here. Undecidability after adding unions, inequalities, integrity constraints or a numerical transformation of the query count must likewise be reduced to this exact plain-CQ problem. No approximation tolerance or complexity-class upper bound is requested.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

cards.context:
With duplicates, a join multiplies tuple multiplicities and projection adds contributions of different assignments. Queries returning the same set of answers can therefore produce different numbers of copies.

Every proposed counterexample is a finite database with exactly computable counts. Exhaustively searching databases will eventually discover a counterexample when one exists, but gives no stopping rule for true containment.

The join-on-free theorem allows existential variables but forbids joins between body atoms through those variables in the contained query. Its decidability result therefore covers more than projection-free queries, while keeping a restriction absent from this target.

The literature relates bag-bag and bag-set containment by transformations of the query input. This does not justify silently treating the same original relations as sets; repeated atoms can affect the original bag comparison.

Nearby undecidability results add unions, comparisons or a transformation of the count. The June 2025 CQ-versus-UCQ paper still leaves the ordinary two-CQ inequality open.

cards.title: Dichotomy for deletion resilience of relational queries
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite relational schema and every fixed Boolean union of conjunctive queries \(q\), is \(\operatorname{RES}(q)\) either in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?

An input consists of a finite bag database \(D\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It belongs to \(\operatorname{RES}(q)\) if at most \(k\) individual tuple occurrences can be deleted so that \(q\) becomes false. All occurrences may be deleted, and all relation arities and self-joins are allowed.
cards.definitions:
A schema is a finite list of relation names of positive integer arity. A bag database gives an explicit list of tuple occurrences for each relation; duplicates are allowed and count as separate deletions. Domain values are finite binary strings. Multiplicities are represented by repeated occurrences, not exponentially compressed binary counts. The budget k is written in binary. Input length is the bit length of these lists and the budget.

The fixed query is a finite disjunction of Boolean conjunctive queries. Each disjunct is an existentially quantified, nonempty finite conjunction of relational atoms using variables, with no constants, equality, inequality, negation or function symbols. Every variable occurs in an atom. A disjunct is true when a variable assignment maps every atom to a tuple whose remaining multiplicity is positive. Repeated uses of one relation and disconnected conjunctions are permitted. Query truth uses the support of the remaining database, while deletion cost counts occurrences. The empty database therefore makes the query false. The minimum deletion cost is called its resilience; it is zero if the query is already false.

Only D and k vary in RES(q); the schema and query are fixed, so running-time constants and polynomial degree may depend on them. Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np). NP-completeness means membership in NP and polynomial-time many-one hardness for every NP language. The proposition asks whether an intermediate complexity can occur anywhere in this family. It does not demand an effective syntactic classifier or the stronger algebraic characterization from the source, and it does not assume P differs from NP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition. Results for a restricted query family do not settle its universal scope. A conditional negative result must retain its unproved assumptions and is not an unconditional refutation.
cards.why: Resilience measures how fragile a database answer is under deletion of records. A complete complexity dichotomy would identify whether all such fixed-query deletion problems have a tractable or NP-complete behavior, including repeated tables and higher-arity relations.

cards.title: Exponential growth base of the diagonal Ramsey numbers
cards.formal:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(R(n,n)\) be the least \(N\) such that every red–blue coloring of the edges of \(K_N\) contains a monochromatic \(K_n\). Determine whether the exponential base
\[b=\lim_{n\to\infty} R(n,n)^{1/n}\]
exists. If it exists, determine \(b\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). If it fails to exist, prove divergence.
cards.definitions:
The complete graph \(K_N\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and one edge for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. The coloring assigns either color to each edge. A monochromatic \(K_n\) is a set of \(n\) vertices whose pairwise edges all have the same color. Finite Ramsey’s theorem makes \(R(n,n)\) a positive finite integer. Set \(b_n=R(n,n)^{1/n}\), taking the positive real root. The elementary bound \(R(n,n)\le\binom{2n-2}{n-1}\) bounds this sequence.

If the limit exists, \(R(n,n)=(b+o(1))^n\). The numerical tolerance applies to the base \(b\) itself. Convergence means that for each real \(\eta>0\) there is a threshold beyond which \(|b_n-b|<\eta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one of two outcomes. For convergence, prove that \(b_n\) has a limit, supply an independently specified real \(a\), and prove \(|a-b|\le1/100\). After proving convergence, [certified bounds](definitions.html#numerical-answers) on \(b\) of width at most \(1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. For divergence, prove that \(\liminf b_n<\limsup b_n\), or an equivalent failure of convergence. Narrow bounds on the two limiting extrema alone leave the existence question open.
cards.why: This is the classical quantitative question for two-color graph Ramsey theory. It asks how many vertices force a clique of a given size even in the coloring that avoids it for as long as possible.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.
cards.why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.

cards.context:
The classical lemma forces a sunflower only after a factorial-sized threshold. The conjecture would replace this by an exponential whose base is independent of the set size.

Modern bounds remove most of the classical growth but still have a base growing logarithmically with the set size. The robust sunflower method has its own obstruction at that scale, which does not settle ordinary sunflowers.

Sunflower structure supports computational lower bounds and other combinatorial reductions. A uniform exponential threshold would strengthen the general principle used in such applications.

progress.text: The primary breakthrough gives bounds with a base polylogarithmic in the uniformity, improving the classical factorial threshold while retaining Conjecture 1.3.

Rao’s journal survey, in the checked September 2025 author manuscript, states the conjecture as open and surveys an \(O(r\log k)^k\) bound. It distinguishes the necessary logarithmic dependence for robust sunflowers from the ordinary target.

sentences: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets with one common pairwise intersection.
The conjecture fixes the number of petals and asks how many equal-sized sets force that structure.
It asks for an exponential threshold whose base depends only on the petal count.
The ground set is any finite set, and the core may be empty.
Known logarithmic-base bounds and limitations for robust sunflowers leave the ordinary exponential conjecture open in the checked sources.

cards.title: Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite set \(U\) and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) containing a nonempty member and closed under union, is there an element \(u\in U\) belonging to at least \(|\mathcal F|/2\) members of \(\mathcal F\)?
cards.definitions: The power set \(2^U\) consists of all subsets of U. A family is a set of distinct subsets, with no multiplicities. Closure under union means that A and B in the family imply that their union is also in it. The frequency of u is the integer \(|\{A\in\mathcal F:u\in A\}|\). Empty members are permitted, but the family consisting only of the empty set is excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that some element belongs to at least half the members of each permitted union-closed family. To refute the assertion, give one such finite family and prove that every element belongs to strictly fewer than half its members.
cards.why: A basic closure principle for set systems, connected to information inequalities through entropy methods.

cards.title: Hadamard matrices of every order divisible by four
cards.formal: For every positive integer \(n\), does there exist a \(4n\)-by-\(4n\) matrix \(H\) whose entries belong to \(\{-1,1\}\) and satisfy \(HH^{\mathsf T}=4nI_{4n}\)?
cards.definitions: Matrix multiplication is over the real numbers. The superscript T means transpose, and \(I_m\) is the m-by-m identity matrix. The displayed equation says that different rows have dot product zero; each row has squared length 4n. Such a sign matrix is called a Hadamard matrix. The target is existence at every stated order, with no efficiency requirement on a construction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof that the required sign matrix exists for every positive \(n\). A refutation must give one multiple \(4n\) for which every sign matrix fails the orthogonality equation.
cards.why: Orthogonal sign patterns are basic objects in coding, signal design and combinatorial constructions.
